Machining/Milling

Climb and Conventional Milling

Which way the work is fed past a turning cutter decides whether each chip starts thick or thin, which way the cut pulls on the work, and why backlash in a feed screw matters.

Feed direction decides whether each chip starts thick or thin

Feed direction decides whether each chip starts thick or thin

A milling cutter takes metal off in small slices, one slice per tooth. Whether each slice starts thick and ends thin, or starts thin and ends thick, comes down to one thing: which way the work is fed past the turning cutter.

Climb milling
Also called down milling. Where a tooth is cutting, it moves the same way the work is fed. Each chip starts thick and ends thin.
Conventional milling
Also called up milling. Where a tooth is cutting, it moves against the feed. Each chip starts thin and ends thick.
Feed per tooth
How far the work moves while the cutter turns from one tooth to the next. It sets how thick a chip can get.
Width of cut
How far the cutter reaches into the side of the work, measured across the cutter. Machinists also call it the radial depth of cut.

How to read the drawings on this page. Each drawing is a slice straight across the fluted part of an end mill, seen looking down its axis from the spindle; the small side view in the corner marks where the slice is taken, the way a section view does on a drawing. This sketch places the cutter’s axis horizontally, with the table below it; screen-down is toward that table. It is not a top view of a vertical spindle. From the spindle end a standard right-hand cutter turns clockwise. The cutter stays where it is and the work is fed past it, the way a mill table carries the work. Every Work feed arrow is the work’s motion. On a machine that moves the cutter instead, nothing changes: the cutter simply travels the opposite way to that arrow.

The cutter is the same in both modes and spins the same way. What switches climb to conventional is the direction of feed relative to the side of the cutter that is doing the cutting. The down/up force arrows belong to this horizontal arrangement. A top view of a vertical end mill would show forces across the table, not axial force into or away from it.

Watch one tooth take its chip; Interactive

Watch one tooth take its chip

The dashed gold outline is the slice of metal the cutting tooth has taken so far, drawn where it was. The solid gold shape is that metal as a chip, curling off the cutting edge into the flute. The curled chip is scaled to fit the flute at this exaggerated feed; its drawn size is not a thickness measurement. Play it, or drag the tooth through the cut, and use the dashed slice to compare thickness.

Each chip forms on the edge, rides out in the flute and is thrown clear

Each chip forms on the edge, rides out in the flute and is thrown clear

A chip does not stay where the slice was. The cutting edge shears it off the work, it slides along the face in front of the edge and curls into the flute, and the flute carries it round until it is thrown clear. Where that happens depends on the direction of feed.

Swipe the four moments sideways on a narrow screen, or focus the drawing and use the arrow keys to scroll.

Reading the cutter

  • Cutting edge: the tip of each tooth, the only part that touches the finished surface. The tooth that is cutting is outlined in blue.
  • Rake face: the face just in front of the edge. The chip slides along it as it forms.
  • Flute: the curved valley in front of each tooth. The chip curls in it and is carried out of the cut in it, so a flute packed with chips cannot take the next one.
  • Core: the solid centre, hatched because the drawing cuts through it. In this illustrated family, more flutes leave a thicker core and less room for chips. Actual proportions depend on the tool design.

The chip is drawn shorter and thinner than the slice so it fits the flute at a feed drawn many times too large. A continuous metal chip usually becomes shorter and thicker through deformation; IIT Kharagpur’s chip-formation lesson explains the change. The path it takes is illustrative; coolant, tool geometry and the material affect actual chip motion. The cutter’s flutes and chip space follow Harvey Performance’s end mill anatomy.

Six things to try in the demo; Checklist

Six things to try in the demo

  • Choose Compare both and step until each tooth has only just entered the work. Which chip is already thick, and which is barely there?
  • Drag Tooth position in the cut from 0% to 100%, once in each mode. Watch the uncut-thickness readout: in climb it runs down from the peak, in conventional it runs up to it.
  • Set the width of cut to 50%. The tooth now cuts through a quarter of a turn and the chip reaches the full feed per tooth. Drop it to 10%: the peak falls to 60% of the feed. At the same feed, a narrower cut makes a thinner chip.
  • Raise the feed per tooth and watch the dashed uncut slice grow thicker. Its thick-to-thin trend stays the same. The curled chip is scaled to fit the flute and may stop growing on screen; compare thickness using the dashed slice.
  • Follow one chip from start to finish. Pause just before a tooth leaves the work, then step forward. In which mode is the thick end of the chip at the curled tip, and in which is it still on the edge? Where does each chip go once it is free?
  • Watch the red-orange arrow, the pull of the cut on the work. In climb it pulls the work the way it is already going and presses it down. In conventional it pushes back against the feed and lifts. Keep that in mind for the card on backlash.
Starting thin means rubbing; starting thick means a bite

Starting thin means rubbing; starting thick means a bite

A real cutting edge has a rounded tip. When the uncut layer is extremely thin, the edge can push and rub the metal before a chip forms. The peripheral cuts shown here make that difference visible.

  • Conventional milling starts every chip at zero, so every tooth rubs before it bites. Rubbing makes heat and wears the edge. Look at where the tooth enters, too: on the finished surface, the one you are keeping.
  • Climb milling starts the chips shown here at their thickest, so the tooth bites at once, with a knock each time a tooth enters.

That is the main reason climb milling is often the preferred direction when the machine can hold the work steady against it. Whether it can is the next card.

Which way the cut pulls on the work

  • Climb: the teeth drag the work along the way it is already being fed, and tend to push it down onto the table in the peripheral arrangement shown.
  • Conventional: the teeth push back against the feed and tend to lift the work in this arrangement, so whatever holds the work has to resist that lift.
Backlash: why climb milling depends on the machine; Watch out

Backlash: why climb milling depends on the machine

A feed screw moves the table by turning inside a nut. Unless the drive is built to take it out, there is some clearance between the screw’s thread and the nut. That clearance is called backlash, and it lets the table shift a little while the screw stands still.

  • Conventional: the cut pushes the table back, against the feed. That holds the nut against the flank of the thread the screw is driving with, so the gap stays on the far side and the table moves only as fast as the screw turns.
  • Climb: the cut pulls the table forward, the way it is already moving. If there is clearance, the table can slide across it ahead of the screw, and the cutter takes a bigger bite than the feed was set for, all at once. That sudden, oversized bite is hard on the cutter and on whatever is holding the work.

This is a question to ask about a machine, not a rule. How much clearance a feed drive has, and whether it is built to take it out, differs from machine to machine. This page does not tell you which direction to use on any machine you will meet. Ask the person responsible for that machine.

Supporting detail: Addendum 1 — Why some machines climb mill without trouble.

A slot is both at once

A slot is both at once

When the cutter is buried across its whole width, cutting a slot, each tooth enters at one wall and leaves at the other. Its chip starts thin, is thickest halfway across, and ends thin. The first half of the sweep moves against the feed, like conventional milling, and the second half moves with it, like climb milling, whichever way the work is fed. That is why the demo stops at half the cutter’s diameter: past that point the two can no longer be pulled apart.

Machining/Milling

Diagnosing Milling Chatter

Use the finish, setup and cutting conditions as evidence, then check the whole force path before changing one permitted variable at a time.

A repeating mark or loud cut is evidence, not a diagnosis

A repeating mark or loud cut is evidence, not a diagnosis

A common mechanism, regenerative chatter, is self-excited: one cutting edge leaves a waviness that changes the chip thickness seen by the next edge, and the changing force can reinforce the motion. That mechanism does not describe every vibration or finish defect. A repeating surface pattern and a strong sound can be clues; they do not prove the cause by themselves.

Supporting detail: Addendum 2 — Several faults can look or sound like chatter.

Stop the cut before inspecting or changing the setup; Watch out

Stop the cut before inspecting or changing the setup

End the cut with the approved machine procedure before approaching or changing anything. Use Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for the operating rules.

Do not tune around a part, tool or holder that moved. A shifted workpiece, incomplete seating, damaged edge or visibly slipping tool is a mechanical problem to correct or report before another cutting trial.
Record the evidence before trying another cut

Record the evidence before trying another cut

Record where the symptom began, where it appears on the part, which operation and tool were active, and the actual speed, feed, engagement and holder projection. This creates a comparison for the next check instead of relying on sound or memory.

Trace force through the complete cutting system

Trace force through the complete cutting system

Route suspected machine or spindle faults to authorized staff

Route suspected machine or spindle faults to authorized staff

After the cutter, holder, workholding, path and chips have been checked, a persistent symptom is evidence worth giving to authorized staff. Abnormal motion or a visibly damaged or contaminated interface also calls for that route. It does not prove one component failed. Do not remove covers, adjust bearings or gibs, or service a drawbar; manufacturer guidance treats those as separate checks for trained personnel.

Check the holder, collet and cutter as one assembly

Check the holder, collet and cutter as one assembly

Confirm the correct holder and collet, complete seating, clean contact surfaces under the approved procedure, adequate shank engagement, and no visible damage. Compare tool and holder projection with the last stable setup. Inspect for wear, chipping, built-up material and chip damage. Check runout only with the approved instrument and method; compare it with the tool, holder and job requirements. See Mill Toolholders and Collets, End Mill Anatomy and Cutter Selection and Tool Stickout and Deflection.

Check the fixture, workpiece and support

Check the fixture, workpiece and support

Check that the fixture is seated and secured, the work is against its locators, clamps direct force into supports, and the part is not perched or springing. A symptom confined to an unsupported end, thin wall or one clamping orientation points first toward support and force direction. Do not keep tightening until the part distorts. See Milling Vises and Strap Clamps.

Check engagement, path and chip evacuation

Check engagement, path and chip evacuation

Compare where the pattern begins with changes in radial or axial engagement, entry and exit, cornering, cutter engagement, and chip evacuation. A clean straight wall followed by chatter in an inside corner is evidence to inspect the corner path and the sudden engagement change. Packed or re-cut chips call for the approved chip-control method and a review of the operation, not an automatic speed change. See Milling Operations and Cutting Fluids and Application Methods.

It changed with a longer tool or holder

It changed with a longer tool or holder

Check: tool projection, holder projection, shank engagement and both interfaces. Next: restore the shortest permitted assembly that reaches the feature, then repeat the same cut conditions.

Straight walls are clean; an inside corner chatters

Straight walls are clean; an inside corner chatters

Check: the engaged arc, chip load through the corner and programmed path. Next: use an approved path or engagement change, then compare the same corner again.

Only an unsupported or thin area vibrates

Only an unsupported or thin area vibrates

Check: workpiece support, clamp-force path and local flexibility. Next: improve support or revise force direction without distorting the work; verify the setup before cutting.

One edge is chipped or marks repeat once per revolution

One edge is chipped or marks repeat once per revolution

Check: edge condition, chip re-cutting, holder seating and runout. Next: correct the physical cause or replace the damaged tool before tuning speed.

It persists after the student-controlled setup checks; Practice

It persists after the student-controlled setup checks

Check: after the cutter, holder and workholding are verified, ask whether the symptom still follows the same path, engagement or chip condition. Next: if it persists across different permitted cutting conditions, stop and give the complete evidence to authorized staff. It is evidence for inspection, not proof of a spindle fault.

Practice chatter diagnosis

Clear mechanical causes and unnecessary leverage first

Clear mechanical causes and unnecessary leverage first

  1. Clear mechanical causes first. Verify seating, condition, projection, support and chip clearance. Do not use a parameter change to hide motion or damage.
  2. Reduce unnecessary leverage. Shorten the permitted tool and holder projection, improve support, or choose a more suitable assembly. Keep the required shank engagement and feature clearance.
Review engagement and cutter geometry after the setup is sound

Review engagement and cutter geometry after the setup is sound

  1. Review engagement and force direction. A smaller radial or axial engagement, different entry, or revised corner path may reduce the force variation. Stay inside the approved process and tool limits.
  2. Reconsider cutter geometry. Diameter, flute count and pitch, helix, edge geometry and material suitability can change force and excitation. Record the selected tool and why it was changed.
Run one permitted speed trial

Run one permitted speed trial

A stable speed can be higher or lower. Change to one permitted speed, then compare the same feature. Do not assume that slowing down is always the answer.

Review feed when speed changes

Review feed when speed changes

If the trial is intended to preserve feed per tooth, calculate the matching table feed rather than changing chip load accidentally. Too little feed can rub; excessive feed can overload the edge. Use Feeds and Speeds and the tool maker's data.

Record the controlled result

Record the controlled result

Record the observation, the one intentional change and the result. If two settings move together to preserve a stated quantity such as feed per tooth, record both and the quantity held constant. That is one controlled trial, not two unexplained changes.

Manufacturer references behind this diagnostic order

Manufacturer references behind this diagnostic order

  • Haas: Avoid Chatter on Your Mill is the existing public demonstration.
  • Haas TG0100: Mill Chatter Troubleshooting separates tool wear, projection, chip load, engaged flutes, toolpath, corners, coolant, drawbar force and machine support. Its drawbar and foundation actions belong to authorized machine work.
  • Tormach: Chatter separates tool wear, toolholding, workholding and toolpath causes. Its drawbar, pressure and gib instructions are machine-specific maintenance—not generic student steps.
  • Sandvik Coromant: milling vibration guidance connects workpiece and machine stability with overhang, engagement, force direction, pitch and toolpath.
  • Seco: vibration in machining explains resonance, overhang and why a stable speed may be above or below the current speed.
  • Seco: end-mill wear patterns distinguishes chipping, built-up edge and chip-evacuation damage.
Machining/Milling

End Mill Anatomy and Cutter Selection

Read end mill geometry, compare flute counts and tool materials, and choose a cutter for the material and operation.

The shank is held; the cutting edges remove material; the flutes carry chips

The shank is held; the cutting edges remove material; the flutes carry chips

  • Flutes are grooves beside the teeth that provide room for chips. The sharp edges bordering them do the cutting.
  • Helix angle describes the spiral relative to the tool axis. It affects how the edge enters the cut and the direction of cutting forces; it is not the spindle's rotation direction.
  • Cutting diameter is the diameter swept by the cutting edges. Shank diameter fits the holder and may differ from cutting diameter.
  • Overall length (OAL) runs from tool tip to shank end. Length of cut (LOC) is the axial cutting-edge length, not permission to cut that entire depth in one pass.
  • Length below shank (LBS) runs from the start of a reduced neck to the tip, so it includes both relieved neck and LOC. It is not the neck-only length.
  • Square end makes a flat-bottom form with a sharp nominal corner. A corner-radius or bull-nose end rounds that corner. A ball end has a rounded tip for curved surfaces.
  • Center-cutting geometry can cut at the tool center, allowing axial entry when the manufacturer permits it. Flute count alone does not prove a tool can plunge; check its entry method and limits.

Holder-face projection is the mounted distance from holder face to tip. Pulling the same tool farther out changes projection and insertion, not OAL, LOC or LBS. Follow the tool and holder makers' gripping requirements. Use Mill Toolholders and Collets for the holder system, Tool Stickout and Deflection for the cost of extra reach and Milling Operations for the shapes these cutters produce.

Supporting detail: Addendum 3 — Public anatomy reference.

Compare catalog reach with mounted holder projection; Interactive

Compare catalog reach with mounted holder projection

3D model boundary: separately closed cutting, neck and shank display solids meet at the catalog boundaries. They are an illustrative display mesh, not watertight manufacturing CAD. Abrupt shoulders and runout are schematic. Swept transverse sections show fluted side surfaces; flat display caps do not establish center-cutting end-face geometry.

The models use illustrative dimensions, not a catalog recommendation. A reduced neck creates clearance behind the cutting length; it does not by itself prove that the tool is stronger, safe at a particular depth or suitable for a particular holder projection.

Choose flute count for chip space and engagement, not material alone

Choose flute count for chip space and engagement, not material alone

FlutesUseful starting pointCheck before choosing
2Generous chip space, often useful for aluminum slots.Geometry, edge strength and the maker's slotting recommendation.
3Common aluminum-specific choice balancing chip space with another cutting edge.That the tool is designed for the material and engagement; three flutes alone are not a material specification.
4Common for steel and for cuts where chip space is less restrictive.A full-width slot can pack the smaller flute spaces. Do not assume more teeth always improve removal rate.

A side cut and a full-width slot load the same cutter differently. Select the actual tool's data for the operation, then use Feeds and Speeds for the calculations and Climb and Conventional Milling for feed direction.

Supporting detail: Addendum 4 — Why the two-for-aluminum, four-for-steel rule is only a starting point.

Match HSS, carbide and coating to the job and machine; Practice

Match HSS, carbide and coating to the job and machine

High-speed steel (HSS) is relatively tough and often economical. It can be a useful choice at lower cutting speeds, especially where the setup cannot take full advantage of carbide. Cobalt HSS is an HSS family with improved hot hardness.

Cemented carbide retains hardness at higher cutting temperatures and is stiffer than HSS, but is less tolerant of impact and poor support. A carbide tool does not make a loose setup rigid. Select its grade and geometry as well as its material.

Coatings change wear, friction and heat behavior. TiN and TiCN are familiar options; AlTiN/TiAlN are common on tools for hot-running ferrous applications. For aluminum, choose an uncoated polished tool or a coating explicitly recommended for that alloy, such as TiB2 where specified. Color is not a reliable selection method, and no coating guarantees a fixed multiple of tool life.

Job examples: for an aluminum slot, start by comparing aluminum-specific two- and three-flute tools with enough chip space. For steel side milling on a rigid setup, a steel-rated four-flute carbide tool may be a good starting point. For a modest-speed, interrupted job, a suitable HSS tool may be more forgiving. Check the manufacturer's recommendations before selecting the cutting data.

Practice cutter selection

Supporting detail: Addendum 5 — Check the coating's material recommendation.

Face mills and fly cutters cover broad flat surfaces

Face mills and fly cutters cover broad flat surfaces

A face mill uses several cutting edges, often replaceable inserts, to machine a broad face. Match its diameter, insert geometry, holder and power demand to the machine and part.

A fly cutter carries a single cutting point that sweeps a circle. It can make a broad finishing pass, but its single edge and interrupted loading need suitable rigidity, balance and cutting data. It is not simply a face mill that can use the same feed setting.

Check tram when a broad facing pass leaves steps. Cutter selection belongs with machine alignment, toolholding and the operation being planned.

Machining/Milling

Feeds and Speeds

How a cutting speed and a cutter diameter set the spindle speed, how the spindle speed, flute count and chip load set the table feed, how width, depth and feed set the volume of metal removed, and how that volume and the material set the cutting power.

Two numbers come from cutting data; two go into the machine

Two numbers come from cutting data; two go into the machine

A milling setup is described by four numbers. Two describe what each cutting edge goes through, and they come from cutting data for the tool and the material. The other two are what you actually set on the machine, and you work them out from the first two.

Cutting speed
How fast the cutting edge moves through the material: the speed at the outside of the cutter. Written in surface feet per minute (SFM) or metres per minute (m/min). Also called surface speed. Comes from cutting data.
Feed per tooth
How far the work moves while the cutter turns from one tooth to the next, in inches or millimetres per tooth. Also called chip load, because it sets the size of the bite each tooth takes. Comes from cutting data.
Spindle speed
How many turns the cutter makes each minute, in revolutions per minute (rev/min, usually said RPM). Set on the machine.
Table feed
How fast the work moves past the cutter, in inches or millimetres per minute. Also called the feed rate. On a machine that moves the cutter instead, it is how fast the cutter travels. Set on the machine.

"Speeds" are the cutter turning; "feeds" are the work moving. That is all the phrase feeds and speeds means. The two are set separately on the machine, and the rest of this page is about how they depend on each other, how much metal they remove, and the power that takes.

Spindle speed: the turns it takes to reach the cutting speed

Spindle speed: the turns it takes to reach the cutting speed

Cutting speed is a distance per minute, measured at the edge of the cutter. In one turn, a point on that edge travels once around the cutter: its circumference, π × D. So the spindle speed is the cutting speed divided by the distance one turn covers, once the two are in the same units.

Spindle speed (rev/min) = 12 × cutting speed (SFM) ÷ (π × cutter diameter in inches)

The 12 is there because cutting speed is in feet and the diameter is in inches: 12 inches to the foot. In metric units the same idea needs a 1000, millimetres to the metre:

Spindle speed (rev/min) = 1000 × cutting speed (m/min) ÷ (π × cutter diameter in mm)

Worked example, with illustrative numbers. A 0.5 in cutter, with cutting data that calls for 300 SFM: 12 × 300 ÷ (π × 0.5) = 2,292 rev/min. The 300 SFM is there to make the arithmetic concrete. It is not a recommendation for any tool or any material. The feed value below is illustrative too; use the later material guide for the carbide starting bands.

Look at where the diameter sits: underneath. Halve the diameter and the spindle speed doubles. A small cutter has to turn faster to give its edge the same cutting speed, which is why small cutters so often ask for more speed than a machine has. That case has its own card below.

Table feed: each tooth takes one chip load as it passes

Table feed: each tooth takes one chip load as it passes

Each time a tooth passes, the work should have moved one feed per tooth. The number of teeth passing each minute is the spindle speed times the number of flutes, so:

Table feed = spindle speed × flutes × feed per tooth

Worked example, continued. A 4-flute cutter at 2,292 rev/min, with a feed per tooth of 0.002 in: 2,292 × 4 × 0.002 = 18.3 in/min. The units work out on their own: turns per minute, times teeth per turn, times inches per tooth, leaves inches per minute.

Turned around, the same relation tells you what chip load a feed gives. That is the way to check a feed someone else has set:

Feed per tooth = table feed ÷ (spindle speed × flutes)

Flutes here means the teeth that actually take a chip in each turn. For an ordinary end mill that is simply the number of flutes.

Removal rate: width × depth × table feed

Removal rate: width × depth × table feed

Two more numbers describe the cut itself. The width of cut is how far the cutter reaches sideways into the work, across the direction of feed. The depth of cut is how far down its side the cutter is buried, along its axis. A side cut can be no wider than the cutter; a wider path takes more than one pass.

While the table feeds, the cutter sweeps through the work and leaves a channel behind it. In a stretch of time the cutter travels table feed × time, and the solid metal it takes out in that stretch is a slab as wide as the cut, as deep as the cut, and as long as that travel. Per minute, that is the material removal rate:

Removal rate (in³/min) = width of cut (in) × depth of cut (in) × table feed (in/min)

The front of the cut is curved, because it is the cutter’s own shape. The slab’s two ends are the same curve, one travel apart, so whatever the curve, the slab holds exactly width × depth × travel.

Worked example, continued. The same cutter, 0.1 in wide (20% of its diameter) and 0.5 in deep, at 18.3 in/min: 0.1 × 0.5 × 18.3 ≈ 0.917 in³/min, or 15.0 cm³/min. In 5 seconds the cutter travels 1.53 in and removes 0.0764 in³.

That is the volume of solid metal. Once it is chips, the same metal lies loose and takes up far more space, so the removal rate is not the size of the chip pile.

Cutting power: removal rate times the energy each cubic inch takes

Cutting power: removal rate times the energy each cubic inch takes

Cutting a cubic inch of a given material takes roughly a given amount of energy. That is its specific cutting energy, and it is why the same cut needs more power in steel than in aluminum. Written as power per unit of removal rate, it turns a removal rate straight into power:

Cutting power (hp) = removal rate (in³/min) × unit power (hp per in³/min)

Cutting power (W) = removal rate (mm³/min) × specific energy (J/mm³) ÷ 60

The 60 turns minutes into seconds, because a watt is a joule per second. One mechanical horsepower is 745.7 W.

Worked example, continued. For 6061-T6 aluminum the guide in the calculator gives a band of 0.16 to 0.30 hp per in³/min. At 0.917 in³/min that is about 0.15 to 0.28 hp, or 110 to 210 W. The same cut in 304 stainless steel, whose band is 0.65 to 1.3 hp per in³/min, needs about 0.60 to 1.2 hp.

The answer is usually a band. Some table rows give one factor; that still produces an estimate, not a measured certainty. Published bands cover a family of materials over a range of hardness, and the energy a real cut takes also depends on chip thickness and cutting-edge geometry. Treat the band as the size of the job, not a prediction to the watt.

Three different powers get called “the power”, and they are not the same:

  • Cutting power is what the cutting edge spends. That is the estimate above.
  • Motor shaft power is more, because the belts, gears and bearings between the motor and the cutter lose some on the way. If the drivetrain passes on 80% of what the motor delivers, the motor must deliver the cutting power ÷ 0.8.
  • Electrical power drawn from the supply is more again, because the motor and its drive lose some too.

None of these tells you whether a machine can take the cut. A spindle motor’s rating is not necessarily available at every speed, and power is only one limit: the tool, the holding and the machine’s stiffness are others. Use the estimate to compare cuts and to see why a cut is heavy, not to approve one.

Calculator: from material guidance to removal and power; Interactive

Calculator: from material guidance to removal and power

Choose a material to see generic carbide starting ranges for it, then enter the cutter, the cutting data and the cut. Nothing is filled in for you. Each result appears as soon as the fields it needs are filled, and says what it is still waiting for until then. Use the middle of these ranges fills in only the cutting speed and feed per tooth.

How to read the drawings. You are looking at a block of work from the front, a little above and to the right. The cutter feeds to the right along the front top edge. Gold is the solid metal removed in the time shown, drawn where it was before the cutter took it. The dashed blue curve is where the front of the cut stood when that time began; the outlined cylinder is the cutter now. The three labeled axes use the same length scale, and the drawings in one comparison share that scale, so a slab twice as long is twice the volume. The block around the cut is there only to hold it; its size means nothing. The cut is already underway when the interval starts; only the gold volume counts toward that interval.

The comparison below the drawings prices the setup’s removal rate in every material. The cut is the same in every row; only the energy per cubic inch changes.

Things to try in the calculator; Checklist

Things to try in the calculator

  • Before typing anything, read the results. Each one names the fields it is waiting for.
  • With 6061-T6 aluminum chosen, enter a 0.5 in diameter and 4 flutes, then press Use the middle of these ranges. Cutting speed and feed per tooth fill in at 400 SFM and 0.00415 in/tooth. Nothing else changes.
  • Enter a width of 0.1 in and a depth of 0.5 in. Check the removal rate against width × depth × table feed in the arithmetic.
  • Change the material to 304 stainless steel. The drawings, the table feed and the removal rate stay exactly as they were; only the power estimate moves. The guide now marks your cutting speed as above its range for stainless, but the calculator leaves your entries alone.
  • Hold the table feed and drag the spindle speed to 200%. The slab does not change and nor does the removal rate: the same metal comes off, in chips half as thick.
  • Now hold the chip load and do the same. The table feed doubles, the slab grows twice as long in the same time, and the removal rate and power estimate double.
  • Switch to metric and back. The cut and every result stay the same, written in other units, and any field you left empty stays empty.
  • Try a width larger than the diameter. The calculator refuses it: that is more than one pass.
  • Enter a 0.125 in cutter with a 4,000 rev/min machine top speed. Compare the speed the cutting speed asks for with the speed the machine can reach, and where the cutting speed actually reached sits against the guide.
When the machine cannot turn as fast as the formula asks

When the machine cannot turn as fast as the formula asks

Because small cutters ask for high spindle speeds, the formula can easily give more than a machine’s top speed. A 0.125 in cutter at 300 SFM asks for 9,167 rev/min. On a machine that stops at 4,000, it runs at 4,000.

  • Work the feed from the speed the spindle really turns. At 4,000 rev/min, with 2 flutes and 0.0008 in per tooth, that is 4,000 × 2 × 0.0008 = 6.4 in/min. Each tooth then takes the chip load you meant it to.
  • The cutting speed is what you give up. At 4,000 rev/min the edge of a 0.125 in cutter moves at π × 0.125 × 4,000 ÷ 12 = 131 SFM, not the 300 the data asked for.

Working the feed from the speed that was asked for, rather than the one the spindle is turning, gets the chip load wrong by the same ratio. A feed worked from 9,167 rev/min would give each tooth 9,167 ÷ 4,000 = 2.3 times the chip load intended.

The same applies to a machine that offers only certain speeds, through belts or gears: set the nearest speed it has, and work the feed from that one. The calculator’s machine top speed box does this for a top speed.

Generic ranges are a starting point, not your tool’s data; Watch out

Generic ranges are a starting point, not your tool’s data

What determines the surface speed?

Start with the material and its hardness, then the cutting tool. Carbide is a tool material, not one universal cutting edge: its grade, coating and geometry matter, as do coolant and how steadily the setup can cut. A harder material generally calls for a lower starting speed. Once that surface speed is chosen, the diameter determines the RPM; a smaller cutter must turn faster to reach the same surface speed.

What determines the feed per tooth?

Choose a bite the cutting edge can carry and the flute can clear. That is why the guide changes with cutter diameter: small cutters generally take smaller bites. Width and depth of cut, a full-width slot, a long tool and a flexible setup change the loading and chip clearance. The number of flutes then tells you how many of those bites happen per turn; it does not by itself choose the size of each bite. Use the diameter-based range as a starting point, with its stated engagement, and refine it from the actual tool’s cutting data.

The arithmetic on this page is exact. Its inputs are the part that takes judgement. The ranges in the calculator are generic starting bands for solid-carbide end mills, by material family, from published toolmaker tables. The cutting data for your tool comes first: normally the toolmaker’s for that tool, that material and that kind of cut, or the person responsible for the machine.

Cutting data accounts for things these formulas cannot see: the exact grade and hardness of the material, the tool’s coating and geometry, how far it reaches out of the holder, coolant, and how the setup is held. The guide’s feed-per-tooth ranges assume a side cut about 20% of the cutter’s diameter wide; a full-width slot or a long reach needs the tool’s own data. A calculator turns data into machine settings. It cannot tell you whether the data suit your cut.

Supporting detail: Addendum 6 — Feed per tooth is not always the thickness of the chip.

Machining/Milling

G-code and Toolpaths

How a CNC mill reads a program line by line: rapid and feed moves, absolute and incremental coordinates, units, arcs and a drilling cycle. Build a program from blocks and watch it cut a simulated block.

A CNC program combines motion and settings in blocks

A CNC program combines motion and settings in blocks

A CNC mill moves its tool by reading a program from the top down, one line at a time. The language most mills read is called G-code. Each line holds a few words, and together they say where the tool goes next, how fast, and what the spindle and tool are doing.

Start with CNC Control Fundamentals for the control and machine types, CNC Axes and Offsets for coordinate references, and CNC Program Structure for common Fanuc-style milling codes. G- and M-code meanings vary by control. The simulator below uses its own documented subset; check the machine's manual for real programs.

Word
A letter and a number, such as X20, G1 or F300. The letter says what the number means: X, Y and Z are positions, F is the feed rate, S the spindle speed, T a tool number. G and M words are codes that choose what kind of move or machine action the line is.
Block
One line of the program. Machinists often call a line a block; in the simulator below, each block you snap into place is one line of G-code, with the same number.
Work zero
The point the program’s numbers count from. Here, as in Milling Operations, X 0, Y 0 is the front left corner of the block and Z 0 is its finished top face. The uncut stock starts at Z +1. Positions refer to the tip of the tool, on its centre line: Z −3 is 3 mm below work zero and 4 mm below that raw top. A pointed drill reaches its programmed Z at its tip; the full-diameter hole is shallower.
Modal
Most codes stay in force until another code from their group replaces them. After a G1, a line with only X80 is still a G1 move; a feed rate set with F remains available until changed. Not every word is modal. For ordinary G0/G1 moves, an omitted axis stays in place; it does not repeat the preceding incremental displacement.

Read the program above from the top. Line 2 sets millimetres, absolute positions and the XY plane. Line 3 puts tool 1, a Ø10 end mill, in the spindle, and line 4 starts the spindle at 2500 rpm. Lines 5 and 6 move the tool through the air to just above the start of the slot. Line 7 feeds it to Z −3, cutting 4 mm below the raw top at Z +1. Line 8 feeds it along the closed-ended slot, and line 9 lifts it clear. Line 10 stops the spindle and line 11 ends the program.

Rapid moves put the tool in place through the air; feed moves cut

Rapid moves put the tool in place through the air; feed moves cut

  • G0 is a rapid move. The control uses its rapid positioning rate, subject to machine limits and applicable overrides. It is for getting the tool to where a cut starts, through the air, never for cutting.
  • G1 is a feed move. The tool moves in a straight line at the feed rate set by F, here in millimetres per minute. It can cut or feed through air.
  • The spindle has to be turning first. S sets its speed in revolutions per minute, M3 starts it turning clockwise seen from above, and M5 stops it. T1 M6 changes to tool 1.
  • A move goes in one straight line. G1 X80 Y40 Z-2 moves all three axes together and they all arrive at once. An axis left out of the line stays where it is: G1 X80 moves along X only.

A rapid into metal is a crash: the tool arrives at full traverse speed with nothing to say it should be cutting. The simulator stops a rapid at the point where it would touch the block and says so. It does the same if a feed move reaches the metal with the spindle stopped.

This simulator moves a rapid in one straight line, the way the LinuxCNC G-code reference describes G0. Controls differ in how they move during a rapid, so check how the one you use moves before you count on the path a rapid takes.

G90 and G91, G20 and G21: two modes that change what every number means

G90 and G91, G20 and G21: two modes that change what every number means

G90, absolute
A number is a position, measured from work zero. With the tool at X 10, G1 X30 moves it to X 30.
G91, incremental
A number is a distance from where the tool is now. With the tool at X 10, the same G1 X30 moves it 30 mm, to X 40.
G21, millimetres
X30 means 30 mm and F300 means 300 mm per minute with the simulator's G94 feed mode.
G20, inches
The same X30 means 30 inches, which is 762 mm, and, with G94, the feed rate is in inches per minute. A millimetre program read in inches asks for moves 25.4 times as long.

Because these modes change the meaning of every line after them, a program sets both near its start, before the first move. The simulator insists on it: a move before G20 or G21 and G90 or G91 have been set stops the program, and so does a change of units after the machine has started moving.

Work through a point list in Absolute and Incremental Positioning. Units and feed mode are separate settings; G95, where supported, uses feed per spindle revolution.

G2 turns clockwise and G3 counterclockwise, seen from above; Practice

G2 turns clockwise and G3 counterclockwise, seen from above

An arc move cuts along part of a circle in the XY plane (G17) at the feed rate. Its direction is the way it turns as seen looking down on the work from above: G2 clockwise, G3 counterclockwise. The line gives the arc’s end point with X and Y, and its centre in one of two ways.

  • I and J say where the centre is, measured in X and Y from the point where the arc starts. That is the usual mode, G91.1, and it holds even while G90 makes every X and Y a position. G90.1 makes I and J a position too in this simulator. Those decimal codes are not universal; check the control's centre-mode rules.
  • R gives the radius instead, and the control works out the centre. A positive R selects an arc of up to half a turn, a negative R the longer way round in the convention used here. An R arc cannot be a full circle, because a circle through one point has no single centre; a full circle uses I and J with its end point the same as its start.

Worked example. The tool is at X 72, Y 15, moving right along the bottom of an outline. G3 X80 Y23 I0 J8 puts the centre 0 in X and 8 in Y from the start, at X 72, Y 23. Turning counterclockwise about it, the tool rounds a corner of radius 8 and ends heading up the right-hand side at X 80, Y 23. The end point has to lie on the circle: change J8 to J6 and the start radius is 6 mm while the end radius is √(8² + 2²) = √68, about 8.246 mm, so the simulator stops at that line instead of guessing.

In the diagram, absolute endpoints and start-relative centres give G03 X22 Y18 I0 J10 from A to B, then G02 X12 Y8 I-10 J0 back to A. Each start point needs its own centre offsets. Radius format can instead use G03 X22 Y18 R10 for the first arc under the stated convention.

G17 uses X/Y and I/J; G18 uses X/Z and I/K; G19 uses Y/Z and J/K. I, J and K correspond to centre components along X, Y and Z. Judge arc direction looking from the positive normal axis toward the plane: +Z for XY, +Y for XZ, +X for YZ. The simulator supports XY arcs only.

Practice quarter arcs

A drilling cycle packs a whole hole into one line

A drilling cycle packs a whole hole into one line

G81 X15 Y15 Z-8 R2 F120 drills a hole at X 15, Y 15. The tool moves there at rapid, comes down at rapid to R, the height just above the work where feeding begins, feeds down to Z, the drill-tip depth, and rises back up at rapid.

  • How high it rises. In this simulator G99 rises to R between holes, and G98 rises to the height the tool was at when the cycles began, or to R if that is higher. The simulator needs one of the two before the first G81.
  • The cycle is modal. After a G81, a line with only X or Y drills another hole with the same depth, R and feed. G80 ends the cycle; after it, a line with only X or Y is an error until a G0 or G1 says how to move.
Without cutter compensation, program the tool centre path

Without cutter compensation, program the tool centre path

With cutter compensation off, as in this simulator, X and Y describe where the centre of the tool goes. The metal is cut by its edge, one radius further out. A Ø10 end mill fed along Y 30 cuts a slot from Y 25 to Y 35. To leave a wall at X 80 with the metal beyond it cut away, the centre runs along X 85. Milling Operations works through the same rule for a shoulder and a pocket.

Controls can do that offset for you with cutter radius compensation, G41 and G42. The simulator does not model it, so every program here is written as the path of the centre, and a line with G41 or G42 stops with a message. CNC Axes and Offsets explains left/right compensation and tool-length offsets.

Simulator: build a program from blocks and watch it run; Interactive

Simulator: build a program from blocks and watch it run

Pick a program, change it, and run it on a simulated block of metal in a vise. Every block is one line of G-code; the same interpreter reads it whether you build it from blocks or type it, and the machine runs exactly what it reads.

How to drive it. Press a block in the program to open it and change its numbers; leave a number empty to leave that word out of the line. Add a block from the row above the program, either by pressing it, which puts it after the open block, or by dragging it into place. Drag a block by its handle to move it; with the keyboard, focus the handle and press Alt with ↑ or ↓. Play runs the program, Step runs one block and stops, Back goes back one block and Restart starts again with fresh stock. The block that is running is outlined in gold, and its move is drawn in gold on the views; press a move in the top view to open the block that makes it. Any change to the program puts the simulation back to its start, so it always shows the program as it now is.

Things to try in the G-code simulator; Checklist

Things to try in the G-code simulator

  • Step through the slot program one block at a time. Watch the machine state change at blocks 2, 3 and 4 before anything moves.
  • Make the slot deeper and shorter, then run it again. Which numbers did you change?
  • Drag the Spindle on block below the first feed move, and read why the machine stops.
  • Open block 7 of the slot program and switch it from G1 to G0. What does a rapid do when it meets the metal?
  • Change the slot program to G91. Before you press Play, work out where its first move will go.
  • In the arcs program, swap one G3 for a G2, and see which way that corner turns now.
  • In the holes program, try G99 instead of G98, then add a fifth hole.
  • In the G-code text, type a line the simulator does not read, such as G41 or M7, and read what it says.
What the simulator reads, and what it leaves out

What the simulator reads, and what it leaves out

The simulator reads a small part of G-code, modelled on the way the LinuxCNC control reads it. Any other code, or a line that is not G-code at all, stops the program at that line with a message saying what is wrong. Nothing is skipped.

Motion
G0 rapid, G1 feed, G2 and G3 arcs in the XY plane, G81 drilling cycle and G80 to end it.
Modes
G17 XY plane, G20 inches, G21 millimetres, G90 absolute, G91 incremental, G90.1 and G91.1 for I and J, G94 feed per minute, G98 and G99 for the drilling cycle. G40, G49 and G54 are read as the settings the simulator always has: no cutter compensation, no tool length offset, and its one work offset.
Machine
M3 spindle on, M5 off, M6 tool change, M8 and M9 coolant on and off (shown, with no effect on the cut), M2 or M30 program end: stops spindle and coolant, restores G90 and G1, and leaves the tool at its last position.
Words
X Y Z positions, I J arc centre, R arc radius or drilling R plane, F feed rate, S spindle speed, T tool, N line number, and comments in brackets or after a semicolon.
Tools
T1 Ø10 end mill, T2 Ø6 end mill, T3 Ø6 drill, T4 Ø12 spot and chamfer tool, T5 Ø50 face mill: the tools of Milling Operations, with the same rules about what each can cut.
  • Some rules are the simulator’s own. It needs units and distance mode set before the first move, a speed before M3, G98 or G99 before a drilling cycle, and, for a tool change, the spindle stopped and the tool at Z +20 or higher. A real control may be less strict, or strict about different things.
  • Only straight down and straight across, through metal. The block is modelled as a height above each point, so the tool can cut moving along Z alone, or in X and Y at one height. A move in X or Y and Z at once is followed exactly through the air, but stops if it would reach the metal: ramping and helical moves are not modelled.
  • Arcs are cut as short straight chords, each within 0.01 mm of the true arc. They are drawn as true arcs.
  • Simple timing. Feed moves run at their F and rapids at 5000 mm per minute, with no acceleration, no blending of one move into the next, and no time for tool changes.
  • Not a check of a real program. The speeds and feeds in the examples are round teaching numbers, not cutting recommendations; Feeds and Speeds is about choosing them. A program that runs here has met only this simulator’s rules. Controls differ in the codes they accept, in their starting modes and in how they change tools, so a program for a real machine is checked against the manual for its control. See CNC Programming and Prove-Out for graphics, dry run, single block and overrides; follow Equipment Operating Procedure for machine use.

Supporting detail: Addendum 7 — How the simulator reads and runs a program.

Machining/Milling

Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

Identify common keys, choose a shaft or hub cutting method, and check slot location, width, depth and fit.

A key joins the shaft slot to the hub slot to transmit torque

A key joins the shaft slot to the hub slot to transmit torque

A key is a separate piece fitted between a shaft and the bore of a hub, such as a pulley or gear. Contact between the key and slot faces transfers turning force. Here, keyseat means the recess in the shaft and keyway means the matching slot in the hub. Other references sometimes use keyway for both; always identify which part is being cut.

The key does not by itself define how the hub is held against movement along the shaft. Check the assembly drawing for axial retention as well as torque transmission.

Identify the key by its cross-section and seating shape; Practice

Identify the key by its cross-section and seating shape

KeyRecognizing feature
Square parallel keyEqual width and height in cross-section; uniform section along its working length.
Rectangular parallel keyUnequal width and height; uniform section along its working length.
Woodruff keyA segment of a disk, with a curved bottom seated in a matching circular recess in the shaft.
Gib-head keyA tapered key with a projecting head that provides a place to engage it for removal.

For a parallel key, the side fit controls how the turning load is carried. Excessive side clearance permits movement; an overly tight fit can prevent assembly. Verify the specified top clearance too. A tapered key has a different seating action, so do not apply a parallel-key fit rule to it.

Use the drawing's key designation, dimensions and tolerances. Do not choose a key size from shaft diameter alone or assume that half the key height belongs in each part.

Supporting detail: Addendum 8 — Public reference for key forms.

Practice identifying keys

Mill a shaft keyseat with the cutter that matches its end and bottom shape

Mill a shaft keyseat with the cutter that matches its end and bottom shape

An end mill can make a straight, flat-bottom shaft keyseat that ends within the shaft's length. Its diameter leaves rounded ends in plan view; confirm that the key and drawing allow that shape. Use a permitted entry method for the selected cutter.

A Woodruff keyseat cutter is a disk-shaped cutter on a shank. Its diameter forms the curved recess for a Woodruff key and its cutting width establishes the slot width. Match both dimensions to the required recess. Not every tool sold as a keyseat cutter is the correct tool for every key.

  1. Read the keyseat's width, depth, length or cutter diameter, and axial location from the drawing.
  2. Support and secure the shaft against rotation and displacement. Use Milling Vises and Strap Clamps for the setup.
  3. Align the shaft axis with the intended machine travel and locate its centerline using Mill Indicators and Part Zero. Set the cutter's cutting plane or path on that centerline, with the specified axial location and depth reference.
  4. Choose the tool and entry method with End Mill Anatomy and Cutter Selection and plan the cut with Milling Operations. Cut to the planned allowance, measure, then finish to the required dimensions.

Review Equipment Operating Procedure and mill hazards in the safety collection before operation.

Supporting detail: Addendum 9 — Why cutter selection includes more than width.

Broach a through hub keyway; consider slotting when the geometry needs it; Practice

Broach a through hub keyway; consider slotting when the geometry needs it

A conventional keyway broach and guide bushing are useful for a straight keyway through a hub bore. See Broaching for the pass sequence. The same arrangement does not make a closed-end keyseat on the outside of a shaft.

Shaping or slotting uses a reciprocating single-point tool to remove material in successive strokes. A suitable internal slotting setup can make a hub keyway when a through broach is unsuitable. Blind work still needs a planned tool runout and chip space; the method must fit the actual geometry.

Practice choosing a method

Check width, depth and location before using assembly as a fit check; Checklist

Check width, depth and location before using assembly as a fit check

  • Clean the feature and remove burrs without rounding the functional edges.
  • Check width at several accessible positions using a suitable slot gauge, gauge blocks or measuring contacts. Select a tool with enough access and resolution for the tolerance; see Choosing Shop Measuring Tools.
  • Measure depth from the drawing's stated reference. A depth instrument needs a stable reference bridge or fixture on a round shaft; resting it arbitrarily on the curved surface changes the result.
  • For a hub, establish the specified bore-to-keyway measurement with an appropriate internal/keyway gauge or fixture. A reading across the bore and slot includes the bore dimension; it is not automatically the radial slot depth.
  • Check length, axial position and centerline location. Compare actual measurements with the drawing limits.
  • Check the specified key fit and assembly clearance. Investigate interference or unwanted movement instead of forcing the assembly together.

A key that enters the slot is a useful functional check, but it does not prove depth, location or dimensional compliance.

Machining/Milling

Mill Indicators and Part Zero

Choose an indicator for alignment, account for edge-finder radius, and keep machine home, work zero and tool length separate.

A test indicator sweeps with a lever; a dial indicator measures plunger travel

A test indicator sweeps with a lever; a dial indicator measures plunger travel

InstrumentContact motionSetup use
Test indicatorA short stylus pivots through a small angle.Convenient for sweeping a vise jaw or a bore where access is tight.
Plunger dial indicatorA stem moves straight into the body.Useful for displacement checks and alignment when the stem can face the measured motion.

Both can compare alignment. “Dial” describes a display as well as a common instrument name, so identify the contact mechanism. Use the maker's stylus angle for a test indicator; on a common lever design the stylus lies nearly parallel to the measured surface. Align a plunger with the displacement being measured. Incorrect contact angles change the scale factor.

Keep the mounting rigid, preload within the instrument's range and confirm repeatability. During a fixed-jaw sweep, keep the spindle stopped and the contact geometry unchanged. For a bore-centering sweep, turn the spindle by hand using the approved setup method. Follow Equipment Operating Procedure for the machine state during setup.

Supporting detail: Addendum 10 — Contact angle affects the reading.

An edge finder locates the spindle center one tip radius from the edge

An edge finder locates the spindle center one tip radius from the edge

A mechanical edge finder has a spring-loaded contact tip that becomes concentric and then kicks sideways at contact. Use its specified spindle speed and approach method. Electronic edge finders and probes use different signals and procedures; do not assume they rotate like a mechanical edge finder.

Use a clean, defined edge, repeat the approach and account for the contact-tip radius. If the tip is 10 mm in diameter, the spindle center is 5 mm outside the edge at the trigger point. Setting that center position to zero without the radius correction moves every feature by 5 mm.

Example: the left face is X = 0 and positive X goes into the part to the right. At contact from the left with a 10 mm tip, the spindle center is X = −5 mm. Enter that position in the work-coordinate setting method for the control. On approach from a right-hand face, the sign changes. Sketch the spindle center and edge before choosing a sign.

Supporting detail: Addendum 11 — Check both repeatability and the offset sign.

Home the machine, locate the part, then account for each tool's length

Home the machine, locate the part, then account for each tool's length

  • Machine home establishes the machine's reference positions. It does not locate the part.
  • Work zero is the origin chosen on the part or fixture. Its work offset relates that origin to the machine coordinates.
  • Tool length offset accounts for where a particular tool tip lies relative to the control's tool reference.

Choose the origin used by the drawing and program, locate X and Y, and establish Z using the approved touch-off or probing method. Account for any gauge or touch plate thickness. Confirm the active work offset, tool number and tool length before a trial path. Recheck after moving the part or changing how a tool is seated.

Use Vertical Mill Startup, Setup and Shutdown to check the sequence and G-code and Toolpaths to connect coordinates to a program. Tormach's basic-operation reference provides links to work/tool offset instructions; select documentation matching the installed control.

Machining/Milling

Mill Toolholders and Collets

Match the spindle interface, compare tool-gripping mechanisms by five job criteria, and assemble ER collets with the required grip and reach.

The spindle connection and the tool grip are separate choices

The spindle connection and the tool grip are separate choices

A holder has a machine end and a cutting-tool end. “ER” describes a collet system at the tool end; it does not tell you which spindle the holder fits.

InterfaceHow to recognize the idea
R8A taper seats in the spindle and a drawbar threads into the collet or holder to pull it in. A direct R8 collet grips a matching tool shank.
CAT / BTSteep-taper holder families with flanges and retention knobs, also called pull studs, for compatible spindle retention and tool changing. Similar-looking tapers do not establish interchangeability: family, size, flange and retention knob must match the machine.
TTSThe Tormach Tooling System uses a straight holder shank gripped in a compatible collet and a shoulder that seats against the spindle face. TTS is a toolholding system, not a CAT/BT-style taper. Its seated shoulder provides a repeatable axial reference.

Identify the installed interface before selecting a holder. A Tormach name alone does not identify the spindle system or drawbar arrangement.

Supporting detail: Addendum 12 — Public toolholder references.

Compare what actually closes around the tool shank

Compare what actually closes around the tool shank

  • Ordinary keyed or keyless drill chuck: adjustable jaws grip drilling-tool shanks. A key or a hand-operated sleeve closes the jaws. Jacobs and Albrecht are brands, not gripping-mechanism categories. Do not assume an ordinary drill chuck or its mounting is suitable for milling side loads.
  • Weldon / side-lock / set-screw end mill holder: a fitted bore locates the shank and a screw bears on its designated flat. Match the bore, shank and flat. This retention feature does not guarantee that a tool cannot move under every load.
  • ER collet: the nut draws a split collet into a taper, closing it around the shank. Match the series and stated gripping range. A direct R8 collet is a different system.
  • Shrink fit: controlled heating expands the holder bore; cooling around the matching shank produces an interference grip. Tool changes need the compatible heating/cooling equipment and the maker's process.
  • Hydraulic expansion chuck: an actuator pressurizes fluid inside the holder; a sleeve deforms against the shank. The actuating screw pressurizes the system rather than bearing directly on a Weldon flat.
  • Mechanical milling chuck: a mechanical drive compresses the gripping bore or a special collet. Designs differ: some use a nut and needle bearings; Albrecht APC uses gearing and a tapered collet. APC is a milling-chuck product, distinct from Albrecht's jaw drill chucks.
  • REGO-FIX powRgrip: a dedicated unit presses a matching tapered collet into the holder. The retained grip is a mechanical press fit, not an ER nut, thermal shrink fit or hydraulic-expansion sleeve.

Grip the intended shank surface, not the cutting flutes. Keep the tool's specified engagement in the holder while leaving only the reach needed to cut and clear the part.

Supporting detail: Addendum 13 — Manufacturer examples and the drill-chuck exception.

Choose against runout, balance, grip, clearance and total system cost

Choose against runout, balance, grip, clearance and total system cost

Runout concerns the tool's rotating geometry; balance concerns the distribution of rotating mass. Grip must resist the required turning and axial loads. Clearance and reach must work throughout the path. Cost includes the holder, collets or sleeves, setup equipment, inspection, maintenance and change time.

Use this matrix to shortlist actual products. Each cell names a useful check, not a universal quality grade or approval to run at a particular speed. On a narrow screen, scroll the table sideways; keyboard users can focus it and use the arrow keys.

Compare the assembled setup, not just the holder family
MechanismRunout / high-RPM balanceGrip / clearance and reachSystem cost and upkeep
Ordinary drill chuckCheck jaws, mounting and the exact speed rating.Drilling use; body and jaws need clearance.Adjustable diameter coverage; inspect jaws and mounting.
Side-lockVerify the screw/flat assembly's runout and balance.Designated flat; check body and screw clearance.Bore-specific holders; no heat or press unit.
ER colletCollet, nut, shank and seating all contribute.Correct gripping range; nut adds front-end diameter.Collets cover sizes; correct nut, wrench and torque equipment.
Shrink fitCheck the assembled tool, not concentric appearance.Slim-nose options; verify shank match and engagement.Heating/cooling equipment, compatible tooling and change cycle.
HydraulicCheck the sleeve's condition and product specifications.Check the exact milling application and engagement limits.Approved actuation and sleeves; inspection/service requirements.
Mechanical milling chuckClamping configuration can change grip and runout.Roughing candidates; compare the actual body/nut envelope.Maker's wrench and approved parts; mechanism-specific care.
Pressed collet / powRgripCheck the matched collet, holder and complete assembly.Correct collet diameter; compare actual nose profiles.Matching collets and a dedicated press-in/out unit.

Supporting detail: Addendum 14 — A real trade-off within one product family.

Snap the ER collet into its nut before threading the nut onto the holder

Snap the ER collet into its nut before threading the nut onto the holder

  1. Match the ER series, nut, collet and tool shank. Read the collet's actual range; the ER series number is not the tool diameter. Do not force an oversized shank into it or collapse it below its rated range.
  2. Clean and inspect the holder socket, collet, nut and tool shank. Follow the manufacturer's lubrication instructions for the named surfaces; do not treat every taper and gripping surface alike.
  3. Engage the collet's extraction groove with the nut's eccentric retaining ring. Tilt and snap it into place as instructed by the maker.
  4. Thread the nut-and-collet assembly loosely onto the holder.
  5. Insert the tool with the required shank engagement and planned stickout. Tighten to the specified torque using the proper wrench and holding fixture.

Range example: a collet explicitly rated 9–10 mm can grip a 9.5 mm shank; it cannot grip a 10.2 mm shank. This is a reading exercise, not a universal collapse range for every ER collet.

Supporting detail: Addendum 15 — Why the snap matters.

A low runout reading does not establish high-speed balance

A low runout reading does not establish high-speed balance

Runout is the variation seen as a tool or reference shank rotates about the spindle axis. If one cutting edge projects farther than the others, it can carry more of the load. Dirt, damaged seating surfaces, a poor collet fit, the tool, holder or spindle can contribute. Clean and reseat before blaming cutting data; measure against the job and tool requirements.

A geometrically straight assembly can still have uneven mass around its axis. A holder's balance marking may apply without the tool, collet or other fitted parts. Check the complete rotating assembly, the stated measurement conditions and every applicable operating-speed limit. Balancing does not raise a component's permitted speed.

Supporting detail: Addendum 16 — Why adding the tool can change the answer.

Measure the reach you need without losing the required grip

Measure the reach you need without losing the required grip

Physical tool stickout is the unsupported tool length beyond the effective grip. For the bending model, identify the clamp-to-load distance. Holder projection or gauge length refers to dimensions on the holder drawing, often measured from the spindle's gauge reference to a specified holder feature. Flute length is the length of the tool's cutting portion. These are different measurements; read the endpoints on the actual drawing.

A longer holder can move the grip closer to a deep feature while the cutter keeps adequate engagement. It also adds holder projection to the system, so check stiffness and the complete collision envelope. Do not gain reach by pulling a tool out below its required clamping length. Explore Tool Stickout and Deflection for unsupported length and Diagnosing Milling Chatter for the wider cutting system.

Practice choosing the governing constraint before naming a holder

Practice choosing the governing constraint before naming a holder

  • Shallow roughing: start with a milling-rated assembly's torque transfer and axial retention. A matching side-lock holder is one candidate when the tool has the designated flat; compare other approved systems against the job rather than declaring one family the strongest.
  • Deep, narrow feature: compare nose/body clearance and required tool reach. A slim holder may avoid a collision that a large collet nut would create. Verify engagement and the holder's projection as well as the exposed cutter.
  • High-speed finishing with a small cutter: prioritize measured runout, assembly balance and the actual speed limits. A holder family name, shiny finish or high gripping-force claim settles none of those checks.

Supporting detail: Addendum 17 — Check your selection reasoning without a video.

Use short Haas video stops to test the mechanism comparisons

Use short Haas video stops to test the mechanism comparisons

The native explanations and prompts below work without video or network access. The links open selected moments in two Haas videos; they are study references, not this shop's operating procedures or equipment inventory.

Tool Holder Essentials — compare the choices

  • 1:21 — the five criteria. Before watching, choose which criterion governs each of the three situations above. Check: the job determines the priority; one overall winner is not established.
  • 2:28 — drill chucks, 8:34 — side-lock, and 13:13 — shrink fit. Identify what supplies the grip: jaws, a screw on the flat, or thermal interference after cooling.
  • 20:34 — ER, 27:42 — hydraulic mechanism, 29:27 — powRgrip, and 30:54 — Albrecht APC. Predict which needs a nut, fluid pressure, an external press unit or gearing. Check against the mechanism list; similar external shapes do not establish the same grip.

ER Collet Essentials — range and assembly

  • 6:50 — read the collet range. Explain why a series name alone cannot select a tool-shank diameter; use the stated range example above.
  • 12:40 — capture the collet in the nut. Predict the order before playing. Check: nut captures collet first; the assembly then goes onto the holder.
  • 15:50 — torque guidance. Identify where the correct value comes from. Check: the manufacturer of the actual nut, collet and holder combination, not a number generalized from a demonstration.
Machining/Milling

Milling Operations

Make a part on a simulated vertical mill: choose each tool, move it through the metal, and check what is left against the drawing. Facing, shoulders, pockets, slots, drilled, tapped and bored holes, countersinks and chamfers.

A vertical mill shapes a block with a turning tool moved in X, Y and Z

A vertical mill shapes a block with a turning tool moved in X, Y and Z

On a vertical mill the cutting tool turns in a spindle above the work. The work is clamped on the table, the table moves it front to back and side to side, and the tool comes down into it. Every shape the mill makes is the space the turning tool swept through.

X and Y
The two directions across the table. In this lesson X runs left to right as you face the machine and Y runs away from you, toward the back.
Z
Up and down, along the tool. Z+ is up, away from the work, so negative Z is below the finished top face. The raw top is at Z +1, so facing can remove metal at zero or positive Z while taking off that allowance.
Readout
The display that shows where the tool is, in X, Y and Z. A readout on a manual mill is often called a DRO, for digital readout. Here it shows the position of the tool’s tip.
Work zero
The point the readout counts from. In this lesson X 0, Y 0 is the front left corner of the block and Z 0 is the finished top face. Every dimension on the drawings is measured from those same edges and that same face.

On a real knee mill the table carries the work under a spindle that stays put in X and Y. In the simulator you move the tool instead. The readout tells the same story either way: where the tool’s tip is, measured from work zero.

Each kind of tool cuts a shape of its own, and some cannot cut sideways

Each kind of tool cuts a shape of its own, and some cannot cut sideways

Face mill
A wide body with cutting inserts round its rim. It is fed across the work to leave a broad flat face. The one in the simulator takes at most 4 mm in one pass. The inserts sit at the rim, not across the middle, so it is brought down beside the work and then fed in, never pushed straight down into the metal.
End mill
Cuts on its sides and its end. The end mills here are centre-cutting: their end teeth reach the middle, so they can be fed straight down into the metal and then moved across to cut pockets, slots, steps and walls. An inside corner they leave is rounded to the cutter’s own radius.
Spot and chamfer tool
A pointed tool with a 90° point. Fed down, it cuts a cone: the start of a hole, or a countersink round the mouth of one. Run along an edge, it bevels the edge, which is a chamfer.
Drill
Cuts only at its point, as it feeds down along its own axis. It leaves a round hole its own size, with a cone at the bottom from its point. It must never be pushed sideways in the metal.
Tap
Cuts a screw thread into the wall of a hole that is already there. It only goes straight in and straight back out.
Boring head
An adjustable single cutting point on an offset bar. Set to a diameter and fed down a hole, it opens the hole to that size. Its bar has no cutting edge at the centre, so it needs a hole to start in.

This is a teaching rack, not a list of what to buy or use. The sizes are illustrative. A real cutter’s length, number of teeth and depth of cut come from its own data and from the person responsible for the machine.

The tool’s centre runs one radius away from the wall it cuts

The tool’s centre runs one radius away from the wall it cuts

The readout shows where the centre of the tool is. The metal is cut by its edge. To leave a wall at a given place, put the centre one radius away from it, on the side being cut away.

Worked example. A shoulder’s wall belongs at X 75, with the metal to the right of it cut away. A Ø12 end mill has a 6 mm radius, so its centre runs along X 75 + 6 = X 81. Run it along X 75 instead and the wall ends up at X 69, 6 mm too far into the part. That metal cannot be put back.

  • Inside corners take the cutter’s radius. A round tool cannot reach into a sharp inside corner, so a pocket’s corners come out rounded to the radius of the cutter that made them. A drawing that allows R4 at most calls for a cutter no bigger than Ø8.
  • Outside corners stay sharp. Going round the outside of a corner, the tool swings about it and never cuts into it.
  • A slot is the width of the cutter that made it in one pass. A cutter moved in a straight line leaves a groove exactly its own width, with round ends of its own radius.

When a cutter cuts with its side, the metal is on one side of it or the other. With the cutter turning clockwise seen from above, metal on the cutter’s right as it moves is climb milling, and metal on its left is conventional milling. The simulator says which each side cut was. Climb and Conventional Milling explains the difference.

Holes: drilled to size, threaded by a tap, opened up by a boring head

Holes: drilled to size, threaded by a tap, opened up by a boring head

A drill leaves a hole of its own diameter. A hole’s depth on a drawing is measured to where the hole stops being full size, not to the tip of the cone the drill point leaves below that.

A tapped hole starts as a smaller drilled hole

A tap cuts its thread into the wall of a hole, so the hole has to be drilled smaller than the thread first, to the tap drill size. For the common metric coarse threads that size is close to the thread’s outside diameter minus its pitch, the distance from one thread to the next:

Tap drill ≈ thread diameter − pitch. M6×1: 6 − 1 = Ø5.0. M8×1.25: 8 − 1.25 = Ø6.75, drilled Ø6.8.

Drilled too small, the tap has to cut too much metal and can break. Drilled too big, the thread is shallow. The simulator checks the hole against a simplified minor-diameter band and refuses a severely undersize pilot. This does not establish functional thread fit: pitch diameter, thread form and a real thread gauge are separate checks.

Drill deeper than the thread you need

The first few threads of a tap are ground away to a taper so that it can start in the hole. Those threads cut only part of a thread, so full thread stops short of the tap’s tip. In a hole with a bottom, the tap has to go deeper than the full thread you need, and the drilled hole deeper again, past the drill’s point. This simulated tap has a 4-pitch cutting chamfer; real taps vary. The job calls for full thread reaching Z −10 from the finished face. Its countersink removes the first part of the thread, so that is not 10 mm of surviving full-thread length.

Sizes no drill gives

Drills come in fixed sizes. A boring head is set to the size you need and fed down a hole already big enough for its bar, which makes it the tool for a hole of an exact, larger size.

Simulator: make the part on the drawing, then inspect it; Interactive

Simulator: make the part on the drawing, then inspect it

Start by examining the finished Target, then choose a tool and cut Your work. In Compare, gold is metal still to remove and striped red-orange is metal cut past the drawing. The inspection measures the part that is left after every move. Nothing checks which tools you used or in what order: any way of making the right part passes.

How to drive it. Target shows the finished nominal part; Your work shows the block you are making. Compare marks what still needs work, using the drawing’s allowed limits. In Inspect / orbit, dragging and the arrow keys move only the camera. Home restores the view; the View list also offers top, front, below and 2D sections.

Choose a tool and its size, then choose Feed X, Feed Y or Feed Z to drag its tip along that machine axis. The path previews while you drag; releasing starts the feed. Place XY places the centre at the current Z. In these feed modes the arrow keys move the selected machine axis. To go to an exact place, type X, Y and Z under Move to and press Move; the tool goes up before it goes across, and across before it goes down. The handwheel buttons and the selected-axis keys move one step at a time. A move that would break a tool or hit the vise stops where it would happen, and says why. Undo takes back the last move: the one thing a real mill cannot do.

Things to try in the simulator; Checklist

Things to try in the simulator

  • In job 1, load the face mill, move it over the block and try to lower it straight onto the metal. Read why it stops.
  • Lower the face mill to Z 0.00 beside the block and drag it across. Watch the top view and the sections: the raw top is 1 mm above Z 0. Overlap a second pass until the top face check matches.
  • Cut the shoulder with the Ø12 end mill with its centre on X 75 instead of X 81. Read the inspection, then use Undo and cut it again in the right place.
  • In job 2, clear the pocket with the Ø12 end mill and read what the inspection says about its corners. Undo, and clear it with a smaller cutter.
  • Watch the gold as you cut: it is metal the drawing does not keep. Cut one pass a little too deep and see where the striped red-orange appears in the top view and the section.
  • In job 3, try to tap a hole you drilled with the Ø6.0 drill, then one you drilled with the Ø4.2. Then drill Ø5.0 only 10 mm deep and tap it as deep as it will go. How much full thread do you get?
  • In job 4, try the boring head before there is any hole. Then drill one first.
  • Make one part two different ways, for example job 4 with the face mill doing the area round the boss, and again with an end mill. Both pass.
What the simulator leaves out

What the simulator leaves out

The 3D target is a nominal guide sampled at 0.25 mm in X and Y. Its flat floors have the drawing’s depth; its small curved outlines are approximations. The cut surface is derived separately from the analytic tool paths. Neither picture is a dimensional gauge: inspection uses the drawing’s allowed limits, including smaller corners where the drawing says R4 max.
