Complex conical histories or very long cut histories switch to 2D sections to keep the controls responsive. The work is kept, and Undo or a fresh block can restore the 3D view.

The simulator is a model of where metal is and where tools can reach. It does not check speeds, feeds, forces or finish, and passing a job here says nothing about whether a real setup could take the same cuts. Feeds and Speeds is about those numbers.

  • Only straight down and straight across. The tool axis is always vertical and nothing is undercut, so every shape is a height above each point of the table.
  • Tools are exact and rigid. A hole is exactly the drill’s size, a cutter never bends or wears, and edges come out without burrs.
  • Threads are recorded, not drawn. The simulator keeps the size of the hole a thread was cut in and how deep its full thread runs, and checks that later cuts have not taken the metal it is in. It does not model the thread’s form or fit.
  • No chips, coolant or heat, and no limit on depth of cut except where a tool’s cutting edges run out.

Supporting detail: Addendum 18 — How the inspection decides, and what its numbers are.

Machining/Milling

Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

Seat and align a milling vise, support work on parallels or soft jaws, and understand how strap-clamp position divides the clamping force.

Clean contact surfaces before tightening anything

Clean contact surfaces before tightening anything

A vise locates the part against its fixed jaw; the moving jaw supplies the grip. Clean the table and underside of the vise before mounting it. Clean the jaw faces, vise bed, supports and part before loading. A chip trapped underneath changes the position you are trying to establish. Remove raised burrs without rounding away a locating surface.

Choose a grip that leaves access for the cutter while supporting the cut. A part perched high above shallow jaw contact is a different setup from a part seated low in the vise. For the operating rules that govern this work, use Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.

Sweep the fixed jaw, adjust, tighten, then sweep again; Interactive; Practice

Sweep the fixed jaw, adjust, tighten, then sweep again

  1. Mount the vise with its fasteners engaged. Snug one mounting point enough to act as a pivot and leave the other adjustable.
  2. Mount an indicator rigidly with the spindle stopped. Contact a clean, undamaged part of the fixed jaw's locating face with some preload. See indicator setup.
  3. Choose a convenient reference near one end; zero there if it makes comparison easier. Traverse so the contact point follows the jaw toward the other end, keeping contact height and indicator orientation unchanged. Alignment comes from the differences across the sweep, whether or not you re-zero.
  4. Read the difference, then tap the adjustable end of the vise body lightly with a suitable soft mallet. Sweep again. Use the demonstrated indicator response to choose the direction.
  5. Tighten the mounting fasteners to the vise/mounting instructions and repeat the full sweep. Accept the setup against the job's alignment requirement, not an invented universal tolerance.

First use: apply the same small corrective rotation about different illustrative pivots. The tilt can disappear while both ends settle at different common offsets; re-zeroing afterward is optional convenience.

Model: physical jaw position is a + m·x + b·4(x/L)(1 − x/L). Displayed reading = response × physical position − the raw reading stored as zero. A small illustrative rotation d about world pivot P=(p, 0) updates m to m + d and a to a − p·d; the stored zero is unchanged. The fixed 100 mm measuring span is inset 1 mm from each end of the finite modeled face. This is a first-order small-angle model with |d| ≤ 0.001 mm/mm, 0.0001 mm/mm control steps, and total rotation travel ≤ 0.004. The step is model resolution, not real-vise quantization. It does not model adjustment force. The drawing exaggerates deviation and is not a literal scale.

Worked example: over 100 mm, start with left 0.000 and right +0.060 mm. Apply d = −0.0006 about 25 mm: both ends become +0.015 mm, so the tilt is gone but the old zero reveals a common offset. About 50 mm both become +0.030 mm; about 0 mm both become 0.000 mm. Re-zeroing is optional convenience, not an alignment requirement. A real setup is accepted against the job requirement, not a universal tolerance from this model.

Alignment procedure: MIT, Introduction to the Mill, pp. 2–3. The comparison geometry and examples here are original.

Prove the sign first. Check which way the reading changes when the contact is displaced a known small amount toward the indicator body. With the response shown above, a higher right-end reading means that end is nearer the indicator: move it away. A lower right-end reading needs the opposite correction. Reverse the contact arrangement and the tap direction can reverse.

Supporting detail: Addendum 19 — Read the whole sweep, not just two endpoints.

Practice tap direction Practice re-zeroing Practice full-sweep interpretation

Parallels establish height; soft jaws establish a shaped seat

Parallels establish height; soft jaws establish a shaped seat

Parallels are matched support bars placed beneath the part. Choose a height that gives cutter clearance and enough jaw engagement. Keep the planned drilling and milling paths clear of them.

Snug the part, seat it with light downward taps from a dead-blow mallet, then tighten and check the seating again. Check that both supports are contacting; a loose parallel or visible gap means the part may have lifted. A mallet cannot make a chip underneath disappear.

Soft jaws are machinable replacement jaws. A step or pocket cut into them can support a thin part or fit a contour. Machine the pocket with the jaws preloaded in the intended clamping direction, following the vise maker's method. Clean the pocket and check full seating when loading each part; the jaw shape does not excuse insufficient grip.

Put the clamp stud nearer the part than the heel support; Practice

Put the clamp stud nearer the part than the heel support

A strap clamp bridges the part and a heel support. A step clamp has a toothed heel that mates with a step block. Set the heel to the clamp maker's specified height, normally level with or slightly above the part contact. Locate the part against suitable stops and support it beneath the clamping points; a strap pressing on an unsupported span can bend the work.

Place the stud toward the part end of the strap. Keep adequate contact on the part and full seating at the heel. The stud must lie between these contacts. Plan the straps, studs and supports so the tool and holder can pass them.

In the ideal two-contact model, part force = P × b / (a + b). Here P is the downward force from the nut, a is part-contact-to-stud distance, and b is stud-to-heel-contact distance. With P = 6,000 N, a = 20 mm and b = 60 mm, the part receives 4,500 N and the heel receives 1,500 N.

Supporting detail: Addendum 20 — Why the force divides this way—and what the model cannot tell you.

Practice clamp-force sharing

Machining/Milling

Tool Stickout and Deflection

A longer tool reaches farther, but bends much more under the same sideways load. Predict a change, test it, and compare the tool with a fixed baseline.

Experiment: how much does a shorter tool help?; Interactive

Experiment: how much does a shorter tool help?

Predict first: keep the same solid tool, force and material. If its unsupported length drops from 80 to 40 mm, will it bend half as much, one eighth as much, or the same amount?

The length that matters starts at the clamp

The length that matters starts at the clamp

Stickout is unsupported length. Here it is the distance from the rigid clamp face to the point where the sideways force acts. It is not the total tool length, and it is not automatically the flute length.

A force bends the tool and moves its cutting edge away from its unloaded position. The clamp end stays in place and keeps its direction; the bend grows along the unsupported length. In a real cut, force acts over the engaged cutting edges rather than at one perfect point.

Reach is a tradeoff. The tool must reach the feature and clear the work and holder. Within those constraints, reducing unnecessary stickout improves bending stiffness. A larger diameter can also help if the feature has room for it.

Length is cubed; diameter is raised to the fourth power

Length is cubed; diameter is raised to the fourth power

For the ideal solid round tool in this lab, tip bending is proportional to F × L³ ÷ (E × d⁴). Change one input at a time to see which factor is responsible.

½ length → ⅛ bendHalf × half × half. Shortening the unsupported reach is a powerful change.
2× diameter → ¹⁄₁₆ bend2 × 2 × 2 × 2 goes into the denominator. This comparison is for solid round sections.
2× force → 2× bendForce acts linearly. Double E instead, with the other inputs fixed, and bending halves.

Try a combined change: start at L = 40 mm and d = 10 mm, save that baseline, then set L = 80 mm and d = 20 mm. The length contributes 8× and the diameter contributes 1/16×, leaving half the bending at the same load and modulus. The two changes compete.

Supporting detail: Addendum 21 — The calculation and its units.

Use the trend; know what this model leaves out

Use the trend; know what this model leaves out

This is a static, linear-elastic, slender-beam model: a uniform solid round tool, a perfectly rigid clamp, a steady sideways point load at the free end and deflections small compared with the length. Elastic modulus E measures stiffness, not hardness or breaking strength.

The lab starts at E = 600 GPa, a chosen teaching value within Hyperion's published 430–690 GPa range for cemented-carbide wear grades. It is not a universal value for carbide cutters. The force is an assumed input, not calculated from a milling operation.

Flutes and necks change stiffness. The holder, spindle and workpiece can move too, and a milling force changes as teeth engage. Static bending alone does not predict chatter thresholds, surface roughness, fracture, safe loads or guaranteed finished-part error.

The lab flags L/d below 4 and bending above 1% of L as prompts to question this simplification. Those are teaching checks, not certification or safety limits.

Supporting detail: Addendum 22 — Primary references.

Connect the setup to feeds, speeds and removal rate, and explore the path and tool access in Milling Operations.

Machining/Milling

Vertical Mill Anatomy and Motion

Identify what moves on a knee mill or bed mill, and distinguish spindle rotation, quill travel, head tram and part coordinates.

The cutter rotates; feed changes its position relative to the work

The cutter rotates; feed changes its position relative to the work

A vertical mill has a spindle whose axis is vertical in its normal setup. The spindle rotates the tool. The head carries the spindle and its drive; the column supports and guides the machine assemblies. The table carries the workholding.

Do not picture the workpiece as fixed in space. Depending on the machine, the table, head, or both move to feed the rotating cutter through the work. On a typical three-axis vertical mill, X is left–right, Y is front–back, and Z is along the vertical spindle axis.

A CNC position describes the tool relative to the work. A table moving left can therefore produce tool motion to the right relative to the part. Confirm the machine's jog directions and readout before locating a feature. Continue with Milling Operations for what those movements cut.

A knee raises the table; a bed mill supports it without a rising knee

A knee raises the table; a bed mill supports it without a rising knee

AssemblyTypical knee millTypical bed mill
TableTravels along X on the saddle.Supported by the bed and slides; often travels along X.
SaddleTravels along Y on the knee.May provide Y travel beneath the table; layouts vary.
Vertical positioningThe knee raises or lowers the saddle and table.The head commonly travels vertically on the column.
QuillA sliding sleeve gives the spindle a shorter axial feed, useful for drilling and fine depth adjustment.May be absent; the head's Z motion provides the feed.

Identify the actual moving assemblies. “Bed mill” does not mean that every machine assigns Y travel to the head. CNC describes how motion is controlled, not whether the machine has a knee.

The setup checklist follows a Tormach workflow. Use the manual for the installed machine to identify controls and travel; a familiar brand name does not establish its spindle interface, options or limits.

Head tram and vise squareness check two different alignments

Head tram and vise squareness check two different alignments

Tram is the spindle axis's perpendicular alignment to the table in both left–right and front–back directions. An indicator carried around the spindle axis compares points on the table at the same sweep radius. This is an alignment check with spindle power off; head adjustment belongs to the machine-specific procedure.

Squaring the vise makes its fixed jaw parallel to an axis of table travel. It uses a straight sweep along the jaw, not a circular sweep over the table. A square vise does not prove the head is in tram, and a trammed head does not prove the vise is square. See Milling Vises and Strap Clamps.

Supporting detail: Addendum 23 — Why facing can reveal a tram problem.

Machining/Milling

Vertical Mill Startup, Setup and Shutdown

A Tormach-based sequence for preparing the machine, locating the part and tools, checking a path, and closing down.

Use the checklist with the installed machine's procedure

Use the checklist with the installed machine's procedure

This checklist follows a Tormach vertical-mill workflow. Match each control, inspection method and tool-change step to the installed machine and controller. It is a setup reminder for trained users, not a substitute for instruction or the machine manual.

The operating and hazard requirements live in Equipment Operating Procedure, Personal Protective Equipment, Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Metal Chips and Swarf. Complete those requirements before using this sequence.

Startup: inspect, power up, enable and reference the axes; Checklist

Startup: inspect, power up, enable and reference the axes

  • Complete the pre-use requirements in Equipment Operating Procedure and Personal Protective Equipment.
  • Check coolant level and lubrication of the ways—the sliding guide surfaces—using the machine's maintenance procedure.
  • Complete the prescribed guard, emergency-stop and work-area checks in Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping.
  • Confirm the machine and controller have power available. Turn on the controller computer, then the mill as directed by the installed-machine procedure.
  • Reset depressed emergency-stop controls after completing the prescribed checks, then use the machine's Start/enable control to activate its motor controllers.
  • When the controller is ready, reference (home) all installed axes by the machine's procedure. Confirm that referencing completed; homing has not set the part zero.
Part and tool setup: seat, grip, locate and record; Checklist

Part and tool setup: seat, grip, locate and record

  • Plan the datum faces, work zero, tool access and fixture clearance for the intended operations.
  • For a vise setup, clean and inspect the vise and part, remove raised burrs, and check the fixed-jaw alignment. See Milling Vises and Strap Clamps.
  • Fit parallels if needed. Snug the part, seat it with light dead-blow taps, tighten the vise and recheck seating.
  • For table clamping, have the support, locating and clamp arrangement checked against the job and installed procedure; confirm every intended contact is seated and every clamp is firm. Use strap-clamp geometry to review placement.
  • Choose the cutter and matching holder. For ER tooling, capture the collet in its nut, thread the assembly loosely, insert the shank with the planned reach, and tighten as specified. For a set-screw holder, align the designated shank flat and follow its seating method. See Mill Toolholders and Collets.
  • Install the holder using the procedure for the actual spindle and drawbar. For a manual drawbar arrangement, verify completion of its spindle-lock release and spindle-cover closure steps before operation; do not apply that sequence to a different retention system.
  • Set and verify tool lengths and the work offset using Mill Indicators and Part Zero. Confirm the active tool number, units and work coordinate system.
Before cutting: verify the program or manual movement plan; Checklist

Before cutting: verify the program or manual movement plan

  • Confirm cutter, spindle direction, speed, feed, width and depth of cut against the tool data and Feeds and Speeds.
  • For programmed work, load the intended program and check the displayed path, tools, offsets and limits. See G-code and Toolpaths.
  • Perform the approved air-cut or dry-run procedure with verified clearance. If that method changes offsets or modes, restore and verify them before cutting the part.
  • For manual movement, confirm the selected axis, direction, jog rate and increment. Use a low approach rate near a surface and incremental motion for fine positioning, as directed in the machine procedure. Select cutting feed from the tool data rather than treating a low approach rate as a cutting-feed prescription.
  • Complete the cutting-readiness checks in Equipment Operating Procedure, then perform the operation and its planned measurements.
Shutdown: end operation, shut down the controller and restore the work area; Checklist

Shutdown: end operation, shut down the controller and restore the work area

  • Finish the operation and complete the stopping and measurement requirements in Equipment Operating Procedure.
  • Follow the installed Tormach shutdown sequence. In this workflow: depress emergency stop, shut down the controller computer normally, then remove its power and turn off the mill.
  • Complete cleanup using Metal Chips and Swarf and Equipment Operating Procedure. Return tools and leave the work area ready for the next user.

Use the machine-specific instructions for any required parking position, tool removal, lubrication or power sequence. These details vary with the machine and its options.

Machining/Turning

Lathe Operations

Identify lathe parts, choose workholding and tools, and explore turning operations in a simulator before studying tapers and threads.

Identify the parts that rotate, guide and feed

Identify the parts that rotate, guide and feed

Headstock and spindle
The headstock supports the rotating spindle and its drive. The spindle carries the chuck, faceplate or other workholding. Its axis is the reference for turning.
Bed and ways
The bed supports the assemblies. Its guide surfaces, called ways, guide carriage travel and locate the tailstock.
Tailstock
Supports the far end of work with a center, or holds axial tools such as drills and machine reamers. Its quill extends along the spindle axis when aligned.
Carriage, cross slide and compound rest
The carriage moves along the bed. The cross slide moves across the axis. The compound sits above it and swivels to guide short angled movements. The tool post holds the cutting tool on the compound.
Apron
The assembly on the front of the carriage contains feed mechanisms and controls.
Feed rod and leadscrew
On machines with separate drives, the feed rod powers ordinary turning or facing feeds; the leadscrew synchronizes threading. Some lathes combine functions, so identify the actual drive arrangement before selecting a feed.
Half-nuts and quick-change gearbox
The half-nuts close around the leadscrew to drive the carriage during threading. The gearbox selects ratios for feeds or thread pitches; its chart tells you which control combinations produce each ratio.
Choose workholding for the shape and the surface that must run true

Choose workholding for the shape and the surface that must run true

Running true means the reference surface is centered on the spindle axis, with little measured runout. Gripping a part does not automatically establish that alignment.

Three-jaw scroll chuck
Moves its jaws together for quick gripping of round or suitable hexagonal stock. Self-centering is convenient, but does not promise zero runout, especially after removing and replacing a part.
Four-jaw independent chuck
Moves each jaw separately. Useful for square or irregular work, intentional offsets, or indicating an existing surface true. Adjustment takes more time.
Collet
Grips around a matching stock shape over a limited size range. Useful for repeated work and small diameters; choose the correct collet and its permitted clamping range.
Centers and drive dog
Centers locate work through prepared center holes. A dog clamped to the work transmits torque from a drive plate; the centers provide support. Useful when several surfaces must share the center-hole axis or the work must be removed and returned.
Faceplate
Provides slots or mounting features for clamping work that does not suit chuck jaws. The fixture must locate the intended axis and account for the off-center mass.
Steady rest
Mounts on the bed and supports a long workpiece at a fixed position. It can support work when the end must remain accessible for drilling or boring.
Follow rest
Mounts to the carriage and travels with the tool. It supports slender work near the cut to reduce bending under cutting force. Its support contacts must suit the diameter being supported.

For why a chuck key must never remain in the chuck, and for rotating-work precautions, see Machine Hazards and Housekeeping. See Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf for protection and chip handling.

Match tool travel to the feature, and set the edge on center

Match tool travel to the feature, and set the edge on center

Facing feeds across an end to establish a plane perpendicular to the axis. Straight turning feeds parallel to the axis to make a cylinder. Shoulder turning joins a cylindrical diameter to a step face; the tool needs clearance to reach both surfaces without its holder or unused edge contacting the work.

Center drilling prepares the seat for a supporting center. It is not automatically the best starting method for every drill. Tailstock drilling makes an axial hole; reaming removes a controlled small allowance to improve hole size and finish. Select that allowance from the reamer maker. A reamer generally follows the existing hole, so it is not a reliable way to correct a misplaced hole. Boring uses a single-point tool to enlarge an existing hole and establish its surface relative to the spindle axis.

Grooving makes a recess; parting continues a similar radial cut until the part separates. Chamfering makes a bevel at an edge. Form knurling presses a pattern into the surface and increases the diameter over the raised points; cut knurling is a different process.

Use spindle center height as the starting reference for ordinary turning and threading tools, then follow any tool-specific instruction. An off-center edge changes the effective rake and clearance. In facing, a tool that cannot reach the axis leaves a small central nub. Boring also needs clearance between the tool and the curved hole wall.

Supporting detail: Addendum 24 — Rake and chipbreakers depend on the whole cutting setup.

Continue with Turning Tapers and Single-Point Threading. Cutting speed and feed belong on Feeds and Speeds; dimensional acceptance and finish belong on Tolerances and Fits and Surface Texture and Finish.

A lathe spins the work and moves the tool on two slides

A lathe spins the work and moves the tool on two slides

In ordinary turning the work rotates while the tool feeds along it or toward its center. This simulator models parts that are round about the spindle’s axis. The shape comes from where the tool is put against the turning work, and in what order.

Chuck
Grips the bar and turns with the spindle. The jaws hold one end; the tool works on the part of the bar that sticks out.
Carriage (Z)
Carries the tool along the bed, parallel to the axis. On this page Z minus is toward the chuck and Z plus toward the tailstock.
Cross slide (X)
Moves the tool straight toward or away from the axis. The simulator’s X readout is the diameter the tool would cut. On a real lathe, find out whether a dial or readout shows diameter or radius before you trust it.
Tailstock
At the far end of the bed, on the centerline. It holds the center drill, the drills and the countersink, which feed straight along the axis.
Z0
Where the drawing’s finished front face belongs. Every length on the drawings is measured from the front face.

How to read the simulator’s picture. It is the lathe seen from the front, with the whole work in one of two views; the switch under the picture changes view at any time without changing the work. Section cuts the work in half along its centerline, the way a section drawing shows a part: metal is hatched, a hole shows open, and a thread or knurl shows as its profile. Normal shows the outside, as you would see the part on the machine, with its thread and knurl; a hole is drawn as a dashed hidden line, and a tool working inside the part is hidden by it. Tools on the cross slide come in from above, in the plane the section is cut on, so a tool and the metal it cuts are in the same plane.

The dashed blue outline is the drawing, placed at Z0. Tinted metal is still to come off. A heavy red-orange dashed line marks work that is already smaller than the drawing allows. On each tool, the gold edge is the part that cuts and the small ring is the point the readout follows.

Before using a real lathe, read Machine Hazards and Housekeeping. The chuck key stays in your hand until it is out of the chuck.

Lathe simulator: make the part on the drawing; Interactive

Lathe simulator: make the part on the drawing

Each target is shown in a complete Normal outside view and a complete Section through its centerline. Dashed lines in Normal identify hidden internal features. Section thread bands are schematic crest/root envelopes; the knurl remains a surface callout. Dimensions are nominal inches; the simulator’s feature table gives the limits.

Pick a part and read its drawing (Drawing opens it). Then make it from bar: choose a tool, start the spindle, and move the tool against the work. Measure the part against the drawing whenever you stop.

  • Move the tool by dragging it in the picture, one slide at a time as if you were turning one handwheel; with the handwheel buttons, which repeat while held; with the arrow keys once the picture is selected; or by typing a position and pressing Feed to Z or Feed to X. Stop feed, or Escape, stops a feed part-way.
  • The spindle has to be running for anything to cut, and stopped before you change a tool, change the drill size or thread pitch, or measure the part. A caliper or micrometer never goes on turning work.
  • Each tool does only its own kind of work. When a move would ask a tool for something it cannot do, the simulator stops the tool there and says why. What the tool in use can and cannot do is listed under the tool rack. Turn / face offers two actual tools in its Cutting tool selector; stop the spindle before changing between them.
  • Undo takes back one cut at a time. New bar starts the part again, and undo brings the old bar back.
  • Measure compares every feature with the drawing. The list under the simulator says what each feature still needs, or whether it has already gone too far to save.
Each simulator tool has a defined job; its form knurl displaces metal

Each simulator tool has a defined job; its form knurl displaces metal

Facing, turning, drilling, threading and knurling are not the same action with a different shape of tool. Each tool reaches different places and moves in different ways.

Turning tool
The roughing tool supplied here has a 10° lead and a 0.008 in nose radius. Its angled edge reaches ahead of its readout point. Stopping an axial pass leaves an angled shoulder; leave allowance instead of running the nose to the finished shoulder plane.
Facing tool
A square, 1/16 in wide finishing blade set for radial feed. Put its left corner at the finished Z and feed X across the end or shoulder. Its actual sweep removes the allowance and leaves the face flat. Retract clear before moving Z. These are the simulator’s selected tools; other turning tools and settings can both turn and face.
Chamfer tool
A 90° point. Plunged at an edge, each side cuts a 45° chamfer.
Grooving and parting blade
Cuts only on its front edge. Plunged part of the way it makes a groove; plunged to the center, or into the hole, it parts the work off.
Center drill, drill, countersink
Fed from the tailstock along the axis. A center drill makes a small pilot and a 60° seat for a lathe center; a spotting drill has different starting geometry. The twist drill makes the hole and the countersink chamfers its mouth. Choose a real drill’s starting method and spot angle from its maker’s guidance.
Boring bar
Turns the inside of a hole that is already there, the way the turning tool works on the outside. Its bar has to fit in the hole.
Threading tools
Form tools with a 60° point, one for outside threads and one on a bar for inside threads. For a threading pass the carriage is driven by the leadscrew, so the tool moves one thread lead for every turn of the work; for the single-start threads here, lead equals pitch.
Knurling tool
A straddle head with two opposed forming wheels, with left-hand and right-hand diagonal teeth. Their axles lie parallel to Z; together they roll a diamond pattern. Gap Ø is a simulated gap/contact-diameter control. A real tool’s arm adjustment and locking are separate from cross-slide infeed. The picture shows the barrels and axles in side projection; the highlighted rims are the forming contact.

What makes the simulator stop a move. Each of these is something the real tool cannot do, or should not be asked to:

  • The spindle is stopped, so the tool would only rub.
  • More of the cutting edge would be in the work than the tool takes in one pass. Take it in more passes.
  • A part of the tool that does not cut would touch the work: the holder, the top of an insert, the bar of a boring tool, the side of a blade.
  • The tool would hit the chuck jaws.
  • A threading tool is still in the thread when the carriage moves. Back it out first.
  • A knurl is pressed past full depth, or into a shoulder.
  • A drill is three of its own diameters into a cut without being backed out to clear its chips.

The simulator’s limits are teaching values chosen for these four parts. A real tool’s limits come from its maker and depend on the machine, the material and the setup.

Tool shape and setting matter: Sherline’s tool-grinding guide describes cutting edges, clearance and form tools. The particular blade widths, nose radius and operating limits used here are declared teaching choices, not specifications for every lathe tool.

Most parts start with a facing cut and end with parting

Most parts start with a facing cut and end with parting

More than one order can make the same part, and the simulator accepts any order that gets there. Some orders are still better than others, for reasons you can see in the work.

  • Face first. The faced end is the datum: every length on the drawing is measured from it. A sawn end is neither flat nor square to the axis.
  • Rough, then finish. A large step comes off in several passes, and only the last one goes to the size on the drawing. On the stepped pin, stop the roughing passes 0.040 in short of each shoulder, retract clear and change to the facing tool. With its left corner at the final shoulder Z, feed X to the smaller diameter. A deeper shoulder needs more clearance for the angled edge; the facing blade can remove its allowance in slices up to 0.0625 in wide.
  • Drill, then bore to size. The boring bar needs a hole its bar fits in. A center drill is available here to explore its pilot and center-seat shape, but it is not a universal prerequisite for drilling. On a real machine, use the starting method recommended for the following drill.
  • Heavy work before thin sections. Knurling pushes hard on the work. Knurling before the thin sections next to it are turned keeps the work stiff while it happens.
  • Make room for the threading tool. A thread needs somewhere for the tool to stop: a relief groove, or a stop short of the shoulder. Chamfer the end first so the thread starts on a clean edge.
  • Chamfer the back edge before parting. Once the part is cut off, its back edge is out of reach without a second setup.
  • Part off last. The part falls free, and anything not done to it by then needs another setup.

The small Chuck end circle is a separate axial view, looking from the tailstock toward the chuck. Its forward-rotation arrow and animation run counterclockwise in that view. The main picture is longitudinal, not a view along the spindle. See the viewpoint diagram in Haas’s spindle-direction training, page 16.

A thread is cut in several passes along one helix

A thread is cut in several passes along one helix

For a threading pass the carriage is coupled to the leadscrew, so the tool advances exactly one lead for every turn of the work. For the single-start threads here, that is one pitch: 1/16 in for 16 threads per inch. Every pass follows the same helix, so every pass deepens the same groove.

The section uses a schematic thread envelope. Its unhatched bands lie between the surviving crests and dashed roots; they are not solid annular thread teeth. A real single-start helix intersects opposite sides half a pitch apart. The model samples a thread profile for depth checks and preserves its material envelope for later cuts and parting. The carriage still stops at the requested Z, even between full turns. Sandvik explains the lead/pitch relation for single- and multi-start threads.

  • A little deeper each pass. The simulator allows 0.015 in of infeed per pass outside and 0.012 in inside. The thread is done when its roots reach the root diameter on the drawing.
  • Back out before you come back. At the end of a pass the tool is still in the groove. Bringing the carriage back without backing the tool out would cut the crests off.
  • Keep the pitch. A pass at another pitch cuts a second helix across the first: a crossed thread.
  • Leave somewhere to stop. The tool runs into a shoulder unless a relief groove gives it room, which is why the thumb screw has one.

Supporting detail: Addendum 25 — How a manual lathe keeps every pass on one helix.

A form knurl moves metal instead of cutting it

A form knurl moves metal instead of cutting it

The knurling tool makes no chips. Its wheels press a pattern into the turning work, and the metal they push aside has to go somewhere: it rises between their teeth. The diameter over the points ends up larger than the blank was.

Blank
The diameter turned before knurling. On these drawings it is not given: the knurled size is, and you work back to the blank.
Full points
The wheels pressed deep enough that the diamond points are fully formed. Too shallow leaves flat tops; pressing past full depth crushes and flakes the points.
Over the points
The knurled diameter, measured across the crests.

In the simulator the roots sink exactly as far as the crests rise, 0.010 in each at full depth, so a full knurl adds 0.020 in to the diameter. A real knurl’s growth depends on its pitch, the material and how hard it is pressed.

This paired-wheel forming arrangement supports feeding along Z after engagement. Dorian’s straddle setup instructions (H-19) and paired diagonal-wheel example (H-48) describe that combination. The drawing is a generic teaching head, not a dimensioned catalog tool or a setup instruction for a particular machine.

Things to try in the simulator; Checklist

Things to try in the simulator

  • On the stepped pin, try to turn the body from 1.000 to 0.750 in in one pass. Read why the tool stops, then do it in two.
  • Stop a roughing pass short of a shoulder and Measure. Choose Face without cutting and measure again. Then make the radial facing cut: which geometry actually changed?
  • Face the end but stop the cut at X 0.200. Measure: what is left at the center?
  • Face 0.010 in past Z0 and make the rest of the pin to the readout. Measure the lengths. Which ones moved, and why?
  • On the bushing, bring the boring bar to the end before there is a hole. Then drill a 1/4 in hole and try again. Which drill gives the bar room?
  • Drill the bushing without the center drill and read the note under the inspection.
  • On the thumb screw, try a threading pass up to the head before cutting the relief groove.
  • Take one threading pass at 16 per inch, change to 13 and take another. Measure the thread.
  • Knurl the head straight on the 1.000 in bar, without turning a blank first. Measure it against the drawing.
  • On the knurled nut, part the ring off and watch where the blade breaks through.
What this simulator leaves out

What this simulator leaves out

The simulator is about which tool does what, in what order, to what size. It leaves out:

  • Speed and feed. The spindle is on or off. Spindle speed, feed rate and what they do to the cut are on Feeds and Speeds.
  • The cut itself. No tool wear, heat, chatter, deflection or surface finish. A drill cannot wander, so a hole started without a center drill is only noted, not drawn off center.
  • Setups. One setup only: no turning the part around, no second operation, no tailstock center supporting long work.
  • Threads and knurls, simplified. Thread pitch, crests and roots are checked along the required length; pitch diameter and functional thread fit are not verified. The form knurl illustrates displaced material and diameter growth. Its patterned section is schematic, not an exact volume-conservation calculation. Form and cut knurling use different mechanisms.
  • Its numbers. Inch only. The tolerances, the tool limits and the parts are teaching values, not tool-maker data and not a standard.

Tolerances on the drawings mean the same as on Tolerances and Fits: a size on a limit passes.

The starting method for a real hole depends on the drill. For example, Haas distinguishes center drilling from spotting for carbide twist drills; this model does not predict drill wandering.

Machining/Turning

Single-Point Threading

Read thread geometry, distinguish pitch from lead, understand compound infeed and check thread size beyond the outside diameter.

Pitch spaces the teeth; lead sets carriage travel per revolution

Pitch spaces the teeth; lead sets carriage travel per revolution

A thread follows a helix around a cylinder. Pitch P is the axial distance between corresponding points on adjacent teeth. For N threads per inch, P = 1/N inch. A 20-per-inch thread has a pitch of 0.050 in.

Lead is the axial advance along one helix in one complete revolution. A single-start thread has one helix, so lead equals pitch. A two-start thread has two interleaved helices and lead equals 2P. In general, lead = number of starts × pitch. Threading feed follows lead; the examples here use single-start threads.

The crest is the top of a tooth and the root is the bottom of the groove. The sides are flanks. The thread angle is the included angle between flanks in an axial section. This page discusses 60° profiles; other thread forms need other tools and geometry.

Major diameter alone cannot tell you whether a thread fits

Major diameter alone cannot tell you whether a thread fits

Major diameter
The largest thread diameter: across external crests or internal roots.
Minor diameter
The smallest thread diameter: across external roots or internal crests.
Pitch diameter
The diameter of an imaginary cylinder at which thread tooth width and groove width are equal for the ideal profile. It strongly affects flank clearance and fit.

The outside of a screw can measure correctly while its flanks are still too thick. Use the thread designation and its specified limits, not just nominal outside diameter. Tolerances and Fits explains limits; Lathe Operations explains what the simulator's simplified thread check measures.

The tool stays square while the compound feeds near one flank

The tool stays square while the compound feeds near one flank

For a 60° thread, use a tool with the required 60° profile and the specified tip shape. A center gauge, also called a fishtail gauge, checks a ground tool's angle and helps align its bisector perpendicular to the work axis. Set the cutting edge at spindle center height. Swiveling the compound does not mean turning the tool away from square.

A common manual arrangement sets compound travel about 29–30° from the radial cross-feed direction for this thread form. That is about 60–61° from the spindle axis. Check the scale's zero reference before setting it.

Near-flank infeed puts most of the cutting on one edge. Exactly 30° is parallel to a flank in the ideal axial profile; slightly less also gives the other edge a small cut. Tool-maker guidance may call for a different infeed strategy.

Supporting detail: Addendum 26 — Radial depth and compound travel are different quantities.

Keep every pass synchronized with the same helix; Checklist

Keep every pass synchronized with the same helix

The gearbox establishes the relationship between spindle rotation and leadscrew rotation. Closing the half-nuts connects the carriage to the leadscrew so that each spindle revolution advances the tool by the selected lead. An ordinary power-feed setting is not a substitute for a threading setting.

Check the machine's threading-dial chart before re-engaging the half-nuts. On an inch-leadscrew lathe, the engagement pattern depends on how the dial is graduated. With four numbered lines and unnumbered half-lines between them, common on older inch lathes with an 8-TPI leadscrew, an odd number of threads per inch (TPI) can usually be caught on any numbered line, but not on the half-lines (see LeBlond's four-numbered-line chart). On dials numbered 1–8, odd TPI are often restricted to lines of one parity (all odd or all even). Even TPI can usually be caught on any line, numbered or half. Fractional TPI may require returning to the same specified line or keeping the half-nuts engaged. These are examples, not universal dial settings: leadscrew pitch and dial gearing determine which marks work, and the machine's chart controls.

Supporting detail: Addendum 27 — Why only certain threading-dial positions return to the groove.

For some combinations, notably many metric threads on inch-leadscrew lathes, ordinary dial re-engagement will lose synchronization. Such setups commonly keep the half-nuts engaged and use the maker's prescribed return method. Confirm the machine and workholding permit that method; this page supplies no universal reversing procedure.

  • Identify the thread form, hand, pitch, number of starts and required limits on the drawing.
  • Check the machine chart for the gearing and permitted half-nut/dial procedure.
  • Check a light scratch pass with a pitch gauge before deepening the thread.
  • Plan the end of each pass and the return path before cutting to depth.
  • Measure as the thread approaches size; use the specified inspection method to decide when it is finished.

Machine operation and hazards belong on Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf.

Calculate a profile depth only after naming the profile; Practice

Calculate a profile depth only after naming the profile

A 60° angle and a pitch do not, by themselves, specify a finished thread depth. Crest flats, root shape, tip geometry and dimensional limits all matter. Use the actual thread specification and tooling data for a production cut, then measure the result. Total depth is not a per-pass infeed instruction.

For the ideal sharp-V teaching profile used in the practice bank, radial depth is H = P / (2 tan 30°) = (√3 / 2)P ≈ 0.8660254P. This is the full sharp triangle height, not a finished Unified or metric thread depth. Actual truncated or rounded profiles remove less radial material than this sharp triangle.

Supporting detail: Addendum 28 — Verify the formula without a thread-depth table.

Practice thread pitch Practice ideal profile depth Practice compound travel

A pitch gauge checks spacing; wires help measure pitch diameter

A pitch gauge checks spacing; wires help measure pitch diameter

A pitch gauge has toothed leaves that compare with the thread spacing. It identifies pitch and helps detect a wrong gearbox selection, but it does not certify pitch diameter or fit.

In the three-wire method for an external thread, two calibrated wires sit in grooves on one side and a third on the opposite side. A micrometer measures over them. Because the wires contact the flanks, the measurement can be converted to pitch diameter using the correct relation for the thread form and wire size.

Use calibrated wire sizes and their applicable instructions or a verified table. Wire diameter, thread angle and lead-angle effects matter; this page does not supply an unchecked wire formula. A thread micrometer uses dedicated contacts for a similar purpose. Appropriate thread plug or ring gauges check functional acceptance against the specified gauge limits.

Trying a mating nut may reveal gross interference, but it does not establish conformance to a thread class.

Machining/Turning

Turning Tapers

Calculate taper rate, compound angle and tailstock offset, then choose a method and check both slope and size.

A taper changes diameter at a constant rate

A taper changes diameter at a constant rate

A straight taper is a cone, or part of one. Name the large diameter D, small diameter d and axial length of the tapered portion l. Use the same length unit for all three.

Taper rate = (D − d) / l. With inch dimensions, this is taper per inch, often abbreviated TPI. Here TPI means diameter change per inch of length; in Single-Point Threading, the same abbreviation means threads per inch. Write the units to distinguish them.

TPF = 12 × TPI, and TPI = TPF / 12. Taper per foot describes the diameter change over twelve inches; the actual tapered portion need not be a foot long.

Supporting detail: Addendum 29 — Check the rate with a fresh example.

Set the compound to the half-angle measured from the spindle axis

Set the compound to the half-angle measured from the spindle axis

The tool travels along one side of the cone. Its angle to the spindle axis is the half-angle α; the angle between the two sides is the included angle 2α.

α = atan((D − d) / (2l)) = atan(TPI / 2). Use degree mode for a setting in degrees. A rate of 0.050 in/in gives α = 1.432°, while the included angle is 2.864°.

Swivel the compound so its travel makes that half-angle with the spindle axis, then feed along the compound. The taper length is limited by compound travel. Check how the lathe labels its scale: a scale measured from cross-slide travel uses the complementary angle, 90° − α.

Supporting detail: Addendum 30 — Why the factor of two belongs in the angle formula.

Tailstock offset uses the full supported work length

Tailstock offset uses the full supported work length

For a shallow external taper turned between centers, offsetting the tailstock tilts the work while the carriage still travels parallel to the bed. The usual small-angle setup estimate is offset ≈ TPI × L / 2 = (D − d)L / (2l).

L is the total work length between the effective center support points, approximated by the total part length in elementary problems. It is not just the length l of the tapered portion. Center-hole geometry matters in an actual setup. Use inches for L when the taper rate is in in/in; if given TPF, first divide it by 12.

For a rate of 0.050 in/in and L = 8.000 in, the estimate is 0.200 in even if only 3.000 in is tapered. Machine offset capacity and the center arrangement limit this method. Check a trial cut and restore center alignment before straight turning.

Supporting detail: Addendum 31 — Why this is an estimate rather than an exact setting.

Choose the taper method for length, access and support

Choose the taper method for length, access and support

Compound rest
Useful for short external or internal tapers. The compound guides the tool at the half-angle, but its limited travel restricts length.
Tailstock offset
Useful for shallow external tapers between centers. It changes the work axis and does not provide a method for boring an internal taper.
Taper attachment
A guide coordinates cross-slide motion with carriage travel. It can produce internal or external tapers within its travel and angle limits while the work stays aligned with the spindle. Connection and cross-feed arrangements depend on the attachment.
Form tool
A shaped cutting edge produces a short taper by feeding across the axis. A wide edge engages much of the cut at once, increasing cutting load and the tendency to chatter.

Start with Lathe Operations for the machine and workholding. Use Feeds and Speeds for cutting conditions and Surface Texture and Finish for the finish left by the cut.

A matching taper needs both the right slope and the right size; Practice

A matching taper needs both the right slope and the right size

Measure diameters at two known axial positions to check the rate. A correct rate can still leave the entire taper too large or too small. A suitable taper plug or ring gauge checks the mating geometry; contact pattern and seating position answer different questions.

Morse tapers are commonly used for centers and tool shanks. Jacobs tapers commonly join a drill chuck to its arbor. They are separate families: identify the exact mating designation before selecting a tool or adapter. No dimensions or angles should be inferred from the family name alone.

No standard taper table is reproduced here. Use the specified component drawing and verified manufacturer or standard dimensions for a real fit; see Tolerances and Fits.

Practice taper rate Practice half-angle Practice offset

Machining/Drilling and Threading

Drilling on a Drill Press or Mill

Plan hole location, workholding, starting, chip evacuation and depth before drilling, then inspect and deburr the result.

Locate and secure the work before starting a hole

Locate and secure the work before starting a hole

A drill press feeds a rotating drill along its spindle axis. A mill adds controlled table positioning, which helps place a pattern of holes from drawing datums. On either machine, the hole follows the relationship between spindle, tool and workholding.

Clamp the work or hold it in a suitable vise or fixture rather than by hand; see Machine Hazards for why. Round stock needs support that prevents rolling, such as a properly clamped V-block arrangement. Provide clearance for a through drill without drilling into the table, vise or supports.

For the operating rules, use Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf. The sequence here assumes those requirements and the machine's operating instructions have been met.

A spot starts the hole; a pilot removes the center material

A spot starts the hole; a pilot removes the center material

Spot drilling makes a short starting feature to help locate the next drill. A center drill is primarily designed to produce a center hole for supporting work between centers; its small pilot and conical portion make it different from a spot drill. Select a starting tool compatible with the following drill, rather than treating the two tools as interchangeable.

A pilot hole is a smaller hole drilled before a larger one. It can reduce the thrust required at a conventional drill's chisel edge. It is not automatically required: some drill geometries are intended to enter solid material. Follow the drill maker's starting-hole and pilot recommendations.

Supporting detail: Addendum 32 — Why “always center drill first” is too broad.

Choose speed and feed for this drill and material; Practice

Choose speed and feed for this drill and material

Use Feeds, Speeds and Removal Rate for the surface-speed-to-RPM calculation. For drilling, its diameter input is the drill's cutting diameter. Surface speed is a cutting condition; RPM is the spindle setting. They are not the same quantity.

Feed per revolution describes how far the drill advances each turn. Select cutting data for the tool material, work material, diameter, depth and coolant arrangement. A generic material table is a starting reference only when its tool assumptions match. Use an available machine setting consistent with the tool and machine instructions.

Practice drill RPM

Plan chip evacuation and full-diameter depth

Plan chip evacuation and full-diameter depth

Peck drilling advances in stages with retractions to break or evacuate chips. The needed stroke and retraction depend on the drill, material, hole depth and fluid delivery; there is no universal peck distance. Do not add a peck cycle to a tool that calls for continuous feed without checking its instructions.

For a blind hole, distinguish the depth reached by the tip from the depth that has the full drill diameter. The conical point extends beyond the full-diameter portion. A tapped blind hole also needs space for the tap's lead-in and chip clearance. For a through hole, account for breakthrough and the drill point below the work.

If chip shape, sound, thrust or finish changes unexpectedly, stop and inspect the setup before resuming; use Metal Chips and Swarf for chip handling.

Supporting detail: Addendum 33 — Why changes in the cut matter.

Check the hole before calling it finished; Checklist

Check the hole before calling it finished

  • Confirm the hole location, required diameter and whether it is through or blind.
  • Check the tool, starting method, workholding, exit clearance and depth plan.
  • Set suitable speed, feed and chip-evacuation conditions.
  • After drilling and stopping the machine, inspect the hole and remove burrs without changing the specified feature.
  • Measure the required dimensions and complete any specified finishing operation.

Deburring removes the raised edge left by cutting. It does not automatically mean making a large countersink. Preserve the drawing's edge requirements and inspect the exit side too.

Machining/Drilling and Threading

Reaming, Boring and Hole Seats

Choose a finishing operation by the feature needed: a sized bore, a cylindrical recess, a conical seat or a flat bearing surface.

Choose the operation from the finished shape

Choose the operation from the finished shape

Needed featureOperation
Improve the diameter and finish of a nearly correct holeReam
Enlarge an existing hole with control of its axis and diameterBore
Cylindrical recess with a flat shoulder for a fastener headCounterbore
Conical seat for a matching flat-head fastenerCountersink
Local flat bearing surface around a holeSpot face
Ream for size and finish; bore when the axis needs control

Ream for size and finish; bore when the axis needs control

A reamer removes a small amount of material with multiple cutting edges. Prepare an undersize hole with enough material for the reamer to cut, rather than rub. Too much allowance overloads the tool; too little may leave the previous surface. Use the reamer maker's allowance for that diameter and material, not one stock allowance for every hole.

A reamer tends to follow the existing hole. Do not rely on it to relocate a badly misplaced or crooked hole. Boring enlarges an existing hole with a cutting edge whose path can be set relative to the machine axis. With a suitable setup and enough material left to clean up, it can correct location and straightness as well as diameter.

Use Tolerances and Fits to interpret the size limits and select inspection methods. See Lathe Operations for boring and threading on the lathe.

Supporting detail: Addendum 34 — A nominal tool size is not a finished-hole guarantee.

Match the head seat to the fastener drawing

Match the head seat to the fastener drawing

A counterbore has a cylindrical wall and a flat shoulder. A countersink has a conical seat. The screw head must match that seat's included angle; the thread diameter alone does not determine the head angle or the countersink diameter.

A spot face removes enough surface material to create a local flat seat for a head, nut or washer. It is useful on a rough or uneven surface. A spot face and a counterbore may use similar tools, but their required depth and purpose differ.

Read the specified diameters, depths and angle before cutting. A tool used only to break a sharp edge is not necessarily producing a fastener seat to size. Do not substitute a preferred cutter angle for the drawing requirement.

Test the choice before choosing the cutter; Practice

Test the choice before choosing the cutter

A smooth pin hole already on location suggests reaming. A hole whose axis must be corrected suggests boring, if there is enough material. A socket-head screw recessed into a cylindrical pocket suggests counterboring. A conical flat-head seat suggests countersinking.

Practice choosing hole operations

Machining/Drilling and Threading

Tap Drills and Tapping

Estimate a cutting-tap drill, distinguish thread percentage from engagement length, and plan tap geometry, alignment and depth.

Subtract the pitch to estimate a cutting-tap drill; Practice

Subtract the pitch to estimate a cutting-tap drill

A tap makes an internal thread in a prepared hole. Start by reading the full thread callout. For common straight Unified and metric cutting taps, a useful roughly 75% thread estimate is:

  • Inch: drill diameter ≈ nominal major diameter − 1/TPI. Both diameters are in inches; TPI means threads per inch.
  • Metric: drill diameter ≈ nominal major diameter − pitch. Both dimensions are in millimeters.

This is an estimate, not a final hole specification. Use the major diameter, not the minor or pitch diameter. Select the actual drill from the tap maker's chart for the material and required thread. Do not apply this cutting-tap estimate to forming taps, pipe threads or insert-installation taps.

ThreadEstimateCutting-tap chart comparison
1/4-200.250 − 1/20 = 0.200 inNo. 7, 0.2010 in
M6 × 16 − 1 = 5.00 mm5.00 mm
3/8-160.375 − 1/16 = 0.3125 in5/16 in, 0.3125 in

Supporting detail: Addendum 35 — Chart basis and the approximation's limits.

Practice the inch estimate Practice the metric estimate

Thread percentage is not percent of bolt strength; Practice

Thread percentage is not percent of bolt strength

Percent thread describes how much thread height the hole permits relative to a reference profile. With the same cutting tap, a larger prepared hole leaves less thread height; a smaller hole leaves more material for the tap to remove and generally increases tapping torque.

It does not describe how far the screw enters the hole. That is engagement length. Nor does 75% thread mean 75% joint strength. Material, engagement length, thread geometry and loading all affect the joint. More thread height is not automatically a better choice.

Supporting detail: Addendum 36 — Keep percentage and fraction separate.

Practice thread-percentage reasoning

Taper, plug and bottoming describe the tap's lead-in

Taper, plug and bottoming describe the tap's lead-in

The chamfer is the gradual lead-in where the first teeth progressively cut the thread. A taper tap has a long lead-in that helps starting; a plug tap has a shorter lead-in; a bottoming tap has the shortest of the three and reaches full thread closer to the bottom of a blind hole.

A bottoming tap still has a lead-in. It cannot produce full thread all the way to the physical bottom. For hand tapping, start with a tap that can establish alignment, then use a bottoming tap when the required depth calls for it. Leave room for incomplete threads, chips and the drill point.

Chamfer style is separate from chip direction. A spiral-point cutting tap generally pushes chips ahead and needs exit space; a spiral-flute cutting tap can draw chips back toward the entrance. Select a tap intended for the material and through or blind hole.

Use a guide to start a hand tap square; Checklist

Use a guide to start a hand tap square

  • Confirm thread size, tap type, drill size, actual hole size and required full-thread depth.
  • Prepare the hole entrance as specified. Clamp the work or hold it in a vise rather than by hand; see Machine Hazards for why. Choose the tap maker's recommended lubricant for the material.
  • Align the tap with a suitable tapping guide. With a spindle used as a guide, keep it unpowered and follow the approved hand-tapping setup.
  • Turn with a suitable tap wrench while maintaining alignment. Follow the tap's chip-breaking instructions; do not force a tap whose resistance rises unexpectedly.
  • Keep within the planned travel, withdraw appropriately, clean and inspect the thread with the specified gauge or inspection method.

To help prevent broken taps, use the correct tap drill, maintain alignment, clear chips as the tap's instructions specify, use the recommended lubricant and do not force the tap. Reverse-to-break-chip routines depend on tap design; do not apply one hand-tapping rhythm to every tap.

For injury hazards, operating rules and chip handling, see Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf.

Power tapping needs a machine and holder designed for it

Power tapping needs a machine and holder designed for it

Machine tapping coordinates spindle rotation with axial travel at the thread's lead. Depending on the machine, that may use synchronized rigid tapping or a suitable tapping attachment. The machine, holder, tap, reversal and depth control must work together. An ordinary drill-press setup is not automatically a power-tapping setup.

A cutting tap removes chips. A forming tap displaces suitable ductile material to make the thread without cutting chips. Forming taps require their own, generally larger, prepared-hole sizes and suitable lubrication. A cutting-tap drill can be much too small for a forming tap of the same thread size.

Use the machine's instructions and the approved shop procedure for tapping equipment.

Supporting detail: Addendum 37 — Why the local setup decides what is permitted.

Machining/Drilling and Threading

Thread Callouts and Threaded Fasteners

Decode inch and metric thread names, distinguish thread fit from strength, and choose fastener features by their function.

Read diameter, spacing, series and class separately; Practice

Read diameter, spacing, series and class separately

In 1/4-20 UNC-2B, 1/4 is the nominal major diameter in inches, 20 is the number of threads per inch, UNC is the Unified coarse series, and 2B identifies the internal thread's fit class. The major diameter is the largest thread diameter; it is not the diameter of the hole drilled before tapping.

UNF identifies the Unified fine series. At a given nominal diameter, fine threads have more threads per inch and therefore a smaller pitch than coarse threads. In M6 × 1, M identifies a metric thread, 6 is the nominal major diameter in millimeters, and 1 is the pitch in millimeters. It does not mean one thread per inch.

Practice reading a callout

Thread class controls fit, not fastener strength

Thread class controls fit, not fastener strength

Unified external thread classes are 1A, 2A and 3A; internal classes are 1B, 2B and 3B. A means external, as on a screw; B means internal, as in a tapped hole. Class 1 permits a looser fit, class 2 serves general applications, and class 3 uses closer dimensional control.

The class number is not a material grade or a load rating. A class 3 thread does not by itself make a stronger bolt. Read the drawing for the required class and use the appropriate inspection limits. M6 × 1 alone does not specify a metric tolerance class; do not append an inch A/B class to it.

For the general distinction between a nominal dimension, its tolerance and a mating fit, see Tolerances and Fits. Exact thread acceptance limits require the applicable specification and gauges.

Pitch is spacing; lead is travel per revolution

Pitch is spacing; lead is travel per revolution

Pitch is the axial spacing between adjacent thread crests. For an inch thread, pitch in inches = 1/TPI. A 20-TPI thread has a pitch of 0.050 in. Lead is the axial travel in one complete relative revolution.

On a single-start thread, lead equals pitch. On a multiple-start thread, lead equals pitch times the number of starts. Right- and left-hand threads move in opposite axial directions for the same rotation. Look for a left-hand designation rather than forcing a fastener that does not start normally.

The lathe topic owns the process of single-point thread cutting. The tapping topic explains preparing and making internal threads with taps.

Choose the fastener by how it locates and clamps the parts

Choose the fastener by how it locates and clamps the parts

PartFunction and selection question
Bolt or screwA bolt commonly passes through clearance holes and uses a nut; a screw commonly engages a tapped part. Names overlap in catalogs, so check the actual product specification.
Cap screwA headed screw, often with a hex or socket drive. Choose the head clearance, bearing seat, thread and specified material properties, not just appearance.
Set screwIts point bears on a mating part, such as a shaft, to resist relative motion. Point shape and the mating surface matter; it is not simply a small clamping bolt.
StudA headless threaded member, often installed in one part with a nut on the exposed end. Check which end engages the part and how much usable thread remains.
NutProvides the mating internal thread. Match thread size, pitch and required properties; head shape alone does not establish compatibility.
WasherProvides a bearing surface beneath a head or nut. Choose its size, hardness and type for the joint rather than assuming every washer also locks it.
Threaded insertProvides an internal thread in a parent material or repairs a damaged thread. Follow that insert system's hole, tap and installation requirements.
Engagement, grade and locking are separate decisions

Engagement, grade and locking are separate decisions

Engagement length is the axial length of mating threads carrying load. There is no single diameter multiplier that establishes adequate engagement for every combination of screw and parent material. Use the joint design or fastener-system requirements, and ensure the screw does not bottom before it clamps.

Strength identification must come from the specified fastener grade or property class and its traceable markings or documentation. Thread fit class and head style are not substitutes. Do not assign a strength grade to an unidentified fastener from its appearance.

A flat washer is not a locking device. A lock washer or thread-locking compound is not a guarantee against loosening in every joint. Use the specified locking method; for a compound, follow its compatibility, preparation, cure and removal instructions.

Supporting detail: Addendum 38 — Check the entire joint before substituting a fastener.

Machining/Drilling and Threading

Twist Drills and Drill Sizes

Identify the parts that cut and guide a twist drill, compare point shapes, and read the four common drill size systems.

The lips cut; the flutes give chips a way out

The lips cut; the flutes give chips a way out

A twist drill makes a round hole with cutting edges at its point. The lips run from the center region toward the outside diameter. The helical grooves are flutes: they provide space for chips and a route for cutting fluid. The web is the central core between the flutes.

The chisel edge crosses the center of a conventional point. It pushes material aside with substantial thrust. Narrow strips called margins run along the outside of the drill body and help guide it in the hole. The relieved body behind them reduces rubbing. The shank is the portion held by the machine.

Point angle and split point describe different features

Point angle and split point describe different features

118° and 135° are included point angles, measured across the point in an axial view. A 135° point is flatter and shorter than a 118° point of the same diameter. A 118° point is common on general-purpose drills; 135° points are common on drills intended for tougher materials. Select the complete tool for the material and setup, not by angle alone.

A split point has extra grinding near the center to reduce the chisel edge and improve starting behavior. “135°” does not automatically mean “split point.” A split point is also not a guarantee that the hole will be located accurately without a suitable setup.

Supporting detail: Addendum 39 — Why a damaged or uneven point makes a poor hole.

Read the diameter system before selecting the drill

Read the diameter system before selecting the drill

SystemWhat the marking means
Fractional inchA diameter in fractions of an inch, such as 1/4 in. Convert the fraction when a calculation needs a decimal.
NumberA size label, such as No. 7. In the common numbered series, a larger number means a smaller drill. The number itself is not a diameter.
LetterA size label from A toward Z, increasing in diameter. Look up the actual diameter; letters are not equal increments.
MetricA diameter in millimeters, such as 5.0 mm. It is not interchangeable with a nearby inch size just because both fit in the chuck.

Read the marking and confirm the cutting diameter when identification is uncertain. A drill index is storage, not proof that someone returned the drill to the correct slot. Use the specified diameter and a checked chart when selecting a tap drill.

Match the shank to the holder and the hole to the job

Match the shank to the holder and the hole to the job

A straight shank fits an appropriate chuck or collet. A reduced shank is smaller than the cutting diameter; it does not increase the machine's drilling capacity. A taper shank fits its matching taper socket or approved adapter, rather than being gripped as though it were a straight shank.

Choose enough flute length and reach for the hole, with as little unnecessary projection as the setup permits. A drill's nominal diameter does not guarantee a finished hole's size, location or surface finish. Plan the drilling sequence, then choose a finishing operation if the drawing calls for it.

Machining/CNC

Absolute and Incremental Positioning

Convert between positions and signed moves, and trace the endpoint of a program as its distance mode changes.

G90 gives a destination; G91 gives a signed change

G90 gives a destination; G91 gives a signed change

In common milling usage, G90 makes axis values absolute coordinates in the active coordinate system. G91 makes them signed changes from the current position. Neither command moves an axis by itself. Units and work offsets still matter.

Increment = next position − current position. Reverse the calculation with next position = current position + increment. Keep a separate running total for every axis.

For an ordinary G00/G01 move, an omitted axis stays in place. In G90, X0 requests X zero; in G91, X0 requests zero X movement. Do not reuse an omitted incremental value from the preceding block.

These G90/G91 meanings must not be assumed on every lathe. Some turning controls use X/Z for absolute and U/W for incremental coordinates, and use G90 for a turning cycle. Check the control before translating a mill program to a lathe.

One path can be written as points or as moves; Practice

One path can be written as points or as moves

Start at A = (6,4) mm. Visit B = (26,4), C = (26,19), then D = (11,19). Z is unchanged; these are coordinate exercises with no cutting setup implied.

MoveAbsolute destination, G90Increment, G91
A → BX26 Y4X20 Y0
B → CX26 Y19X0 Y15
C → DX11 Y19X−15 Y0

Supporting detail: Addendum 40 — Check the conversion in both directions.

Practice point-list conversion

Trace the active mode before evaluating each block; Practice

Trace the active mode before evaluating each block

Assume millimetres, one unchanged work coordinate system, no compensation and an initial position (6,4,12). This is a paper trace, not a machine-ready program. F120 is an arithmetic example.

G21 G90 G94
G01 X26 Y4 F120

G01 X26 Y4 F120Absolute(26,4,12)
G91 Y15Incremental(26,19,12)

M30 ends this trace; it is not a command to move to zero. For arcs, the endpoint mode and centre mode are separate questions: see G-code and Toolpaths. For a broader view of modes use CNC Program Structure.
