Machining/CNC

CNC Axes and Offsets

Identify mill and lathe axes, distinguish machine and work zero, and separate work offsets from tool compensation.

Describe tool motion relative to the work with a right-handed frame

Describe tool motion relative to the work with a right-handed frame

Use your right hand: thumb along +X, index finger along +Y and middle finger along +Z, with all three perpendicular. Equivalently, curling from +X toward +Y makes the thumb point along +Z. Z runs parallel to the principal spindle axis.

On a conventional vertical mill viewed from the front, +X is to the right, +Y is toward the back and +Z raises the tool away from the work. These are tool-relative-to-work directions. If the table moves instead of the tool, its physical motion is opposite the tool-relative motion.

For a basic lathe, Z is along the spindle and +Z is away from the headstock. X is radial; positive X values commonly describe the tool side of the centreline. A slant bed or rear turret changes what this looks like from the operator's position. Do not infer axis signs from screen orientation. Two-axis turning normally uses the XZ plane.

A lathe X value may describe diameter or radius; Practice

A lathe X value may describe diameter or radius

In diameter programming, X24 describes a surface 24 mm in diameter, 12 mm from the spindle centreline. In radius programming, the same surface is X12. Z distances are not halved.

For a change from diameter 30 mm to diameter 26 mm, the X coordinate changes by −4 mm in diameter mode, but the tool moves only 2 mm radially inward. Confirm the control's convention for absolute X, incremental X and arc-centre words separately; do not halve every number in a turning block.

Practice diameter and radius

Machine zero belongs to the machine; work zero belongs to the setup

Machine zero belongs to the machine; work zero belongs to the setup

Machine zero is the machine coordinate origin. A reference-return or homing procedure establishes the machine's position reference; the home position need not be the coordinate origin. Work zero is a chosen datum on the part or fixture, such as a corner, hole centre or faced end.

Common milling codes G54 through G59 select stored work coordinate systems. Selecting G54 does not measure the part, write the offset table or redefine machine zero. The setup procedure establishes the stored values.

With only a translation, machine position = work-zero location in machine coordinates + work position. If the work origin is (100,60) and the program point is (20,15), the machine point is (120,75). This example omits rotation, local shifts and tool offsets.

In common Fanuc-style milling, G53 selects machine coordinates for the block containing it. It does not erase G54 or force G54 to become the next active work system. The previously selected work system remains selected afterward. Tool-offset interaction and permitted motion modes are control-specific; check your control's manual. Machine-coordinate zero is not necessarily a clearance position.

Tool length and cutter radius compensate for different dimensions

Tool length and cutter radius compensate for different dimensions

In common Fanuc-style milling, G43 H... applies positive tool-length compensation: it adds the signed value stored in the selected H register to commanded Z positions so Z can refer to the intended tool-tip position. The offset's sign, established by the touch-off convention, determines the direction of that shift. G43 does not mean an unconditional upward move. Check your control's manual for its offset and touch-off conventions.

For example, H03 selects register 3; it does not mean a length of 3 mm. T selects a tool; H selects offset data. Their numbers may match by shop convention, but the programmer must verify that relationship. G49 commonly cancels length compensation.

Supporting detail: Addendum 41 — Why positive compensation can use a negative offset.

G41 offsets a cutter to the left of the programmed path looking in the direction of travel; G42 offsets it to the right. G40 cancels it. These are not clockwise/counterclockwise commands. Moving along +X in XY, left is +Y. On many mills a D word selects cutter compensation data; check whether that register stores radius, diameter or a wear adjustment.

Compensation needs suitable entry and exit moves. Do not add a full radius correction to a CAM path that already includes that correction. Turning tool nose compensation also depends on nose radius and tool orientation; it is not simply a milling H offset.

See G-code and Toolpaths for tool-centre paths without compensation. Tormach's PathPilot guidelines describe H-based tool offset selection; CIMCO's Fanuc milling lesson illustrates left/right compensation.

Machining/CNC

CNC Control Fundamentals

How a control turns a program into motion, how feedback works, and what changes between milling and turning.

CNC repeats programmed motion; the operator still defines the process

CNC repeats programmed motion; the operator still defines the process

Computer numerical control (CNC) uses a program to command machine motion and functions. On a manual machine, the operator directs each move with handwheels or power-feed controls. On a CNC machine, the operator prepares the tools, workholding and coordinate references, then checks the programmed sequence.

CNC can repeat a complex path consistently. It does not remove variation from tool wear, deflection, temperature or setup errors. Programming and setup take time, so CNC is not automatically faster for every one-off job.

The machine control unit (MCU) reads program blocks, keeps track of active settings, calculates intermediate positions along a path, and sends commands to the axis drives and machine functions. The drives supply power to the motors. The control also presents positions, settings and alarms to the operator.

Feedback distinguishes open-loop and closed-loop motion

Feedback distinguishes open-loop and closed-loop motion

SystemHow position is controlledWhat that means
Open loopThe drive sends motion commands without measuring actual position back into that positioning loop.The control may not detect a missed step. A displayed commanded position is not proof of actual position.
Closed loopA sensor reports position or motion; the drive/control compares feedback with the command and corrects error.Excessive following error can produce an alarm. Feedback does not make the mechanics error-free.

A stepper motor advances through commanded angular steps and is often used in open-loop systems. A servo system uses feedback to regulate motion. Closed-loop stepper systems also exist: motor type alone does not tell you whether feedback is present.

Supporting detail: Addendum 42 — Where the sensor sits matters.

Milling rotates the cutter; turning rotates the work

Milling rotates the cutter; turning rotates the work

Basic machineCutting motionCommon programming concerns
Three-axis vertical millA rotating cutter moves relative to the work along X, Y and Z.Tool lengths, cutter radius, XY contours and hole locations.
Two-axis latheThe work rotates while a cutting tool moves along X and Z.Diameter/radius convention, tool geometry and wear offsets, tool nose radius and changing work diameter.

Machines with live tooling, extra linear axes or rotary axes extend these basic cases. A mill's tool changer and a lathe's turret do not necessarily use the same tool-selection commands. Learn the geometry in CNC Axes and Offsets, then compare Milling Operations and Lathe Operations. For cutting data use Feeds and Speeds; for milling direction use Climb and Conventional Milling.

G-code is a family of control dialects

G-code is a family of control dialects

These pages describe common Fanuc-style milling usage, with turning differences called out. G- and M-code meanings vary by control, machine type, options and configuration. Check the machine's own manual before applying a code or example. These examples teach interpretation; they are not production programs.

PathPilot is Tormach's machine control. Tormach publishes PathPilot programming documentation and post-processor guidelines. Select documentation for the actual machine and software version. A general description does not establish its installed tools, options or setup.

Continue with CNC Program Structure and CNC Programming and Prove-Out. Use G-code and Toolpaths to explore a deliberately limited teaching interpreter.

Machining/CNC

CNC Program Structure

Read program identifiers, startup modes, machine functions, feed modes and drilling cycles in common milling G-code.

A block can combine motion, settings and machine functions

A block can combine motion, settings and machine functions

A word is a letter and value, such as X12 or F100. A block is a line of words. The control applies its execution rules; words are not necessarily executed in left-to-right typing order. N numbers label blocks and are often optional. Many Fanuc-style programs use an O number such as O2468 as the program identifier. File naming, percent delimiters and identifiers vary by control.

A modal command stays active until replaced or cancelled within its group. G01 can remain active while G90 changes to G91, because motion and distance mode are different groups. A startup line sets specific modes; it does not clear every stored setting or offset.

A safe-start line declares assumptions; it does not prove the setup

A safe-start line declares assumptions; it does not prove the setup

A common milling startup example is G17 G21 G90 G94 G40 G49 G80: XY plane, millimetres, absolute endpoints, feed per minute, cutter compensation cancelled, tool-length compensation cancelled and canned cycles cancelled. This is a reading example, not a universal restart line. Cancelling an offset changes the coordinate relationship; startup and restart sequences must match the actual control and tool position.

  1. Identify the program and establish required units, plane and modes.
  2. Select the intended work coordinate system and tool; apply the correct offset data.
  3. Establish spindle, feed and coolant settings for the operation.
  4. Perform positioning and machining blocks, including any cycle cancellation.
  5. Use the machine-approved retract and shutdown sequence, then end the program.

The order and motion details around tool changes and offset activation require the machine manual. See CNC Axes and Offsets and CNC Programming and Prove-Out.

Separate spindle, tool and coolant commands from motion; Practice

Separate spindle, tool and coolant commands from motion

These are common Fanuc-style meanings, not a promise for every machine.

CodeCommon meaningRead with it
M03 / M04 / M05Spindle clockwise / counterclockwise / stopS sets the speed value. Direction is conventionally viewed from the spindle toward the work; confirm machine orientation.
M06Tool change on many millsT selects a tool. The changer may be manual or automatic; offset activation is a separate issue.
M08 / M09Flood coolant on / coolant offAvailable coolant systems and auxiliary M codes depend on the machine.
M30End program and commonly reset/rewindIt does not command a return to machine or work zero, and does not mean automatically run another part.

For example, S1800 M03 requests 1800 rpm in a fixed-rpm mode; it is not a cutting recommendation. A lathe using constant surface speed interprets S differently. See Feeds and Speeds.

Practice code meanings

Units, feed mode and plane answer different questions

Units, feed mode and plane answer different questions

SettingCommon milling interpretation
G20 / G21Inch / millimetre length units.
G94 / G95Feed in units per minute / units per spindle revolution, where supported.
G17 / G18 / G19XY / XZ / YZ plane for plane-dependent operations such as arcs.
G00 / G01Rapid positioning / straight-line motion at programmed feed.
G02 / G03Clockwise / counterclockwise arc in the selected plane.

In G21 G94, F90 means 90 mm/min. In G21 G95, F0.15 means 0.15 mm/rev; at 600 rpm that corresponds to 90 mm/min. G20/G21 alone does not choose the time basis. Some lathes use G98/G99 for feed mode, while mills commonly use those codes for drilling return levels.

Rapid path shape depends on the control and can differ from G01. G01 may feed through air as well as cut. Learn the motion and arc geometry in G-code and Toolpaths, including the existing simulator; learn distance modes in Absolute and Incremental Positioning.

G81 and G83 repeat a drilling sequence at hole locations

G81 and G83 repeat a drilling sequence at hole locations

A canned cycle packages repeated motions. In common milling use, G81 feeds a drill to depth then retracts; G83 divides the depth into pecks with retracts for chip clearance. X/Y locate the hole, Z specifies the drill-tip depth, R specifies a return/approach plane, F sets feed, and Q commonly specifies peck depth for G83. Q is not the final hole depth.

With G90 on a conventional mill, Z and R are coordinates in the active work system. Incremental canned-cycle rules need separate study in the manual. G98 commonly returns to the initial level and G99 to R; choose a return level for the actual setup. G80 cancels the cycle. Modal hole cycles can drill again at subsequent position blocks.

The simulator in G-code and Toolpaths demonstrates G81, not G83. See Tormach's programming reference for control-specific modes and cycles, and the Haas lathe manual for examples of meanings that differ from milling.

Machining/CNC

CNC Programming and Prove-Out

Follow the CAD-to-CAM-to-post chain and use graphics, dry run, single block and overrides to check a program against its setup.

CAD describes the shape; CAM plans how to cut it

CAD describes the shape; CAM plans how to cut it

CAD supplies design geometry and drawings. CAM uses geometry plus the programmer's stock, tool, workholding, operation and cutting-data choices to calculate toolpaths. Depending on the operation, CAM may work from 2D profiles or a 3D model; a solid model is not always required.

A post-processor translates CAM output into the syntax and conventions for a particular machine/control combination. Selecting the wrong post can change tool calls, arc format, offsets or startup behavior. Review the posted code as well as the CAM preview.

Supporting detail: Addendum 43 — Other ways to create a program.

Each prove-out aid answers a different question

Each prove-out aid answers a different question

Prove-out compares the intended operation, posted code and actual setup. Follow Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping for safety requirements; this page explains program-checking concepts, not a machine operating procedure.

AidUseful forLimit
Graphics or simulationInspecting path shape, endpoints, sequence and modeled interference.A missing clamp, wrong tool model or incorrect offset can make the preview disagree with the machine.
Dry runObserving a trial cycle under the control's defined test conditions.It may substitute feed rates; the name does not guarantee no motion or no contact. Use the manual's procedure.
Single blockAdvancing through blocks while comparing position and active modes with expectations.One canned-cycle block may contain several motions. Not every internal action stops separately.
Feed overrideAdjusting eligible feed motions during observation.It need not affect rapids, tool changes or synchronized operations. Rapid override may be a separate control.
Review the program against the setup before a supervised trial; Checklist

Review the program against the setup before a supervised trial

  • Match the posted file and revision to the intended part, machine and post-processor.
  • Identify the active units, plane, distance mode and feed mode at each operation.
  • Compare work offsets, tool numbers and offset registers with the documented setup.
  • Trace the first approach, tool changes, cycle returns and final retract against the modeled stock and fixtures.
  • Check that the actual setup matches what the preview includes; resolve any discrepancy with the instructor before proceeding.
  • Identify the manual's dry-run, single-block and override behavior before using those functions in a supervised trial.
  • After an edit, repeat the affected checks; compare the first part's measured features with the drawing.

Practise interpretation with G-code and Toolpaths and explore the existing 3D/WebGL milling lab in Milling Operations. A successful simulation only establishes behavior within that model. It does not approve a program for a real machine.

Machining/CNC

CNC Turning Profiles and Cycles

Account for a rounded tool nose on tapers and arcs, then distinguish roughing, finishing, grooving and threading cycles.

A rounded tool nose does not cut at the imaginary sharp tip

A rounded tool nose does not cut at the imaginary sharp tip

A turning insert has a rounded corner, called its nose radius. Touching off along X and Z establishes an imaginary tip: the intersection of the two tangent reference lines. There is no cutting material at that intersection. The actual contact point moves around the nose as the direction of the surface changes.

Axis-parallel cuts can reach the measured diameter or face with the corresponding touch-offs. On a taper, chamfer or arc, simply driving the imaginary tip along the desired surface leaves a profile error. Account for the nose radius with a calculated toolpath or the control's tool nose compensation. See Turning Tapers for taper geometry.

Supporting detail: Addendum 44 — Why a good diameter measurement does not prove a taper is correct.

Compensation needs nose radius, tip orientation and a clear entry and exit

Compensation needs nose radius, tip orientation and a clear entry and exit

In common Fanuc-style usage, G41 selects compensation to the left of the programmed direction of travel and G42 to the right; G40 cancels it. Judge the side in the control's XZ-plane convention. Do not choose a code from the screen's apparent left or right, or assume one code means every outside cut.

Enter the actual nose radius and the control's tip orientation, which tells it where the imaginary tip sits relative to the nose centre. Select the correct tool-offset register, use the manual's lead-in and lead-out requirements, and check the resulting path with CNC Programming and Prove-Out. Tip numbers differ by control; there is no universal number table here.

Do not apply full nose-radius compensation again to a path already corrected for that radius. Check whether a CAM post expects full geometry compensation, wear-only compensation or no control compensation.

Supporting detail: Addendum 45 — Where to check the control behavior.

A roughing cycle removes layers while leaving stock for finishing

A roughing cycle removes layers while leaving stock for finishing

A G71-type roughing cycle uses a defined final profile to generate repeated stock-removal passes, commonly along Z for outside or inside turning. The programmer supplies the applicable cut depth, retract and finish allowance. A G70-type finishing cycle follows the defined profile to remove the remaining allowance.

Read the control's cycle definition before entering parameters. One-block and two-block formats differ. A depth word may be radial while an X allowance is diametral; the same letter can mean different things in different blocks. P and Q commonly identify the first and last numbered profile blocks. Check the referenced blocks, permitted profile direction changes, return path and compensation rules.

Supporting detail: Addendum 46 — Why no universal cycle template is shown.

Grooving repeats plunges; threading synchronizes feed with rotation

Grooving repeats plunges; threading synchronizes feed with rotation

A grooving or peck cycle divides a plunge into smaller advances and retracts. Some formats repeat the plunge at different Z positions to make a wider groove. G75 is one common outside/inside grooving family; face-grooving and peck-drilling families may use other codes. Check peck size, final depth, groove width and tool-width convention separately.

A G76-type threading cycle makes repeated synchronized passes with increasing depth. The thread lead determines the axial advance per spindle revolution. The cycle also needs control-specific information about final size, infeed, pass depth and runout. Use Single-Point Threading for pitch, lead and thread form; a threading cycle does not choose those dimensions for you.

Formats differ by control, so no complete parameter syntax is universal. See the Haas G75 reference and the G70/G76 entries in its lathe workbook as examples. CNC Turning Program Walkthrough spells out ordinary moves so the sequence can be read without decoding a cycle.

Machining/CNC

CNC Turning Program Walkthrough

Trace an original facing, outside roughing, chamfering, finishing and cutoff sequence with every block explained.

Read the setup assumptions before the first block

Read the setup assumptions before the first block

Illustrative; check your control's manual. This is a reading example in a common Fanuc-style lathe dialect, not a machine-ready file. Read CNC Program Structure for blocks and modes, CNC Turning Setup and Offsets for offsets, and CNC Turning Spindle and Feed Modes for S and F. The mill simulator in G-code and Toolpaths cannot validate this lathe program.

The invented part is 20 mm in diameter and 25 mm long, with a 1 mm × 45° front chamfer. The chamfer runs from X18 Z0 to X20 Z−1: the 2 mm diameter change is a 1 mm radial change. Stock is 24 mm diameter with its raw face at Z+0.5. G54 has Z0 at the finished face and X0 on the spindle centreline. Stock and clearance extend beyond Z−28; workholding is farther toward negative Z.

Assume diameter programming and absolute X/Z endpoints; this dialect does not need G90 for absolute moves. T0101 selects station 1 and offset 1: a right-hand OD/facing tool with a 0.4 mm nose radius, suitable for the illustrated cuts. Its imaginary tip and radius are set, and G42 is the correct side for this setup's finish contour. T0202 selects a 2 mm wide cutoff tool and offset 2. Its Z reference is the edge toward positive Z, so Z−25 puts the blade in the interval Z−27 to Z−25. The cutoff tool is capable of the illustrated small travel past centre.

The example assumes X60 Z10 is an already-verified tool-change clearance location for both tools and the turret sweep, and starts there with spindle and coolant off. These coordinates are not a general clearance rule. All speeds, feeds and the 1800 RPM ceiling are teaching values, not material recommendations. Verify the real setup, tool calls, compensation entry/exit, centre crossing and file delimiters using CNC Programming and Prove-Out and the Safety collection.

Face the end, then leave a small allowance on the outside diameter

Face the end, then leave a small allowance on the outside diameter

Every parenthesized comment explains its block. G01 remains active until G00 replaces it; X/Z values here are destinations. Facing travels slightly past the centre to account for the rounded nose. Roughing uses two explicit lengthwise passes rather than a control-specific canned-cycle format.

Compensate the chamfer and finish, then cut off at fixed RPM

Compensate the chamfer and finish, then cut off at fixed RPM

The finish contour uses the same tool at a smaller feed. Nose compensation is active for the chamfer and OD; it is entered ahead of the face and cancelled after departing the finished contour. See CNC Turning Profiles and Cycles for why a sharp-point assumption would give the wrong chamfer.

G00 X16.0 (POSITION AHEAD OF THE FACE FOR THE COMPENSATED ENTRY)

File-start/end percent delimiters, tool-call behavior and supported startup codes must be supplied or adapted as required by the target control. No bar-feeder or parts-catcher sequence is implied.

Trace the modal state and finished dimensions on paper; Checklist; Practice

Trace the modal state and finished dimensions on paper

  • Mark where S means RPM and where it means metres per minute; locate the preceding RPM clamp.
  • Confirm that every F value is interpreted in mm/rev under G99.
  • Calculate the radial depth of each OD pass and the two chamfer endpoints.
  • Locate the nose-compensation entry and departure, and identify the selected offset register.
  • Check that the cutoff blade's positive-Z edge leaves the intended 25 mm length.

The syntax conventions can be compared with the Haas lathe programming reference. This original example is not copied from a manufacturer program. A paper trace establishes intended geometry and modal state; actual prove-out still follows CNC Programming and Prove-Out.

Spot a feed-mode error

Machining/CNC

CNC Turning Setup and Offsets

Read lathe X and Z coordinates, identify tooling and workholding, and separate part location from tool geometry and wear.

Read X as a size and Z as a position along the spindle; Practice

Read X as a size and Z as a position along the spindle

Start with CNC Control Fundamentals for how CNC works and Lathe Operations for the cuts a lathe makes. Here the work rotates and the ordinary turning tool moves in the XZ plane. Z runs along the spindle; positive Z is away from the headstock in the basic arrangement shown. X moves radially, even when its displayed value is a diameter. A slant bed or rear turret changes the view, so check the machine's axis diagram.

Confirm diameter or radius programming before reading an X value. For a 28 mm diameter, diameter mode uses X28 and radius mode uses X14. Moving from X28 to X24 in diameter mode removes 2 mm radially. Z is not halved. Confirm incremental and arc-centre conventions separately.

Use Absolute and Incremental Positioning for coordinate arithmetic. On many Fanuc-style lathes X/Z are absolute endpoints and U/W are increments; G90 can be a turning cycle. Do not paste a mill's G90/G91 startup into a lathe program.

Practice lathe X commands

The tool arrangement determines how the next cutter reaches the work

The tool arrangement determines how the next cutter reaches the work

A turret indexes a selected tool station into working position. Gang tooling mounts several tools on a slide; moving the slide brings the selected tool into position without turret indexing. Each tool still needs the correct offsets and a checked approach path.

Live tooling powers a rotating cutter on the lathe for operations such as drilling or milling. A C axis controls the spindle's angular position, allowing the work to be indexed or rotated under position control. These are options, not features of every CNC lathe. Some machines also add a Y axis. Live-tool and spindle-mode commands belong to the machine's manual.

Supporting detail: Addendum 48 — Why an extra axis changes the work a turning center can do.

Match the workholding and automation to the part

Match the workholding and automation to the part

  • A chuck grips with jaws. A self-centering chuck moves its jaws together; independent jaws permit individual adjustment. Jaw style and setup determine which shapes can be held.
  • A collet closes around a matching stock size and shape. Its useful size range depends on the collet design.
  • A tailstock center supports the free end of suitable work. It does not replace the chuck or collet that drives the work.
  • A bar feeder advances bar stock for successive parts. A parts catcher receives a separated part. Their timing and interlocks are machine-specific; neither is assumed in an ordinary two-axis program.

For operating requirements use the Safety collection and CNC Programming and Prove-Out. No particular shop machine or installed option is assumed here.

Locate the part face once, then locate each tool relative to it

Locate the part face once, then locate each tool relative to it

Use CNC Axes and Offsets for machine zero, work zero and the general offset relationship. On a lathe, a common part datum is Z0 at the finished face and X0 on the spindle centreline. Establish the Z work shift using the control's documented reference-tool, probe or touch-off method. Allow for any material still to be faced away.

For X touch-off, the reference is a measured diameter. In a trial-cut method, a tool cuts a short cylindrical surface and that diameter is measured; the control's measurement function uses the known size to establish that tool's X geometry. Use the manual's procedure for the actual machine, including which table receives the value. Do not enter the measured diameter as though it were automatically the raw geometry-offset value.

Stored informationWhat it describes
Work shift or work offsetThe part datum, especially its Z location.
X and Z tool geometryThe position of each tool's reference tip relative to the established reference system.
X and Z wearSmall dimensional corrections after measurement, separate from the basic tool setup.
Nose radius and tip orientationThe rounded cutting corner and how its imaginary tip relates to it; see CNC Turning Profiles and Cycles.

Check whether an X wear entry is interpreted radially or diametrally, its sign, and whether the control adds to or replaces the existing value. A work-offset change affects the shared datum; a tool correction addresses one tool. Selecting G54 does not measure or store a new zero. G53 does not erase the offset table.

Supporting detail: Addendum 49 — Control example: separate geometry and wear fields.

Machining/CNC

CNC Turning Spindle and Feed Modes

Calculate constant-surface-speed RPM, apply an RPM ceiling, and distinguish feed per revolution from feed per minute.

G96 changes RPM with diameter; G97 holds a requested RPM; Practice

G96 changes RPM with diameter; G97 holds a requested RPM

In the Fanuc-style lathe convention used here, G96 selects constant surface speed (CSS). S gives cutting speed: surface feet per minute with inch units, or metres per minute with metric units. G97 cancels CSS and makes S an RPM value. Confirm the actual control's units and code meanings.

Use the work diameter at the cutting point, not the insert size. From Feeds and Speeds:

  • Inch: RPM = SFM × 12 / (π × diameter in inches).
  • Metric: RPM = cutting speed in m/min × 1000 / (π × diameter in mm).

At 180 SFM on a 1.5 in diameter, RPM = 180 × 12 / (π × 1.5) = 458 RPM, rounded to a whole RPM. At 90 m/min on a 30 mm diameter, the result is 955 RPM. These are arithmetic examples, not recommended cutting data.

Practice CSS calculations

Set the maximum RPM before enabling constant surface speed; Interactive; Practice

Set the maximum RPM before enabling constant surface speed

Establish an appropriate spindle-speed ceiling for the actual setup before G96. On the Fanuc-style lathe convention here, G50 S1800 limits requested speed to 1800 RPM. The number is only an illustration; determine the permissible limit from the machine, workholding, tooling and setup documentation. Other controls use different commands or parameters.

G50 S1800 (ILLUSTRATIVE RPM CEILING)
G96 S90   (METRIC CSS: 90 METRES PER MINUTE)
G97 S600  (LEAVE CSS: REQUEST 600 RPM)

As diameter approaches zero during facing, CSS requests increasing RPM. Once the clamp is reached, RPM stays limited and surface speed falls. At the centre, a nonzero surface speed cannot be maintained at any finite RPM. Use CNC Programming and Prove-Out and the Safety collection for the required operating checks.

Supporting detail: Addendum 50 — Calculate where a speed ceiling starts to matter.

Worked example: 240 SFM, 2 in stock outside diameter (OD), and a 1000 RPM clamp. These are teaching values, not cutting recommendations. D* = 240 × 12 / (π × 1000) = 0.917 in.

One setpoint, three cutting diameters
D (in)RPMSFMClamped?
2458.37240No
0.51000130.9Yes
010000Yes

At 2 in: 240 × 12 / (π × 2) = 458.37 RPM. At 0.5 in, CSS would request 1833.46 RPM; the clamp gives 1000 RPM and π × 0.5 × 1000 / 12 = 130.90 SFM. At D = 0, the model commands the clamp RPM and surface speed is zero.

This ideal steady-state model uses π without rounding in the calculations. Displays round RPM and surface speed to two decimal places, diameters to three; trailing zeros are omitted. It assumes the commanded RPM is reached immediately and omits acceleration and other machine limits. Unit changes load a fresh teaching preset. For operating checks, see CNC Programming and Prove-Out and the Safety collection.

Explain the RPM clamp

Read the feed mode before interpreting F; Practice

Read the feed mode before interpreting F

In this common Fanuc-style lathe convention, G99 means feed per spindle revolution and G98 means feed per minute. With inch units, G99 F0.006 means 0.006 in/rev; G98 F0.006 means 0.006 in/min. With metric units, the corresponding lengths are millimetres. Codes vary: the milling return-level meanings of G98/G99 do not apply here.

Feed per minute = feed per revolution × RPM. At 800 RPM, 0.006 in/rev gives 4.8 in/min. If CSS increases RPM while G99 holds F constant, the feed per minute increases too. If G98 holds feed per minute constant, feed per revolution changes with RPM.

Set the intended feed mode explicitly. See CNC Program Structure for modal behavior and CNC Turning Program Walkthrough for a commented turning example.

Supporting detail: Addendum 51 — Reference for the code convention used here.

Practice feed conversion

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Bench Work with Hand Tools

Hold a part in a bench vise, saw by hand, choose and clean files, and remove burrs without losing the intended shape.

Use the vise to make the part steady

Use the vise to make the part steady

A bench vise holds the part while both hands control the tool. Clamp near the working area with enough material between the jaws to resist movement. Excessive projection makes the part flex and chatter. Use suitable soft jaw covers when the ordinary jaws would mark a finished surface, and support long pieces.

Keep the cut or filing area accessible. A thin-walled part may need shaped support so clamping does not distort it. Check dimensions with Choosing Shop Measuring Tools and place lines using Shop Layout and Angle Measurement. For hazards and precautions, see Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment, and Metal Chips and Swarf.

A conventional hand hacksaw cuts on the push stroke; Practice

A conventional hand hacksaw cuts on the push stroke

Install the blade with its teeth pointing away from the handle for the conventional push-cut setup, and tension it according to the frame's instructions. Choose pitch for the material actually crossed by the teeth: thin sections need finer teeth. Apply the three-teeth rule of thumb from Saw Blade Selection.

Start a shallow groove with controlled strokes. Once established, use long, even strokes that spread the work over the blade. Apply cutting pressure on the forward stroke and ease it on the return. Keep the blade aligned with the cut instead of twisting it to steer back to the line. Ease pressure as the cut nears completion and plan support for the separated piece.

Practice blade direction

File cut and coarseness are separate choices; Practice

File cut and coarseness are separate choices

A file removes small chips with many teeth. Choose its shape to reach the surface: flat for a flat face, round for a round opening, or half-round for both flat and curved areas. A safe edge has no cutting teeth, allowing work close to an adjoining surface that should remain uncut.

Single-cut files have one family of parallel tooth cuts; they are useful for controlled finishing and draw filing. Double-cut files have crossing cuts that divide the teeth into smaller cutting points; they commonly suit faster stock removal.

Coarseness describes tooth spacing. Common grades run from rough, coarse, bastard, second-cut, smooth, to dead smooth, from coarser to finer. Availability varies. Compare grades within the same file family and length; the name alone is not a universal tooth-spacing measurement. “Second-cut” is a coarseness grade, not another name for double-cut.

Practice file choice

Keep the file flat and its teeth clear

Keep the file flat and its teeth clear

Fit a suitable handle to a tanged file. For ordinary forward filing, guide the file with both hands, keep it level, apply pressure on the cutting stroke, and ease pressure on the return. Rocking rounds the edges of a surface intended to stay flat. Check progress frequently rather than filing past size.

For draw filing, hold a suitable single-cut file crosswise to the work and move it along the surface, with its length across the direction of travel. Use light, controlled pressure and orient it so the teeth cut on the working stroke. This helps blend marks and refine a flat surface.

Chips lodged in the teeth are called pinning; they can scratch the work. Clean with a file card, brushing with the tooth grooves to clear trapped chips. Store files so their teeth do not rub against other tools.

Supporting detail: Addendum 52 — File selection and care resources.

Remove the burr without changing the required edge

Remove the burr without changing the required edge

Deburring removes the thin unwanted lip left by cutting. Use a file for accessible straight edges, a suitable swivel-blade deburring tool for edges it can follow, or a suitable countersinking tool for a hole entrance. Match the cutter to the material and edge shape.

Take light passes and inspect the result. Removing a burr does not authorize a large chamfer or a rounded edge. Preserve the drawing's dimensions and edge requirements; if an edge break is specified, make that feature deliberately.

Scribers mark; hammers and punches move or indent material

Scribers mark; hammers and punches move or indent material

A scriber makes a fine line with a hard point. Use it for the marking method described in Shop Layout and Angle Measurement, rather than as a substitute for a punch.

A ball-peen hammer supplies controlled blows for appropriate metalworking tasks. A soft-face hammer can reduce surface marking when positioning a part; it does not guarantee that a delicate surface will be unmarked.

A center punch makes an indentation for locating a drill start. A pin punch drives a pin with a flat-ended tip sized for that pin. Choose the tool for the task: the pointed center punch is not a pin driver. Detailed measuring and layout procedures belong in Shop Layout and Angle Measurement.

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Cutoff Sawing

Choose a saw for the blank, hold the material securely, and leave enough material for the next operation.

Saw a blank with room for finishing

Saw a blank with room for finishing

Sawing often turns a long bar or a large plate into a manageable blank: the starting piece for machining. Plan both the material left for finishing and the kerf, the slot removed by the saw. Kerf is material lost between pieces; it is not finishing allowance.

Choose allowance from the required finished dimensions, cut quality, and later operations. A saw cut is not automatically a finished datum surface. Check dimensions and squareness before using it to locate the next cut. See Choosing Shop Measuring Tools and Shop Layout and Angle Measurement.

Match the saw's motion to the cut

Match the saw's motion to the cut

SawHow it removes materialTypical use
Power hacksawA straight blade moves back and forth, cutting on one stroke and relieving on the other. Cutting-stroke direction depends on the machine.Occasional straight cutoff work; the return stroke does no cutting.
Horizontal bandsawA continuous toothed loop advances through material clamped in a vise.Bar, tube, and structural sections cut to length. Miter capability depends on the head or vise design.
Vertical bandsawThe band passes through a table while the work is fed along a path.Straight cuts and curved outlines in plate; see Vertical Band Machining.
Cold circular sawA toothed circular blade shears chips.Repeatable cutoffs where squareness and surface finish matter. Inspect for burrs even when the cut looks clean.
Abrasive cutoff sawA thin abrasive wheel grinds through the section.Cutoff work suited to the wheel's material rating, including some hardened materials. Heat and cut quality can require further finishing.

“Cold” distinguishes chip cutting from abrasive or friction cutting; it does not mean zero heat. Use Saw Blade Selection for toothed blades. An abrasive wheel has its own selection rules.

Hold every piece, including pieces in a bundle; Checklist

Hold every piece, including pieces in a bundle

NEVER hand-hold material for a horizontal saw cut. Use the machine's vise or a suitable fixture. Support long material at the saw's working height so it does not tilt the clamped piece. Arrange support for the cutoff without trapping the blade as the cut closes.

Nesting means arranging several pieces for one cut. Clamping the outside of a bundle does not prove that its inner pieces are held. Use a nesting arrangement and clamping system approved for the machine, and select the blade for the resulting section.

  • Identify the material, section shape, finished size, and finishing allowance.
  • Confirm that the vise or fixture grips each piece and that long stock is supported.
  • Account for the kerf when locating the cut or setting a length stop.
  • Plan how the cutoff will be supported as the blade breaks through.
  • After cutting, inspect the blank and remove the burr before the next setup.

At break-through, the last connection between blank and stock disappears. Cutting resistance changes, and a thin lip of displaced metal may remain at the edge: a burr. See Bench Work with Hand Tools for deburring, and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment, and Metal Chips and Swarf for hazards and precautions.

Choose speed, feed, and coolant together

Choose speed, feed, and coolant together

Band speed is the distance the blade travels per minute, usually stated in feet/min or m/min. Feed is the rate or force that advances the blade into the work. They are different adjustments. Material grade and hardness, blade material, tooth geometry, and section shape all affect the starting settings.

Use the blade maker's cutting chart for the actual material, then follow the machine manual for setting it. Follow the blade maker's break-in procedure for a new blade. There is no single speed table or fixed percentage adjustment that fits every saw. Connect these terms to Feeds and Speeds.

On a saw designed to use cutting fluid, the fluid helps lubricate the cut, carry away heat, and clear chips. Use the approved fluid, concentration, and delivery method. Some abrasive cutoff systems are dry and others are wet; do not add coolant to a dry-only setup.

Supporting detail: Addendum 53 — Why finer teeth do not fix every bad cut.

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Grinding Wheels and Abrasives

Match the abrasive to the material, distinguish grit from grade, and read the five main fields of a conventional wheel specification.

A grinding wheel cuts with many small grains

A grinding wheel cuts with many small grains

A bonded wheel holds abrasive grains in a supporting material called the bond. The grains act as small cutting edges. Spaces between them provide room for removed material and, in wet grinding, fluid. Grains can fracture or pull free as the wheel works; dressing restores a useful cutting surface when that renewal is insufficient.

Choose the complete wheel for the machine, material and operation. Abrasive type alone does not establish suitability: shape, dimensions, bond, speed rating and permitted grinding surfaces also matter. See Offhand Grinding and Precision Grinding.

Match the abrasive to the work material

Match the abrasive to the work material

AbrasiveGeneral starting applications
Aluminum oxideSteels, including high-speed steel (HSS) tool bits. Different formulations serve different grinding conditions.
Silicon carbideCast iron, some nonferrous materials, and brittle nonmetals; also conventional carbide-tool grinding with a suitable wheel.
Cubic boron nitride (CBN)A superabrasive used for hardened steels and HSS.
DiamondA superabrasive used for cemented carbide, ceramics and other hard nonferrous materials. It is not the general choice for steel grinding.

These are selection starting points, not permission to use any wheel containing that abrasive. In particular, a standard bench wheel for steel is not a wheel for aluminum. Confirm the manufacturer's application listing.

Supporting detail: Addendum 54 — Manufacturer resources for abrasive selection.

Grit is grain size; grade is how firmly grains are held

Grit is grain size; grade is how firmly grains are held

Grit size: within the same conventional grit-number system, a lower number means coarser grains and a higher number means finer grains. Coarse grit generally provides more space for chips and favors material removal; fine grit generally favors smaller scratches. Finish also depends on dressing, feeds, wheel condition and the work material.

Grade: the wheel's resistance to releasing abrasive grains. A hard grade holds grains more strongly; it does not mean that the abrasive mineral itself is harder. A hard work material may need a softer grade so dull grains can release.

Structure: the spacing of the grains. An open structure provides more space between grains than a dense structure. Do not confuse spacing with grain size.

Bond: vitrified bonds are glasslike; resinoid bonds use resin. Rubber and metal bonds serve other applications. Bond choice affects wheel behavior, dressing and permissible operating conditions; no bond name establishes a universal RPM rating.

Read the conventional marking from abrasive to bond; Practice

Read the conventional marking from abrasive to bond

The usual core sequence is abrasive → grit → grade → structure → bond. Prefixes and suffixes may identify a manufacturer's particular abrasive or bond. Some markings omit a structure field. Superabrasive specifications may include concentration and use a different format.

For a teaching example, suppose a supplier defines A 60 J 7 V as aluminum oxide, grit 60, grade J, structure 7 and vitrified bond. The 60 is not an RPM limit; the J is not the hardness of aluminum oxide. Use that supplier's key to interpret J and 7 rather than assuming all manufacturers' grades behave alike.

Supporting detail: Addendum 55 — A manufacturer's explanation of the marking.

Practice decoding a wheel Practice grit selection

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Offhand Grinding

Understand bench and pedestal grinder setup, wheel condition, tool-bit shaping and the difference between rim speed and a wheel's maximum RPM.

Offhand grinding guides the work by hand

Offhand grinding guides the work by hand

A bench grinder mounts on a bench; a pedestal grinder stands on a base. In offhand grinding, the operator guides the work against the wheel, usually supported by a tool rest. This suits shaping and sharpening; it does not provide the controlled workholding and feeds of Precision Grinding.

For a conventional straight bench wheel, the intended grinding surface is usually its outer circumference. Move the work across that surface to distribute wear. Use only the surfaces approved for that wheel and machine; a wheel designed for peripheral grinding is not automatically suitable for side grinding.

Before operating, use Equipment Operating Procedure. Injury hazards and protective measures belong in Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf. This page explains the process, not a machine-specific operating authorization.

Wheel wear changes both rest and tongue-guard clearances

Wheel wear changes both rest and tongue-guard clearances

The tool rest supports the work near the wheel. The tongue guard is the adjustable part of the surrounding guard above the working opening; it is not the transparent eye shield. As the wheel becomes smaller, both clearances need checking and adjustment to the applicable machine instructions and requirements.

Make these adjustments with the wheel stopped and the machine secured according to its operating procedure. Recheck after dressing or wheel replacement. Use the specified clearance limits, not the proportions in the drawing.

Supporting detail: Addendum 56 — Where to check the clearance requirements.

Inspection, ring testing and dressing do different jobs

Inspection, ring testing and dressing do different jobs

Inspection checks condition and suitability before mounting. A ring test is an additional pre-mounting check for applicable vitrified wheels: a light nonmetallic tap produces a sound that a trained person evaluates for indications of cracking. Wheel size, shape and composition limit where the test applies. A clear ring does not replace the other checks.

Truing restores the required wheel shape and concentric running. Dressing renews the cutting surface by removing unwanted material and exposing useful abrasive. An appropriate dressing operation may do both. Use the dresser and method specified for the wheel.

Loading means work material fills the wheel's spaces. Glazing means dull abrasive remains at the surface and rubs instead of cutting effectively. Either condition calls for correction, not simply more pressure.

Supporting detail: Addendum 57 — Why a wheel can glaze, and where ring testing applies.

Shape an HSS tool bit without overheating its edge

Shape an HSS tool bit without overheating its edge

Grinding a high-speed steel tool bit creates the faces that meet at the cutting edge. Clearance behind the edge lets it cut without the adjacent tool face rubbing; rake influences chip flow. The required angles come from the intended tool and work material, not one universal sharpening angle.

Use light, controlled contact and check the shape frequently. Periodic dipping of a warm HSS bit in water can control temperature when the tool's instructions permit it. This is cooling during sharpening, not heat-treatment quenching; do not heat the bit severely and then plunge it into water.

Do not transfer that dipping method to a hot cemented-carbide tip. Sudden cooling can crack carbide. Use the specified dry method or a compatible continuous wet-grinding process. Intermittently quenching hot carbide is not equivalent to supplying coolant throughout the cut.

Supporting detail: Addendum 58 — Carbide needs consistent temperature control.

Aluminum and other soft, ductile metals can smear into and load a standard wheel intended for steel. Use equipment and abrasives specifically approved for the material. Changing from aluminum oxide to silicon carbide by itself does not establish that the whole setup is suitable.

Compare RPM ratings directly; calculate rim speed separately; Practice

Compare RPM ratings directly; calculate rim speed separately

The machine's spindle speed must not exceed the wheel's printed maximum operating RPM. A wheel's grade or grit marking is not that rating. Passing the RPM comparison is only one compatibility check; it does not approve the wheel's mounting, dimensions or application.

Rim speed is distance traveled at the wheel's outside diameter. With diameter D in inches and spindle speed N in revolutions per minute:

SFPM = π × D × N / 12, in surface feet per minute. The 12 converts inches to feet. Use diameter, not radius.

For an illustrative 7 in wheel at 1,750 RPM, π × 7 × 1,750 / 12 = 3,207 SFPM, rounded to the nearest whole foot per minute. This calculation is not a recommended operating speed. A smaller worn wheel has a lower rim speed at the same RPM; that does not authorize exceeding its marked maximum RPM.

See Feeds and Speeds for the same surface-speed relationship. Practice wheel speed Practice the RPM comparison

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Precision Grinding

Follow surface-grinder motions and workholding, plan small downfeed increments, and distinguish surface, cylindrical and centerless grinding.

Controlled motion lets many small cuts produce fine size and finish

Controlled motion lets many small cuts produce fine size and finish

Precision grinding combines an abrasive wheel with controlled workholding and machine feeds. Each active grain removes a small amount. A dressed wheel, stable support, small finishing increments and temperature control can produce accurate dimensions and fine surface texture, including on hardened materials.

A smooth-looking surface is not proof of correct size or flatness. Wheel condition, vibration, heat and workholding can all affect the result. Inspect the drawing's requirements using Surface Texture and Finish and Tolerances and Fits. Choose the abrasive with Grinding Wheels and Abrasives.

Use Equipment Operating Procedure for operating preparation; see Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf for injury hazards and protective measures.

A surface grinder separates table travel, crossfeed and downfeed

A surface grinder separates table travel, crossfeed and downfeed

On a horizontal-spindle reciprocating-table surface grinder, the table carries the work back and forth under the wheel. Crossfeed shifts the contact across the width of the work. Downfeed moves the wheel toward the work in small increments to remove thickness. Other surface grinders use different arrangements, including rotary tables.

After the finishing downfeed, sparking out continues passes without adding downfeed. The wheel can still remove a small amount as elastic deflection relaxes. Spark-out is not a substitute for measuring the part, and the number of passes is process-dependent.

A magnetic chuck holds suitable ferromagnetic work

A magnetic chuck holds suitable ferromagnetic work

A magnetic chuck uses magnetic attraction to hold suitable material such as many steels. It does not directly hold aluminum, brass or every stainless steel. Holding depends on material, contact area, thickness and the chuck's pole arrangement, not simply whether a magnet attracts one corner.

Clean mating surfaces and remove burrs that would lift the part. Use an approved fixture for parts that the chuck cannot hold adequately. A thin part can be pulled flat during grinding and spring back after release, so check the finished condition after removing the holding force.

Follow the chuck's release procedure after grinding. Residual magnetism may require demagnetizing so particles do not cling to the work. Demagnetizing is not the act that secures the work for grinding.

Supporting detail: Addendum 59 — Magnetic holding and release are equipment-specific.

Count downfeed increments separately from table strokes; Practice

Count downfeed increments separately from table strokes

For an ideal plan with constant downfeed, number of increments = total thickness to remove / downfeed per increment. One increment may require many table strokes and crossfeed steps to cover the entire face. State what a “pass” means before using the equation.

Example: removing 0.024 in from one face at an assumed 0.002 in per full-face layer takes 12 downfeed increments. These are arithmetic teaching values, not machine settings. If the division is not exact, use a smaller final increment rather than removing extra stock.

Supporting detail: Addendum 60 — Why a real grinding plan needs more than the quotient.

Practice downfeed counts

Coolant helps control heat and carry away grinding debris

Coolant helps control heat and carry away grinding debris

Grinding fluid can cool the work, lubricate contact and flush away removed particles. Heat changes dimensions during grinding and can alter the work surface. Delivery into the grinding zone, cleanliness and compatibility with the wheel and work material matter as much as having fluid in the tank.

Select the fluid and delivery method for the machine and operation. Do not assume every wheel or grinder permits wet operation. See Cutting Fluids and Application Methods for fluid selection and care, and Coolant Concentration and Mixing for mixing and measurement.

Cylindrical and centerless grinding control round surfaces differently

Cylindrical and centerless grinding control round surfaces differently

Cylindrical grinding commonly rotates work held between centers or in a chuck while a grinding wheel removes material from an outside diameter. Traverse grinding moves along the length; plunge grinding feeds into a selected width. Internal grinding finishes bores and can use rotating work or other machine arrangements.

Centerless grinding supports the work on a blade between the grinding wheel and a regulating wheel. The regulating wheel controls work rotation and, in through-feed operation, helps advance the work axially. The work does not need center holes. Infeed arrangements serve shapes that cannot pass straight through.

Each process needs its own setup and wheel selection. A fine finish alone does not establish roundness, straightness or size.

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Saw Blade Selection

Use section shape, teeth in the cut, tooth form, set, and blade material to narrow the choice before consulting the maker's chart.

Pitch spaces the teeth; gullets carry the chips

Pitch spaces the teeth; gullets carry the chips

TPI means teeth per inch along the blade. A higher TPI is a finer pitch. For evenly spaced teeth, pitch in inches is 1 ÷ TPI. The gullet is the hollow between teeth that provides chip space. Set is the sideways displacement of teeth, making clearance for the blade body in the kerf.

Estimate teeth in the cut before choosing TPI; Interactive; Practice

Estimate teeth in the cut before choosing TPI

As a rule of thumb, aim to keep at least about three teeth engaged. For a uniform pitch crossing one continuous thickness of material:

Estimated teeth engaged = contact length in inches × TPI
Minimum TPI for three teeth = 3 ÷ contact length in inches

Use thickness measured along the tooth line through solid material, not automatically the height of the part. For 0.25 in of continuous contact at 12 TPI, the estimate is 0.25 × 12 = 3 teeth. At the same thickness, the three-tooth calculation gives 3 ÷ 0.25 = 12 TPI.

A calculated minimum is a screening value, not a blade specification. If it falls between available pitches, select a suitable finer option from the maker's chart rather than rounding down. Excessively fine teeth can run out of chip space in thick stock.

Supporting detail: Addendum 61 — Why the answer can be a fraction of a tooth.

Predict first: at mid-depth in the thin-wall tube below, would doubling TPI halve, double, or leave the estimated engagement unchanged? It doubles: the same contact length contains twice as many tooth spacings.

Dashed line = about three teeth; shading = below three. Each plot uses its own vertical scale.

Estimated teeth = solid contact length ÷ tooth spacing; mm per tooth = 25.4 ÷ TPI. Readouts round to two decimal places; calculations keep the unrounded, real-valued estimate. Highlighted tooth tips illustrate one blade position, not a guaranteed integer count.

Round-section minima include the exact entry and exit tangencies, where contact is zero. A flat bar has constant contact through its feed height, including the limiting faces. Rotate the flat bar 90° to swap contact thickness and feed height; rotating a round bar or round tube about its axis changes neither. This model is a straight tooth line crossing an ideal section, with uniform pitch and no blade tilt.

The thick-bar, fine-blade preset highlights the full contact region as a reminder: gullets may fill with chips; check the blade maker's guidance. It sets no numeric upper limit. Tooth count alone cannot predict chip filling. For shop practice and hazards, see Cutoff Sawing and Safety collection.

Practice teeth in the cut Practice minimum TPI

A tube's outside diameter is not its solid thickness; Practice

A tube's outside diameter is not its solid thickness

A solid bar offers continuous material across the blade's path. A tube, angle, or channel presents walls and gaps, and the contact changes as the cut progresses. Select from a chart for tubes or structural sections, using wall thickness, overall dimensions, and orientation as that chart requires.

Thin walls generally need finer teeth than a solid bar of the same outside size. Do not multiply tube outside diameter by TPI and count the empty center as cutting engagement. Nor does simply adding two wall thicknesses describe every stage of a round tube cut.

Variable pitch alternates tooth spacing within a repeating group. It can reduce repeated tooth-impact vibration and suit changing engagement, but it still needs to match the material and section.

Practice tube versus solid selection

Tooth form and set describe different features

Tooth form and set describe different features

Tooth formSelection idea
Regular or standardCommon general-purpose form, typically with a zero rake face. Fine versions suit thinner sections.
SkipWidely spaced teeth with generous gullets, typically zero rake; useful when softer materials and larger chips need clearance.
HookA positive rake face takes a more aggressive bite. Use where the maker recommends it for the material and the machine can support the cut.

Rake describes the angle of the tooth face that meets the material. Exact angles vary by blade; “hook” does not specify one universal angle.

Set patternArrangement and use
RakerA common sequence is left, right, straight. A general-purpose arrangement; the straight tooth is unset.
AlternateSuccessive teeth are set left and right.
WavyGroups of teeth vary their sideways set in a wave. Common on fine-pitch blades for thin sections.

Set pattern does not replace pitch selection. Choose the complete blade specification, not a tooth-form name alone.

Choose blade material and dimensions for the machine

Choose blade material and dimensions for the machine

  • Carbon steel: an economical choice for suitable easy-to-machine materials and lighter service.
  • Bimetal: high-speed-steel cutting teeth joined to a flexible alloy-steel back; widely used for metal cutoff work.
  • Carbide-tipped: carbide cutting tips for applications needing greater wear resistance, with a compatible machine and cutting conditions.

Match blade length and thickness to the machine. Blade width, measured from tooth tip to back, also affects contouring; see Vertical Band Machining. Material name alone does not establish a blade's hardness limit or speed. Use the maker's product chart for the actual alloy and condition.

Supporting detail: Addendum 62 — Manufacturer resources for the next selection step.

Machining/Sawing and Grinding

Vertical Band Machining

Plan contour cuts around blade width and turning radius, and recognize the purpose of blade welding, band filing, and polishing attachments.

A vertical band follows a contour through the work

A vertical band follows a contour through the work

A vertical bandsaw supports the work on a table while a continuous band cuts through it. Moving the work along a marked path allows curved outlines as well as straight cuts. This can remove excess material before milling a profile.

Leave the planned finishing allowance on the retained side of the line, including room for the kerf. Use Shop Layout and Angle Measurement for marking the path and Choosing Shop Measuring Tools for checking the result. Tooth pitch and blade material are covered in Saw Blade Selection; speed and coolant in Cutoff Sawing.

The tightest curve sets the blade-width limit

The tightest curve sets the blade-width limit

A narrow blade can turn a tighter curve; a wide blade better resists wandering in a straight cut. Find the smallest radius on the intended saw path, then use the blade maker's width-versus-minimum-radius chart. Choose a width that fits both that path and the machine.

Radius is measured from the center of a curve to its edge; diameter is twice the radius. A chart's minimum radius is not a guarantee for every blade with that width: blade thickness and kerf clearance matter too. Do not force a wide blade around a tighter corner than its chart permits.

Supporting detail: Addendum 63 — Why relief cuts help with some outlines.

Blade welding closes the loop for some internal cuts

Blade welding closes the loop for some internal cuts

Blades may arrive as ready-welded loops. On equipment designed for it, a suitable open band can pass through a starting hole in the work and then be joined, making an internal contour accessible without a slot from the outside edge.

In general, blade joining involves preparing and aligning the ends, making a butt weld, heat-treating the joint as specified, finishing the weld flush, and inspecting it. The joint must flex around the wheels and pass through the guides. Follow the welder and blade maker's instructions for the exact sequence and settings; not every blade construction is suitable for a shop blade welder.

Supporting detail: Addendum 64 — Why joining includes more than making a weld.

Filing and polishing require their own bands and guides

Filing and polishing require their own bands and guides

Some band machines accept a file band to remove small amounts of material and refine a contour, or an abrasive band to smooth a surface. These are dedicated attachments with matching guides and operating instructions, not ordinary saw blades used differently.

Confirm that the machine supports the attachment before selecting its band, speed, or lubricant. Hand finishing methods are in Bench Work with Hand Tools. For operating hazards and precautions, use Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Personal Protective Equipment, and Metal Chips and Swarf.

Machining/Cutting Fluids

Coolant Concentration and Mixing

Read Brix, apply the product factor, and balance concentrate and water when mixing a fresh charge or correcting a partly full tank.

Zero the refractometer, then multiply Brix by the product factor

Zero the refractometer, then multiply Brix by the product factor

A refractometer measures how a sample bends light. On an analog Brix instrument, read where the light and dark areas meet. Brix is a scale reading; it is not automatically coolant percent.

  1. Find the product's refractometer factor and working concentration range in its technical data sheet. Use the specified method for that product.
  2. Clean the prism. Calibrate to zero with water, using the water and temperature procedure specified for the instrument and fluid. Fluid suppliers commonly specify the water used for mixing.
  3. Remove the calibration water. Apply a representative, well-mixed coolant sample, close the cover and read the light/dark boundary. Avoid sampling a floating oil layer.
  4. Calculate concentration (%) = Brix reading × product factor. Record the result and compare it with the product's range for the operation.
  5. Clean the prism after use. Recheck a doubtful reading; contamination can blur the boundary or bias the result. Use the supplier's alternative test if the sample cannot be read reliably.

There is no universal factor or target range. The SDS explains hazards and handling; the product's technical data sheet supplies the mixing and measurement information. See Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Supporting detail: Addendum 65 — Measurement references.

Add concentrate to water, and state what the ratio means

Add concentrate to water, and state what the ratio means

Water first; add concentrate while mixing. Follow the product's mixing instructions in a clean container or approved mixing system. For emulsions, this lets the emulsifier disperse oil into the water. Adding water to a body of concentrate can form an unstable or inverted mixture that does not disperse properly.

Write the order of a ratio. 24 parts water to 1 part concentrate contains 25 total parts, so its concentrate percentage is 100 × 1 ÷ (24 + 1) = 4.00%. It is not 100 ÷ 24. For water:concentrate = W:1, use C = 100 ÷ (W + 1).

To make 12 L of that 4.00% premix, measure 0.48 L concentrate and 11.52 L water. Put the water in first. This is a volume-based teaching example with additive volumes, not a product recommendation.

Supporting detail: Addendum 66 — Why mixing order matters.

A falling level does not tell you how strong the coolant is

A falling level does not tell you how strong the coolant is

Measure both level and concentration before topping up. Evaporation mainly removes water, raising concentration. Coolant carried out on parts and chips removes both water and concentrate. Adding plain water lowers concentration.

A tank below the target is lean; one above it is rich. Compare with the actual permitted range before deciding it needs adjustment. A tank can be low in volume and rich in concentrate at the same time.

Top up fluid that is still serviceable. Persistent odor, separation, sludge or contamination calls for the evaluation and cleaning decisions in Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance. New premix does not make spoiled fluid sound.

Calculate the premix needed to reach both target level and concentration; Interactive

Calculate the premix needed to reach both target level and concentration

Use the same volume unit throughout. Let V be the current tank volume, C its measured concentration, F the intended final volume, and T the target concentration. Concentrations below are entered as percent numbers, such as 6 for 6%.

Premix volume A = F − V

Premix concentration P = (F × T − V × C) ÷ A

Concentrate to measure = A × P ÷ 100.
Water to measure = A − concentrate volume.

Example: a hypothetical tank has 36 L at 4.0%. Bring it to 48 L at an assumed target of 5.5%. Add A = 48 − 36 = 12 L. The premix must be (48 × 5.5 − 36 × 4.0) ÷ 12 = 10.0%: 1.2 L concentrate added to 10.8 L water.

Check the balance: the tank contains 1.44 L concentrate, the addition supplies 1.20 L, and 2.64 ÷ 48 × 100 = 5.5%. These assumed values teach the calculation; the product must permit the proposed makeup mix.

Stop when the result cannot be made. A must be positive. A negative P means even plain water cannot achieve the target at that final level; P above 100% asks for more concentrate than the addition can contain. A full tank has no top-up space. Seek an approved partial replacement or other correction instead of overfilling. Even a mathematical result between 0 and 100% may be outside the product's permitted mixing method.

Mix the approved addition separately, add it, circulate as specified, then measure again. The calculation assumes accurate volumes, uniform mixing and no losses during the adjustment.

20:1 is not 5%

20:1 water : concentrate
1 ÷ (20 + 1) × 100 = 4.76%

5.00% concentrate
5 parts concentrate in 100 total parts.
95:5 = 19:1 water : concentrate.

Brix needs the product factor

6 Brix × an invented teaching factor of 1.0 = 6.00%. Use the actual product data sheet factor.

Correct a lean sump: account for the added volume

Teaching example: 100 L at 3%, target 5%, capacity 120 L. With x litres of neat concentrate, the balance is 3 × 100 + 100x = 5(100 + x).

x = 100(5 − 3) ÷ (100 − 5) = 2.1053 L. Final volume = 102.1053 L, within capacity. Check: (3 + 2.105263…) ÷ 102.105263… × 100 = 5.00%.

This is a concentrate balance, not an instruction to pour neat concentrate into a sump. Use the product-approved makeup method described on this page.

Predict what water replaces

Start with 100 L at 5%. Losing 20 L of well-mixed coolant leaves 80 L at 5%. Replace it with water: 4 L concentrate ÷ 100 L = 4%. Replace it with 5% premix: (4 + 1) ÷ 100 × 100 = 5%.

If instead only 20 L of water evaporates, all 5 L of concentrate remains: 5 ÷ 80 × 100 = 6.25%. Replacing that water restores 5%; adding 5% premix raises it to 6%. The loss mechanism matters.

For coolant condition and contact guidance, see Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance and Safety collection.

Supporting detail: Addendum 67 — Derive the balance, or solve for an unknown addition volume.

Practice the reading, the ratio and the top-up balance; Practice

Practice the reading, the ratio and the top-up balance

Use fresh hypothetical values to check the method. Every question states its rounding and assumptions; none supplies a shop concentration recommendation.

Practice Brix conversion Practice lean or rich Practice top-up concentration Practice mixing ratios

The practice catalog contains the full Coolant Concentration and Mixing bank.

Machining/Cutting Fluids

Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance

Recognize concentration drift and contamination, decide whether to top up or replace, and work through a general tank-cleaning sequence.

Look for oil, odor, solids and foam—not just a low level

Look for oil, odor, solids and foam—not just a low level

The sump is the reservoir that collects coolant for reuse. It also collects material that does not belong in the cutting fluid.

  • Tramp oil: unwanted lubricant leaking into the coolant, such as hydraulic oil or oil from sliding machine surfaces. Skim the floating layer and investigate its source; it can interfere with fluid condition and concentration readings.
  • Bacteria and odor: water-mixed fluids can support microbial growth. New or persistent bad odor is a reason to investigate, not a test that identifies the organism. Lack of odor does not prove the fluid is healthy.
  • Concentration drift: evaporation tends to make the tank richer; repeated water additions can make it lean. Measure using Brix and the product factor.
  • Chips and fines: chips settle and fine particles collect as sludge. They occupy tank space and can obstruct screens, filters and flow paths.
  • Foam: check concentration, water quality, contamination and air entering the delivery system. Foam is not a reliable concentration measurement.
  • Skin irritation: an overly strong mix can irritate skin; an overly weak mix can lose protection against microbial growth. Irritation is a reason to report exposure and investigate, not to guess a dilution.

Supporting detail: Addendum 68 — Why inspection and measurement belong together.

Top up a serviceable tank; replace fluid that cannot be restored

Top up a serviceable tank; replace fluid that cannot be restored

Use a top-up when the existing coolant is fit for continued use and the problem is level or a correctable concentration. Choose the addition from the measured condition, not from the fresh-fill recipe. A rich tank may need a weaker makeup mix; a lean tank may need a stronger one.

Arrange a cleanout and replacement when contamination, unstable mixing or persistent odor cannot be brought under control by the approved maintenance process, or when the machine/fluid maintenance instructions require it. Investigate leaks and other causes so the fresh charge does not immediately inherit the problem.

Straining removes larger solids; it does not remove dissolved contamination or establish that drained fluid is reusable. Do not return rejected fluid just because it looks cleaner. Do not add household disinfectant or an unapproved chemical to mask odor.

Use the machine and fluid suppliers' maintenance intervals and condition checks. There is no universal calendar changeout interval or guaranteed sump life.

Clean the tank and its return path before refilling; Checklist

Clean the tank and its return path before refilling

Use this as a general sequence with the machine's approved maintenance procedure. Stop the machine and follow its isolation requirements before accessing the tank, pumps or chip-handling equipment. Only run pumps for a cleaning or circulation step when that procedure calls for it and the system is safely reassembled.

  • Identify the fluid, approved cleaner and disposal route. Review Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets, Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf before starting.
  • Stop and isolate the equipment as required by its maintenance procedure. Prepare suitable labeled receiving containers before opening or draining the system.
  • Skim accessible floating tramp oil. Drain or transfer coolant through a suitable strainer to catch larger chips, keeping the destination consistent with the reuse or waste decision.
  • Remove accumulated sludge and chips with the approved tools. Clean accessible screens, filters and return passages; inspect for blocked flow and leaks.
  • Clean dried coolant residue with a compatible cleaner diluted to its labeled instructions. Use the specified contact time and cleaning method; do not invent a stronger mixture.
  • Remove the spent cleaning solution. Rinse and drain as the machine, cleaner and fluid suppliers specify; capture those liquids for the approved waste route. Account for retained liquid before refilling.
  • Reinstall components and guards. Prepare fresh coolant by adding concentrate to water at the product's specified concentration, then fill to the machine's operating level.
  • Restore and circulate the system according to its procedure. Check flow and leaks, measure concentration after mixing, and record the fluid condition, result and service performed.

For a public demonstration, watch Haas's Machine Tool Coolant: Cleaning Your Tank. Its examples distinguish a routine tank cleanout from cleaning an extensively contaminated coolant system. Haas's Machine Tool Coolant: Tools of Coolant is a companion resource.

Supporting detail: Addendum 69 — Supplier instructions determine the cleaning treatment.

Use the safety pages for contact, PPE and waste handling

Use the safety pages for contact, PPE and waste handling

Minimize skin contact with coolant and cleaning liquid. Use the SDS for the actual products and the PPE guidance for exposure control. Use Metal Chips and Swarf for removing and handling solids; this maintenance page does not replace those rules.

Manage spent coolant, removed oil, sludge and cleaning liquid through the approved regulated-waste process. Do not pour them down a drain or onto the ground. The responsible waste handler must determine the applicable classification and disposal route from the fluid, contaminants and local requirements. “Water-based” or “biodegradable” is not disposal permission.

Supporting detail: Addendum 70 — Why the waste route depends on what is in the tank.

Machining/Cutting Fluids

Cutting Fluids and Application Methods

Cutting fluids cool, lubricate, carry chips away and protect surfaces; match the fluid and its delivery to the tool, material and operation.

Cool the cut, reduce friction and carry chips away

Cool the cut, reduce friction and carry chips away

Coolant does more than cool. A cutting fluid removes heat from the cutting zone, lubricates contact between the tool, chip and workpiece, flushes loose chips away, and helps protect the machine and work against corrosion.

Lubrication can reduce material sticking to the cutting edge, called built-up edge. Together with cooling and chip removal, that can improve surface finish and dimensional control. Fluid cannot make up for a dull tool, poor workholding or unsuitable feeds and speeds.

The fluid must reach the cutting zone to do its job. A full tank with a blocked filter or a nozzle aimed away from the cut is not effective delivery.

Choose a fluid family for the operation

Choose a fluid family for the operation

Use a product approved for the machine, work material and tooling. These are general tendencies, not a product selection chart for a particular shop. Check compatibility with seals, coatings and the metals being cut.

FamilyStrength and typical useTradeoff
Straight oil (neat oil)Used without water dilution.
