Strong lubrication suits operations where sliding contact dominates, such as some tapping, broaching and slow cutting.Less cooling than water-based fluids; oil mist, smoke and fire risk depend on the product and process. Not suitable for every machine.
Soluble oil (emulsion)Concentrate disperses oil droplets in water. Combines lubrication with water's cooling for many general machining operations.Needs concentration and contamination control. Water quality affects stability; residue and foam can develop.
Semi-syntheticA water-diluted formulation with less mineral oil than a conventional soluble oil. Often balances cooling, lubrication and cleanliness in general machining.Still needs water-quality and sump maintenance. Foam, residue and compatibility depend on the formulation.
SyntheticA water-diluted formulation without mineral oil. Cooling and visibility can suit grinding and suitable machining operations.Lubrication depends on its additives; do not assume all synthetics suit heavy cutting. Concentration, corrosion protection and contamination still need attention.

Concentrate and working fluid are different. A supplier's oil-content figure for the concentrate is not the percentage to put in the tank. The working concentration comes from that product's technical data sheet.

Supporting detail: Addendum 71 — Why the family name does not settle performance.

Run dry, mist or flood according to the cutting setup

Run dry, mist or flood according to the cutting setup

  • Dry: use when the tool supplier's guidance for that material and operation calls for it. Some carbide milling benefits from avoiding repeated heating and sudden cooling of the edge. Dry does not mean chips or dust need no control.
  • Mist or minimum-quantity lubrication: a designed system meters a small amount of fluid toward the cut when lubrication and access matter more than bulk cooling. It does not provide flood-level heat removal or washing. Use the specified enclosure and mist control.
  • Flood: a continuous flow can remove heat and wash chips from the cut when the setup calls for wet machining. Supply enough flow to reach the edge consistently; a weak, intermittent splash is not the same thing.

Oil mist is liquid droplets carried by air, not a residue-free gas. Neither “all carbide runs dry” nor “more coolant is always better” is a useful rule. Follow the tool and machine guidance for the actual cut.

Supporting detail: Addendum 72 — Why some milling runs dry while other milling needs fluid.

Use Personal Protective Equipment and Metal Chips and Swarf for exposure and chip-handling rules. Continue with Coolant Concentration and Mixing and Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Choosing Shop Measuring Tools

Match the tool to the feature, the allowed size range, and the measurement you need to trust.

Choose from the tolerance and the shape of the feature

Choose from the tolerance and the shape of the feature

Start with what must be measured: an outside size, an opening, a depth, a height, or a small change from a reference.

As a rule of thumb, choose a tool that reads about ten times finer than the total tolerance. This is a starting point, not a standard or a guarantee that the measurement is good enough. Check its specified accuracy, condition, measuring range, and the way its contacts reach the part.

For a size of 0.625 ± 0.001 in, the total tolerance is 0.002 in. A starting resolution target is 0.002 / 10 = 0.0002 in. An outside micrometer reading 0.0001 in is a candidate for an accessible outside diameter. A 0.001 in caliper is too coarse for that rule of thumb.

See Tolerances and Fits for the allowed size range, Reading Measuring Scales for the numbers, and Reliable Shop Measurement for the technique.

Resolution is the increment; accuracy is agreement with a reference

Resolution is the increment; accuracy is agreement with a reference

Resolution
The smallest indicated change or scale increment. A display that changes by 0.0005 in has that resolution; its last digit is not an accuracy certificate.
Accuracy
How closely a measurement agrees with the reference value. Use the instrument's error specification and checks against suitable standards to judge its capability.
Precision
How closely repeated measurements agree under stated conditions. A dirty measuring face can give repeatable readings that are all wrong.

Extra digits cannot remove jaw wear, a tilted contact, dirt, or heat. Record the instrument and units along with the result when the measurement matters.

Use a steel rule for layout and quick size checks

Use a steel rule for layout and quick size checks

A steel rule is useful for stock lengths, approximate sizes, and setting a divider. Read the graduation pattern on the edge you are using: fractional edges may divide an inch into 8, 16, 32, or 64 parts; decimal edges may use 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, or 0.01 in increments. A decimal rule does not ordinarily have 0.001 in graduations.

Place the rule along the distance being measured and look straight at the marks. A damaged end is a poor zero. If you start at the 1 in line instead, subtract 1 in from the far-end reading. Do not use a rule to accept a feature with a tight size tolerance.

Calipers cover outside, inside, depth, and step measurements

Calipers cover outside, inside, depth, and step measurements

Dial, digital, and vernier calipers use a sliding jaw. The larger jaws measure outside sizes; the smaller jaws measure openings. A depth rod reaches down from the end of the beam. On tools with step faces, the back shoulders measure a step.

The readout changes how you read the tool, not how carefully you must position it.
ReadoutUse and readingWatch for
DialQuick mechanical reading: beam scale plus dial remainder.Check the marked value per revolution. Dirt in the rack can disturb the reading.
DigitalDirect numerical display; often offers inch/mm and relative zero.Confirm units and zero mode. Resolution varies by model; a common display increment is 0.0005 in / 0.01 mm.
VernierMain scale plus the aligned vernier division; no battery or dial mechanism.Read the correct scale and its least count. Inch 0.001 in tools can use different main-scale spacings.

Use light contact and keep the jaws square. Measure near the beam where access allows. Long jaws can flex; small inside jaws may not reach the true diameter of a small hole. A caliper's versatility does not make it the best tool for every tolerance.

Micrometers specialize in outside sizes, inside sizes, or depths

Micrometers specialize in outside sizes, inside sizes, or depths

An outside micrometer measures between a fixed anvil and a moving spindle. Choose a range that contains the dimension: a 1–2 in instrument does not start from zero like a 0–1 in instrument. A conventional inch scale reads 0.001 in; a sleeve vernier can add 0.0001 in readings. A conventional metric scale reads 0.01 mm. Digital models differ.

An inside micrometer spans an opening using internal contacts. Rod and two-point types require careful alignment; three-point types have a different contact arrangement. Check the reference and any extension length for the actual tool.

A depth micrometer rests its flat base on the reference face and extends a rod to the lower surface. Keep the base seated. Check the installed rod's range and the scale direction: many depth scales run opposite to an outside micrometer. Do not add a rod length without checking how that instrument is marked.

Indicators show change from a reference

Indicators show change from a reference

A dial indicator commonly has a plunger moving along its axis. A test indicator has a pivoting lever stylus and usually a shorter measuring range. Both are useful for alignment, comparing heights, and observing runout as a part turns.

Read the marked graduation and count revolutions where needed. Zeroing the bezel sets a reference; it does not turn the indicator into an absolute diameter tool. Total indicator reading, or TIR, is the maximum indication minus the minimum during a sweep. From −0.001 to +0.002 in, TIR is 0.003 in.

Use a rigid stand. A magnetic base needs a suitable magnetic support; it will not attach magnetically to granite. For plunger indicators, align motion with the plunger. For lever test indicators, follow the maker's stylus-angle instructions; the lever is normally close to parallel with the surface. These are different geometries.

Supporting detail: Addendum 73 — What a sweep can and cannot establish.

Gauge blocks supply a reference; transfer gauges carry a size; Practice

Gauge blocks supply a reference; transfer gauges carry a size

Gauge blocks have accurately finished opposing faces and a known length. Use suitable blocks to set a height, compare a measurement, or check an instrument. Clean and inspect the faces before wringing blocks together; follow their care instructions. A zero check alone is not a full calibration.

Build stacks from sizes actually present in the set. For example, 1.0000 + 0.1340 + 0.1005 = 1.2345 in uses three blocks if those sizes are available. Do not assume a set contains separate 0.0040 or 0.0005 in blocks.

A telescoping gauge transfers a bore size to an outside micrometer. With light locking friction, set the contacts slightly across the bore at an angle and sweep gently through the diameter; withdraw without changing the setting, then measure across the contacts. Follow the tool's instructions for locking and repeat until the technique is consistent.

A small-hole gauge expands rounded contacts inside a smaller opening. Adjust for light drag, withdraw as its design permits, and measure across the contacts with a micrometer. Neither transfer tool has its own numerical readout. Take readings at several depths and directions; keep them separate to reveal taper or out-of-roundness rather than averaging the shape away.

Practice choosing a tool

Supporting detail: Addendum 74 — Instrument references.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Reading Measuring Scales

Read rules, micrometers, calipers, and verniers by separating the coarse scale from the remainder.

Read the unit and the graduation before the number

Read the unit and the graduation before the number

The same-looking line can mean 0.025 in, 0.5 mm, or something else. Identify the instrument and its scale before adding anything.

On a fractional rule, count spaces from the last whole inch using that edge's denominator. Seven 1/16 in spaces beyond 2 in gives 2 + 7/16 = 2.4375 in. That exact fraction-to-decimal conversion does not make the rule accurate to four decimal places.

On a decimal rule with 0.01 in spaces, eight spaces beyond 1.20 in gives 1.28 in. On a digital caliper, read the displayed unit and confirm whether the tool shows an absolute size or a deviation from a stored zero.

In inch shop speech, a thou is 0.001 in and a tenth often means 0.0001 in, one tenth of a thousandth. Write units and decimals to avoid confusing a shop tenth with 0.1 in.

An inch micrometer adds sleeve plus thimble

An inch micrometer adds sleeve plus thimble

For the conventional 0.001 in micrometer, one turn advances the spindle 0.025 in. The sleeve has a line every 0.025 in; each fourth line marks another 0.100 in. The thimble divides one turn into 25 spaces of 0.001 in.

  1. Read the last sleeve line reached by the thimble edge. Count the 0.100 in intervals and the extra 0.025 in lines.
  2. Read the thimble line at the sleeve's horizontal datum line.
  3. Add the two. Include the range offset for a larger micrometer according to its markings.

Example: sleeve 0.300 in plus two 0.025 in lines, with thimble 18 at the datum:

0.300 + 0.050 + 0.018 = 0.368 in

Watch the rollover. Sleeve 0.375 and thimble 24 gives 0.399 in. The next 0.001 in step gives sleeve 0.400 and thimble 0: 0.400 in. Do not add the old 0.025 in interval again.

A vernier micrometer adds the fourth decimal place

A vernier micrometer adds the fourth decimal place

The sleeve vernier divides a thimble space into ten parts. Read the sleeve and the whole 0.001 in thimble amount first, using the thimble graduation just passed when the datum falls between lines. Then find the sleeve vernier line that aligns with a thimble line.

Example: the last sleeve line is 0.450 in, the datum is between thimble 12 and 13, and sleeve vernier line 7 aligns:

0.4500 + 0.0120 + 7 × 0.0001 = 0.4627 in

The matching vernier line adds 0.0007 in, not 0.007 in. Do not round the thimble to 13 and then add the vernier. If the zero line aligns, add zero; the end line represents the same alignment at the next interval.

A metric micrometer includes the exposed half millimeter

A metric micrometer includes the exposed half millimeter

On a conventional 0.01 mm micrometer, one turn moves the spindle 0.5 mm. The sleeve shows whole millimeters and half-millimeter marks; 50 thimble spaces divide the turn into 0.01 mm increments.

If 8 mm and the following 0.5 mm mark are exposed, and thimble 23 aligns, the reading is 8 + 0.5 + 0.23 = 8.73 mm. If that half-millimeter mark is still covered, the same thimble position gives 8.23 mm.

At the rollover, 8.49 mm is sleeve 8.0 plus thimble 49; 8.50 mm is sleeve 8.5 plus thimble 0. Use the marked unit; these increments are not the inch micrometer's increments converted by eye.

A 0.001 in vernier caliper adds the aligned division

A 0.001 in vernier caliper adds the aligned division

For the 25-division inch vernier used here, each main-scale space is 0.025 in. Twenty-five vernier spaces occupy the length of 24 main-scale spaces, so each vernier space is 0.024 in. Their 0.001 in difference makes the fine reading possible.

  1. Read the last main-scale line at or before the vernier zero.
  2. Find the vernier division that lines up with a main-scale line.
  3. Add its division number × 0.001 in.

Vernier zero just beyond 1.325 in, with division 17 aligned, gives 1.325 + 0.017 = 1.342 in. It is the vernier zero, not the right end of the slider, that locates the coarse reading.

Supporting detail: Addendum 75 — Other 0.001 in verniers can have different spacing.

A dial caliper adds the beam reading and the dial remainder

A dial caliper adds the beam reading and the dial remainder

On an inch dial caliper marked 0.100 in per revolution, the dial's 100 divisions each represent 0.001 in. Read whole inches and completed 0.100 in intervals on the beam, then add the dial reading.

Beam 1.200 in and dial 47 gives 1.200 + 0.047 = 1.247 in. Beam 1.200 plus dial 99 is 1.299 in. At the next thousandth the beam reaches 1.300 and the dial returns to zero.

Some dial calipers use a different travel per revolution. Check the dial markings rather than assuming this example applies. Clean the jaws, close gently, check zero, and confirm the reading again after measuring.

Practice reading a new micrometer or vernier scale; Interactive; Practice

Practice reading a new micrometer or vernier scale

The trainer draws ideal scales with zero error. It teaches reading, not instrument accuracy. Micrometer examples stay within 0–1 in; caliper examples stay below 2 in. Enter the exact indicated reading in inches.

Read these scale positions before uncovering the answers. These examples also serve as the print version of the trainer.

  1. Inch micrometer: sleeve 0.275 in, thimble 24 at the datum.
  2. Vernier micrometer: sleeve 0.275 in, datum between thimble 24 and 0, vernier line 9 aligned.
  3. 25-division vernier caliper: zero past main line 1.150 in, division 8 aligned.
Readings as sums

1. 0.275 + 0.024 = 0.299 in.
2. 0.2750 + 0.0240 + 0.0009 = 0.2999 in.
3. 1.150 + 0.008 = 1.158 in.

Add a micrometer reading to practice Add a vernier reading to practice

Supporting detail: Addendum 76 — Reading references.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Reliable Shop Measurement

Control zero, contact force, alignment, cleanliness, and temperature before trusting the last digit.

Clean, check, measure, and check again; Checklist

Clean, check, measure, and check again

A good reading starts before the scale is read. Use this sequence with the instrument's own instructions.

  • Identify the feature, its limits, and its reference surfaces. Choose a suitable measuring tool.
  • Clean the contact faces and the part. Look for chips, dirt, raised burrs, and damage that would hold the contacts apart.
  • Let the part and instrument settle to the measuring environment. Avoid a freshly cut hot part or a tool warmed by long handling.
  • Check zero or the correct setting reference. Close a 0–1 in outside micrometer gently; use the appropriate setting standard for larger ranges or inside tools.
  • For a critical size, check a suitable known reference near the working size as well. Confirm the instrument is within its required calibration status.
  • Measure with the intended contact force and alignment. Release and repeat to check that you can reproduce the reading.
  • Record the result with units, location, and enough method information to repeat it. Check zero again afterward; investigate any change.

Zero adjustment removes an offset at one position. It cannot repair worn jaws, a damaged screw, or an error that changes along the range. If a tool fails its checks, have it evaluated rather than hiding the error with a new zero.

Use consistent light contact instead of squeezing out a number

Use consistent light contact instead of squeezing out a number

With a micrometer, bring the faces close, then use the ratchet or friction thimble as its maker directs. These devices help repeat the measuring force. They do not make dirt, tilt, or a flexible part disappear.

Use a smooth, slow approach. The required clicks or turns depend on the mechanism; a friction thimble may slip without clicking. Do not force the main thimble after the force-limiting device operates. The spindle lock holds a setting; it is not a clamp for tightening the measurement.

With a caliper or transfer gauge, feel means consistent light contact or drag, not a hard squeeze. Too much force bends jaws and compresses thin parts. Repeated readings should agree because the setup is repeatable, not because the tool has been forced to the expected number.

Keep contacts square and look straight at the scale

Keep contacts square and look straight at the scale

A tilted instrument can span a diagonal rather than the intended distance. For an outside diameter, keep the measuring direction perpendicular to the cylinder's axis. For a two-point inside measurement, the contacts must pass through the bore center in the cross-section while staying square along its length. A single instruction to “always find the largest” or “always find the smallest” does not cover both alignment directions.

Parallax is a reading error from looking at separated scales at an angle: the marks appear to shift against each other. Put your eye square to the reading line. Good lighting helps distinguish a line from a reflection.

For an indicator, keep its intended motion and contact geometry aligned. Preload enough to maintain contact throughout the expected movement, while staying within its usable travel. Do not apply a universal number of needle turns to both plunger and lever instruments.

Abbe error grows when tilt acts through an offset

Abbe error grows when tilt acts through an offset

The scale on a caliper runs along the beam, while the part often touches farther down the jaws. If the moving jaw tilts a little, its tip moves more than the scale location does. The scale misses that extra motion. This is Abbe error.

Picture a door: a small rotation moves the handle much farther than a point near the hinge. Greater distance between the measurement line and the scale line gives tilt more room to create error.

Keep the part near the beam when access permits, use light contact, and avoid loose or worn sliders. An ordinary outside micrometer puts its measurement and screw axes in line, reducing this particular source of error. Alignment still matters.

Supporting detail: Addendum 77 — The offset-and-angle relationship.

Temperature and surface condition can move the result

Temperature and surface condition can move the result

Parts and instruments change size with temperature. Let them approach the same stable measuring conditions; follow the reference temperature and corrections required by the inspection procedure. Avoid direct sun, drafts, and prolonged hand contact with precision tools.

Clean contact faces matter because the instrument measures what touches them. A chip can enlarge an apparent outside size; a raised edge can hold a depth-micrometer base above its reference. Surface peaks can affect contact too. See Surface Texture and Finish for surface condition rather than treating every last-digit change as a size change.

Measure at several positions when taper or out-of-roundness matters. Keep the individual values. An average can hide an oversize region and does not prove the whole feature meets its limits.

For the operating rules around machines, use Equipment Operating Procedure and Machine Hazards and Housekeeping. For the numerical limits themselves, use Tolerances and Fits.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Shop Layout and Angle Measurement

Carry dimensions from a reference onto the work with clear lines, checked centers, and correctly read angles.

Start layout from a reference you can return to

Start layout from a reference you can return to

Layout places lines, arcs, and points on a part to guide cutting or locate features. A neat line is useful only when it is in the right place.

Identify the reference surfaces from which dimensions are taken. Keep using those references rather than measuring each new line from the last one. A layout mark guides the work; it does not prove the finished part is within tolerance.

A surface plate supplies a reference plane for layout and inspection. Clean the plate, the part's supporting face, and the tool base. Support the part so it cannot rock. Use an appropriate angle plate or V-block when the shape needs support.

Protect the plate from impact and abrasive work. Its flatness depends on its size, grade, condition, and calibration; “a surface plate” does not imply one universal accuracy. Follow its specified support arrangement. Level and flat are different: leveling a plate does not repair a worn surface.

Dye makes a fine scribed line easier to see

Dye makes a fine scribed line easier to see

Layout dye adds contrast. Prepare the surface, apply a thin coating as directed, and let it dry before marking. Use Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets for chemical handling guidance.

A scriber scratches a narrow line through the coating. Hold the guide firmly and draw the point along it with light, consistent pressure. Repeated passes can make a wide, ambiguous mark. Scribe only where the drawing and process allow a permanent scratch.

A surface gage carries an adjustable scriber at a fixed height above its base. Set it from a separate height reference, then move the base along the plate to scribe a line parallel to that plane. A surface gage ordinarily has no direct height scale.

A height gage adds a scale or readout. Set its reference correctly, seat the base flat, set and lock the height as intended, and make the line. With a suitable probe it can compare or measure heights. It is not simply another name for a depth gage.

Supporting detail: Addendum 78 — Finding the middle of two heights.

Dividers and trammels carry a distance into an arc

Dividers and trammels carry a distance into an arc

Dividers have two pointed legs. Set their spacing from a suitable scale, hold one point at the center, and swing the other to mark a circle or arc. They can also transfer or step off equal distances.

Trammels put adjustable points on a beam for radii too large for ordinary dividers. Lock the points after setting, support the beam, and check the spacing again before marking.

The point spacing is the radius, not the diameter. For a 3.00 in diameter circle, set 1.50 in between points. Recheck transferred dimensions against the original reference; repeated stepping can accumulate error.

Prick-punch the location; center-punch after checking it

Prick-punch the location; center-punch after checking it

A prick punch has a sharper point for a small, precise location mark at intersecting layout lines. A center punch makes a wider depression to help start a drilling operation. Point angles vary by tool; the important distinction here is the fine locating mark versus the wider starting mark.

Locate the point carefully, bring the punch upright, and make a light mark. Check the location before enlarging it. A heavy first mark is difficult to correct. Support the work on a suitable punching support, away from the precision surface plate.

A punch mark is not a substitute for the machine setup or spotting method needed to locate a hole accurately. Check the finished feature with a suitable measuring method. Use Personal Protective Equipment and Equipment Operating Procedure for the applicable shop rules.

Supporting detail: Addendum 79 — Punch types and their uses.

A combination set uses one blade with three different heads

A combination set uses one blade with three different heads

Square head
Provides 90° and 45° reference faces. With the blade it can lay out right angles, check squareness, or establish an offset or depth. Seat the reference face fully before reading or scribing.
Center head
Its two faces seat on round stock, positioning the blade along a diameter. Scribe one line, rotate the work or head, and scribe another; their intersection locates the center on the end face.
Protractor head
Sets the blade to an angle on a graduated head. Read the scale in the correct direction, lock the setting, and recheck contact with the reference.

Clean the mating faces and blade groove so the head seats properly. Pick the tool's accuracy for the task: a combination set is useful for layout, but it does not automatically replace a precision square or a finer angle instrument.

A universal bevel transfers an angle; a vernier protractor reads it; Practice

A universal bevel transfers an angle; a vernier protractor reads it

A universal bevel has an adjustable blade and stock that can fit against two surfaces. Lock it to transfer or compare an angle. A plain bevel has no numerical scale; obtain the angle from a separate reference.

A vernier bevel protractor combines the adjustable blade with degree and vernier scales. On a 5-minute instrument, each matching vernier division adds 5 arcminutes. 60 minutes = 1 degree, so 5 minutes is 1/12 degree. This is the reading increment, not a universal accuracy claim.

  1. Seat the stock and blade against the intended surfaces. Identify the angle being measured.
  2. Read the whole degrees between the main zero and the vernier zero.
  3. Use the vernier on the same side and in the same reading direction as those degrees. Find the matching division.
  4. Add the matching division number × 5 minutes to the whole degrees.

Example: 32 whole degrees and the seventh matching vernier division give 32° + 7 × 5′ = 32°35′. That is 32 + 35/60 = 32.5833…°, not 32.35°.

Check the contact geometry before reporting an obtuse angle. If the instrument has measured the acute supplement, a reading of 32°35′ corresponds to 180° − 32°35′ = 147°25′ for the required obtuse angle. Do not automatically subtract every reading from 180°.

Practice bevel-protractor readings

Supporting detail: Addendum 80 — Why the 5-minute vernier works.

Check the layout before making a permanent cut; Checklist

Check the layout before making a permanent cut

  • Confirm the reference surfaces and dimension directions.
  • Check each line or center from the intended reference, including radius versus diameter.
  • Verify the height or angle after locking the tool.
  • Check the mark before punching more deeply or beginning the cut.
  • Plan how to measure the finished feature; use Choosing Shop Measuring Tools and Tolerances and Fits.

Drawing views and dimensioning conventions belong in the Engineering Graphics collection. Layout follows those requirements; it does not redefine them.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Surface Texture and Finish

A machined surface has a lay, a waviness and a roughness; a stylus trace and a filter turn them into Ra, Rz and Rt, and a drawing symbol says what is required and how the surface may be made.

A surface has lay, waviness and roughness

A surface has lay, waviness and roughness

Every manufactured surface carries marks from the process that made it. Surface texture describes those marks: which way they run, how far apart they are, and how tall they stand.

Roughness
The finest, closely spaced marks, such as the feed marks a cutting tool leaves at each pass or the scratches of abrasive grit.
Waviness
A longer, gentler undulation that the roughness sits on, for example from vibration or deflection while the part was made.
Lay
The direction of the main surface pattern, set by how the tool or the part moved.
Form
The overall shape, such as a face that is slightly curved. Size and geometric tolerances control form; surface texture is what is left on top of it.
A stylus traces one line, and a filter splits it; Watch out

A stylus traces one line, and a filter splits it

A contact instrument drags a fine stylus along a straight line and records its height. That record is the measured profile. Everything else is worked out from it.

Trace direction
Usually across the lay, so the stylus crosses the marks. If the drawing specifies a measuring direction, that direction governs.
Mean line
A smooth line the filter draws through the measured profile, a weighted average of the heights around each point. This mean line is the waviness.
Cutoff λc
The wavelength where the filter splits the profile. Undulations much longer than λc stay in the mean line; marks much shorter than λc are left over for the roughness. A wave exactly λc long is shared half and half.
Roughness profile
The measured profile minus the mean line.
Evaluation length
The part of the trace the numbers come from. In this lab it is five sections, each λc long. The trace runs one more λc at each end so the filter has heights on both sides of every evaluated point.

The filter decides what counts as roughness, not the size of the undulation. Change λc and the same undulation can move from the waviness into the roughness. That is why a measurement result needs its cutoff, and why a drawing or its standard says which one applies.

Ra, Rz and Rt read the roughness differently

Ra, Rz and Rt read the roughness differently

All three come from the same roughness profile. They answer different questions about it. This lab uses the older ISO 4287 convention with five sections for Rz; the drawing-symbol comparison separately shows older and current graphics.

Ra
The average distance of the roughness profile from its mean line over the evaluation length. Peaks and valleys count alike.
Rz
The average of the sections’ peak-to-valley heights. Each section counts once, whatever is in it.
Rt
The largest peak-to-valley height over the whole evaluation length: the single highest peak to the single deepest valley.

Ra = average of |roughness| over the evaluation length

Rz = (Z1 + Z2 + Z3 + Z4 + Z5) ÷ 5

For the trace above: Ra 1.55 µm; Rz = (6.55 + 6.56 + 6.70 + 6.57 + 6.87) ÷ 5 = 6.65 µm; Rt 7.10 µm.

The values are in micrometres (µm). They can also be given in microinches (µin): one inch is exactly 25.4 mm, so 1 µin is exactly 0.0254 µm, and Ra 1.6 µm is 63.0 µin.

Name the standard. Current documents use the ISO 21920 series. Many existing drawings and instruments use the older ISO 4287 parameters and ISO 1302 symbols. The names Ra, Rz and Rt carried over, but the standards are not identical, so this page says which one each symbol comes from and does not mix them. For a real part, check which standard the drawing invokes.

Surface texture lab: trace a surface and hold it to a drawing; Interactive

Surface texture lab: trace a surface and hold it to a drawing

Change the surface, the trace and the drawing, and watch the numbers. Start with experiment 1.

  • The block is a few millimetres of surface. Lines are the crests of the marks; the blue line is the stylus trace, solid over the evaluation length.
  • The plots are that trace: the measured profile with its mean line, then the roughness profile with its five sections.
  • The drawing holds one requirement against this one trace and writes it as a callout in the view you choose.
Parallel marks 0.2 mm apart, mark height 6 µm, λc 0.8 mm unless stated. Teaching surfaces, not predictions for any process.

The same-Ra experiment is the figure in the next section.

Same Ra, different surfaces

Same Ra, different surfaces

These three roughness profiles all have Ra 1.6 µm. They are not the same surface. All three plots use the same height scale.

  • Ra alone cannot tell these apart.
  • Rz separates the rounded marks from the other two, but not flat tops from narrow peaks.
  • Where the extremes sit, above or below the mean line, separates those two.

One number does not describe a surface. That is why a drawing names the parameter, not just a value.

Reading a surface texture symbol

Reading a surface texture symbol

The symbol’s point touches the line that represents the surface in a drawing view. Its shape says how the surface may be made; the text beside it says what texture is required.

The three process requirements, in the older and the current graphics. Schematic drawings: the standards dimension the symbols exactly.
SymbolOlder, ISO 1302Current, ISO 21920-1Meaning
BasicAny manufacturing process is permitted. This does not forbid machining; it simply does not require it.
BarMaterial removal is required: the surface must be produced by removing material, for example by machining.
CircleMaterial removal is prohibited: the surface must not be machined or otherwise have material removed to meet this requirement.
Current or older
An ISO 21920-1 symbol carries a short separate dash above the short leg, touching neither leg. The older ISO 1302 graphic has none, so the familiar older marks are not the current symbols unchanged.
The requirement
The parameter and its limit, such as Ra 3.2, sit below the long line, to the right of the long leg, in both.
The lay
In an ISO 21920-1 callout the process and the lay sit above the long line. In the older symbols the lay symbol sits beside the long leg, below the line.

A complete specification can state more than this page draws, such as the measuring direction. The process mark is a requirement about how the surface is made; a profile measurement checks the texture, not whether material was removed.

Lay symbols belong to the drawing view

Lay symbols belong to the drawing view

A lay symbol says which way the marks run. = and ⊥ are judged against the plane of projection of the view the symbol is drawn in, not against the page or the screen.

The first two figures are the same surface. Its marks run front to back: parallel to the right side view’s plane of projection, so = there, and perpendicular to the front view’s, so ⊥ there. The arrow shows which way each view looks.

Lay and trace direction are different things. The lay says how the marks run. The trace direction says how they were measured; it is usually across the lay unless the drawing specifies one.

The lay symbols and meanings here are those of ISO 1302:2002.

Older notation: N grades and triangle marks; Interactive

Older notation: N grades and triangle marks

Older drawings may give a roughness grade number or a row of triangles instead of a parameter and value.

Roughness grade numbers

Each grade number stands for one Ra value. A grade is an Ra value: it does not convert to Rz.

Grade numbers and the Ra values they stand for. Microinches are exact conversions, rounded for display.

Triangle marks

One catalog prints a comparison of downward triangle marks with Ra values, under the heading “Extract from JIS B 0601-2001”. It calls the comparison approximate, not rigorous. It gives no acceptance limits, no dates for the marks, and no Rz equivalents, so read it as a rough historical guide.

One requirement, four ways

Slide the Ra limit and compare the current symbol, the older symbol, the grade number and the triangle marks for the same value.

Read the callout; Interactive

Read the callout

Ten short questions on the symbols, the lay, the older notations and what the numbers respond to.

  1. The older ISO 1302 symbol with a circle in its V, and Ra 3.2. May this surface be machined to reach Ra 3.2 µm? No: material removal is prohibited. The circle in the V prohibits material removal. Material removal is prohibited: the surface must not be machined or otherwise have material removed to meet this requirement.
  2. A current symbol with an open V, no connecting material-removal crossbar or circle, a separate identifying dash above the short leg, and Ra 6.3. Does this callout forbid machining the surface? No, any process is permitted. The V has no connecting material-removal crossbar or circle: it is the basic symbol. The separate floating dash identifies ISO 21920; it does not require machining. Any manufacturing process is permitted. This does not forbid machining; it simply does not require it.
  3. A symbol with a bar closing its V, a short separate dash above the short leg, and Ra 0.8. Which standard's graphic is this? ISO 21920-1 (current). The short separate dash above the short leg, touching neither leg, marks an ISO 21920-1 symbol. The older ISO 1302 graphic has no dash.
  4. A block of surface whose marks run front to back. An arrow shows the right side view looking at its right side. The marks run front to back. Which lay symbol belongs on this surface in the right side view? =. The right side view looks along the arrow. Marks running front to back are parallel to that view's plane of projection, so the symbol is =. The same surface takes ⊥ in the front view: the symbol depends on the view, not on the screen or page.
  5. A block of surface whose marks run front to back. An arrow shows the front view looking at its front. The marks run front to back. Which lay symbol belongs on this surface in the front view? ⊥. The front view looks along the arrow. Marks running front to back are perpendicular to that view's plane of projection, so the symbol is ⊥. The same surface takes = in the right side view: the symbol depends on the view, not on the screen or page.
  6. The grade number N8. An older drawing gives grade N8. What does that stand for? Ra 3.2 µm. N8 stands for Ra 3.2 µm (126 µin). Each step of the grade number doubles or halves the Ra value, near enough.
  7. Three downward triangles. In the catalog comparison, which Ra values sit beside three triangles? 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 µm. Three triangles sit beside Ra 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 µm. The catalog calls this comparison approximate, not rigorous. Read it as a rough historical guide, not as acceptance limits.
  8. A current symbol with Rz 6.3. Which N grade means the same as this Rz 6.3 µm requirement? None: grades are Ra values. Grade numbers each stand for an Ra value; N9 is Ra 6.3 µm, not Rz 6.3 µm. Ra and Rz measure different things, and how they compare depends on the shape of the profile, as the same-Ra experiment in the lab shows.
  9. One deep scratch crosses this otherwise even trace. Which number has the largest proportional change? Rt. In the lab, a scratch three times the mark height takes Rt from 7.10 to 23.4 µm, Rz from 6.65 to 10.5 µm and Ra from 1.55 to 1.88 µm. Rt spans the highest peak to the deepest valley over the whole length. Rz averages five section heights, diluting localized extremes; filtering can spread a scratch across section boundaries. Ra averages every point.
  10. A block of surface with parallel marks running front to back, and a stylus trace running left to right across them. The trace on this surface crosses the marks. Traced along the marks instead, Ra would be: Much smaller. In the lab, Ra is 1.55 µm across the marks and 0.328 µm along them: the stylus misses the marks when it runs beside them. Tracing across the lay is the usual choice, but a direction the drawing specifies governs.
What this lab leaves out

What this lab leaves out

The lab is a teaching model of one straight trace. A real measurement and a real acceptance decision involve more:

  • The instrument. A real stylus has a tip radius, and instruments apply a short-wavelength filter and remove the part’s form before filtering. The lab’s stylus is sharp and its part is flat.
  • The filter and parameters. This lab follows the older ISO 4287 teaching convention of five sections for Rz, with a Gaussian mean line having 50% transmission at λc. Dense samples resolve the narrow marks; numerical integration on a coarser grid computes the smooth mean line. This is not a compliant instrument or a complete ISO 21920 inspection setup, and a drawing or standard can call for other settings.
  • The decision. The lab compares one trace with one limit. The drawing and its standard say how many traces are taken, where, and how the results are judged.
  • The process. No trace shows whether material was removed. The process requirement is checked against how the part was made.
  • Scratches and pits. Whether an isolated flaw counts against a texture requirement is for the drawing and its standard to say.
  • Symbols. The drawings are schematic. The lay symbols are those of ISO 1302:2002; the lab writes the same symbols in the ISO 21920-1 lay position. Check the current standard before relying on one there. Inch-drawing (ASME) practice is not covered here.

Sources

  • ISO 21920-1:2021 preview (section 6.2, Figure 4)
  • ZEISS surface parameter poster
  • Mitutoyo, Surface Roughness Measurement (DIN EN ISO 4287:1998 parameters)
  • KEYENCE, surface roughness symbols and lay (ISO 1302:2002)
  • DIATEST Metrologist Reference Book, roughness grade numbers (printed p. 62)
  • MISUMI catalog, printed p. 518: comparison headed "Extract from JIS B 0601-2001"
