Machining/Measurement and Fit

Tolerances and Fits

The permitted size ranges on a hole and a shaft decide whether the two have clearance, interference, or could have either.

A size tolerance gives two limits

A size tolerance gives two limits

Manufacturing produces variation. For each diameter in this lab, the drawing gives a size between two limits. A measured diameter inside that interval passes this size check.

Nominal size
The size a feature is named by, such as Ø0.7500 in. Ø means diameter. Every limit is measured from this number.
Deviation
How far a limit sits above (+) or below (−) nominal. +0.0010 puts a limit 0.0010 in above it.
Limits
Nominal plus each deviation: the largest and smallest sizes that pass inspection. Ø0.7500 +0.0010 / 0.0000 means anything from 0.7500 in to 0.7510 in.
Tolerance
The width of that range: largest limit minus smallest limit. Here, 0.0010 in.

A size exactly on a limit passes. On this page the limits are part of the allowed range: a 0.7500 in hole and a 0.7510 in hole are both good. A 0.7511 in hole is not.

Clearance is the hole size minus the shaft size

Clearance is the hole size minus the shaft size

Put a shaft in a hole and the number that decides the fit is the difference between their two diameters.

clearance = hole size − shaft size

  • Positive: the hole is bigger. There is a gap, and the shaft slides in.
  • Negative: the shaft is bigger. That is interference: on paper the parts overlap, so the shaft has to be pressed in, or it does not go at all.
  • Zero: exactly the same size, called line-to-line. No gap and no overlap.

Clearance is measured across the whole diameter. With the shaft centred in the hole, the gap you would see on each side is half of it:

gap on each side = clearance ÷ 2

Three kinds of fit, decided by the two worst cases

Three kinds of fit, decided by the two worst cases

You do not have to check every pair of parts a drawing allows. Two pairs settle it: the tightest and the loosest.

Tightest legal pair
The smallest hole with the largest shaft. Its clearance is the least any good pair can have:
hole minimum − shaft maximum
Loosest legal pair
The largest hole with the smallest shaft. Its clearance is the most any good pair can have:
hole maximum − shaft minimum
The fit is named by where those two numbers land.
FitTightest pairLoosest pairWhat it means
Clearancegap, or exactly zerogapNo permitted pair has dimensional overlap. Equality has no gap.
TransitionoverlapgapSome good pairs slide together; some have to be pressed.
Interferenceoverlapoverlap, or exactly zeroNo permitted pair has a positive gap. Equality has no overlap.

The zero cases are deliberate. When the tightest pair comes out at exactly zero, every good pair either has a gap or just meets, so this page counts it as a clearance fit and the lab marks it zero at the limit. The same goes the other way for interference.

Fit lab: make two parts, then try them together; Interactive

Fit lab: make two parts, then try them together

Pick a drawing, then set the size each part actually came out at. Watch whether each part passes inspection, and whether the two go together.

  • The section view is the pair you made, cut in half. The gold and blue bands are where each wall is allowed to be.
  • The pair map is every pair the drawing allows. Anything above the diagonal has a shaft bigger than its hole.
The lab’s example drawings. All are made-up teaching limits on a Ø0.7500 in nominal, not values from any standard.
DrawingHole limitsShaft limitsTightest pairLoosest pairFit
Slides freely0.7500 to 0.75100.7480 to 0.7490+0.0010+0.0030Clearance
Could go either way0.7500 to 0.75100.7498 to 0.7506−0.0006+0.0012Transition
Pressed together0.7500 to 0.75100.7515 to 0.7525−0.0025−0.0005Interference
Two good parts can still make a bad pair; Watch out

Two good parts can still make a bad pair

Checking each diameter against its own limits does not by itself check the clearance of the selected pair.

Take the transition drawing from the lab: holes from 0.7500 to 0.7510 in, shafts from 0.7498 to 0.7506 in.

Hole made at 0.7502
Inside 0.7500 to 0.7510. Passes.
Shaft made at 0.7505
Inside 0.7498 to 0.7506. Passes.
Together
0.7502 − 0.7505 = −0.0003 in. The shaft is bigger than the hole. They overlap.

Neither part is wrong. The drawing allows that pair, and that is what transition fit allows. To exclude dimensional overlap for every permitted pair, the tightest pair must have zero clearance or more. To guarantee a positive dimensional gap, it must be greater than zero. Neither check by itself guarantees assembly: shape, surface finish, temperature and the assembly method also matter.

Call the fit from the drawing alone; Interactive

Call the fit from the drawing alone

Read the two callouts, work out the tightest and loosest pairs, and call it before you look.

Five drawings, each on a Ø0.7500 in nominal. Work out the limits, then the tightest and loosest pairs. The answer follows each one.

  1. Hole +0.0012 / 0.0000, shaft −0.0004 / −0.0011. Clearance: +0.0004 to +0.0023.
  2. Hole +0.0008 / 0.0000, shaft +0.0010 / +0.0003. Transition: −0.0010 to +0.0005.
  3. Hole +0.0006 / 0.0000, shaft +0.0018 / +0.0012. Interference: −0.0018 to −0.0006.
  4. Hole +0.0010 / 0.0000, shaft 0.0000 / −0.0007. Clearance, zero at the limit: 0.0000 to +0.0017.
  5. Hole +0.0015 / +0.0005, shaft +0.0007 / −0.0003. Transition: −0.0002 to +0.0018.
What this lab leaves out

What this lab leaves out

The lab compares two diameters and nothing else. A real assembly also depends on:

  • Shape. No hole is perfectly round or straight, and no shaft is either. A shaft can measure in tolerance everywhere a micrometer touches it and still be bent too far to go in.
  • Temperature. Parts grow when they warm up, so the same part can measure differently straight off the machine and an hour later.
  • Surface finish and measurement. A rough surface and an imperfect measurement both blur the last decimal place the drawing asks for.
  • Force. Whether an interference pair can be pressed together, how hard, and what that does to the parts are questions about the material, not about the two sizes.

The limits in the lab are made-up teaching values. Real drawings often take limits from published tables of standard fits; those tables are not reproduced here.

For measuring a real part, start with choosing a measuring tool, reading its scale, and checking the measurement method. See Shop Layout and Angle Measurement for transferring dimensions onto the work.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Automated Manufacturing Cells

See how programmed machining, tool changes, pallet handling and robots work together—and what must be reliable before unattended production makes sense.

NC and CNC put machining motions under program control

NC and CNC put machining motions under program control

Numerical control (NC) directs machine actions using coded instructions. Computer numerical control (CNC) uses a computer-based controller to execute those instructions. This is a base for automation, not a promise that loading, inspection and fault recovery are automatic too.

Programs still depend on correct tools, work location, offsets and a verified setup. See G-code and Toolpaths and CNC Control Fundamentals for the controls and program details.

Tool changers and pallet changers automate different waits

Tool changers and pallet changers automate different waits

An automatic tool changer exchanges cutting tools so a program can perform several operations. Correct tool identification, dimensions and available tool life remain essential.

A pallet changer exchanges work carriers. In a suitable system, one pallet can be loaded at a designated station while another is being machined. The pallet locates the fixture; the fixture locates the part. Dirt at either interface can undo the expected repeatability.

Repeatable fixturing and planned inspection are part of the automation system, not tasks that disappear after a changer is installed.

A manufacturing cell coordinates machines and handling

A manufacturing cell coordinates machines and handling

A flexible manufacturing cell combines machining and handling resources arranged to produce a planned family of parts. Flexibility comes from suitable programs, tools, fixtures and scheduling; it does not mean any part can be run without preparation.

A loading robot uses a programmed manipulator and a gripping device to transfer parts between defined positions. The cell must confirm conditions such as part presence, clamp state and machine readiness before the next action. A robot's repeatable motion does not compensate for a wrongly seated part.

Supporting detail: Addendum 81 — Cell, system and integration describe different scopes.

Lights-out production requires a plan for faults and variation

Lights-out production requires a plan for faults and variation

Lights-out machining means planned operation without an operator continuously attending the machines. It relies on a validated process, sufficient material and tool life, dependable chip and coolant management, and a defined response to faults.

Monitoring may detect tool breakage, missing parts or measurement trends, but only for conditions the system is designed to detect. Automatic compensation and inspection of every part are options, not universal features of automation. Decide what is measured, what stops production and how affected parts are contained.

Unattended operation is a system-level decision under the applicable equipment and facility procedures. These concepts are not authorization to leave a machine running unattended or enter an automated cell. A stopped cycle alone does not establish safe access.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Broaching

See how progressive teeth cut a profile, how a guided keyway broach works, and where rotary broaching differs.

A broach divides a shaped cut among a row of teeth

A broach divides a shaped cut among a row of teeth

In conventional broaching, a tool moves in a straight line relative to the work. Successive cutting teeth reach farther into the material. Rise per tooth is that increase in cutting height between successive teeth; it is not the tooth spacing along the tool. The spaces between teeth hold chips.

Roughing teeth remove most of the allowance. Semi-finishing teeth approach the final profile with smaller cuts. Finishing teeth establish size and finish; several may have the same height. The exact arrangement depends on the tool.

Supporting detail: Addendum 82 — Why the finishing teeth need not keep getting taller.

Push or pull describes the drive; internal or external describes the surface

Push or pull describes the drive; internal or external describes the surface

A push broach is driven from behind; a pull broach is drawn through by its leading end. An internal broach works inside a prepared opening. An external broach works on an outside surface, such as a flat or an external spline. These are separate distinctions: internal does not mean pull-only.

A suitable hole broach can produce a square, hexagon or internal spline; a keyway broach cuts a slot in an existing bore. Conventional through broaching needs an exit path. Choose the tool from the required finished profile and starting-hole specification, not just a nominal shape name.

Repeated parts can justify dedicated tooling because many cutting edges complete the profile in a short cycle. A small keyway set can also suit repair or short-run work. Compare Material-Removal Process Families and Selecting a Material-Removal Process; Vertical Band Machining covers cutting contours with a continuous band instead.

Supporting detail: Addendum 83 — Production advantages depend on the job.

A bushing guides the keyway broach; shims move its cutting edge outward

A bushing guides the keyway broach; shims move its cutting edge outward

The hub is the part surrounding the shaft. A slotted bushing fits its bore and guides the broach. A shim is a thin spacer behind the broach that increases the depth reached on a later pass. Broach, bushing and shims must be a compatible set.

Before operation, use Equipment Operating Procedure and press and mill hazard guidance in the safety collection. Follow the specific press and broach instructions for capacity, alignment, support, stroke, cut length and lubrication.

  1. Check the drawing, prepared bore and required keyway. Select the matching broach, bushing and specified shim schedule.
  2. Seat the bushing in the hub. Insert the broach in its slot for the first pass, normally without a shim on a multi-pass set.
  3. Support the hub squarely on the press bed with clearance below for the entire broach to pass through. Align the ram, tool and guide.
  4. Apply the specified lubricant and press the broach through according to its instructions.
  5. After the completed pass, remove the broach and clean its teeth. If another pass is specified, insert the prescribed shim behind it, reinsert, lubricate and check alignment again.
  6. Repeat with the specified shim stack for each remaining pass. Stop at the prescribed final setup; deburr and inspect as described in Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats.

Do not add a shim after the final pass. One-pass tools and some small broaches require none. Adding arbitrary shims is not a way to correct an uncertain dimension.

Supporting detail: Addendum 84 — Manufacturer reference for the pass sequence.

Count the first pass separately from the added shim passes; Practice

Count the first pass separately from the added shim passes

Rise per tooth and depth per pass are different quantities. For a simple planning exercise, let d1 be the depth reached by the unshimmed pass and s the extra depth from each added shim increment. After N passes, depth is d1 + (N − 1)s.

For a target depth D greater than d1, the minimum count to reach at least the target is 1 + ceiling((D − d1)/s). Ceiling means round upward to a whole number. If the first pass already reaches the target, the count is one. All depths here are measured radially from the original bore surface.

Example: an invented first-pass depth of 1.0 mm and two 0.5 mm increments give 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm: three passes. This is counting practice, not a real broach specification. If rounding upward exceeds the allowed finished depth, that shim schedule cannot make the part to size.

Practice counting passes

Rotary broaching uses an angled end-cutting tool

Rotary broaching uses an angled end-cutting tool

Rotary broaching can make polygon forms such as a hex socket using a special holder on a suitable lathe or mill. A small angular offset makes successive portions of the tool's end engage as the tool and work move relative to one another. It does not use the long row of progressively taller teeth shown above.

It needs a prepared opening for internal work. Tool form, available thrust, material, depth and chip clearance limit the application; a blind socket needs a planned place for the chips. This is a process overview, not a setup procedure.

Supporting detail: Addendum 85 — How the rotary holder produces the cutting motion.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Chemical Milling and Etching

A mask protects selected areas while an etchant dissolves exposed metal; sideways etching limits the detail.

A mask defines where chemical removal occurs

A mask defines where chemical removal occurs

Chemical machining uses a chemical reaction to dissolve exposed material. A protective mask covers areas that should remain. Chemical milling can make shallow recesses or reduce a metal part's weight. Photochemical etching uses a patterned resist and can produce intricate thin-sheet parts, including through openings.

Unlike ECM, ordinary chemical etching does not use an external machining current between a tool and the work. Select an etchant compatible with the particular material; “chemical machining” does not name one chemistry that works on everything.

Allow for sideways etching beneath the mask

Allow for sideways etching beneath the mask

Etching can spread sideways beneath the mask edge as well as into the surface. This undercut limits narrow lands, corner sharpness and dimensional control, especially as etch depth increases. The mask design must compensate for the etching behavior. Surface finish depends on the material and chemistry. Chemical removal avoids a cutting-induced thermal HAZ, but that is not the same as saying the chemical bath has no temperature requirements.

Supporting detail: Addendum 86 — Why thin-sheet patterns are a useful application.

Compare Electrochemical Machining and Selecting a Material-Removal Process. Safety reference: Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Electrical Discharge Machining

Sinker and wire EDM use controlled sparks to shape conductive work, with a gap between electrode and finished surface.

EDM needs an electrically conductive workpiece

EDM needs an electrically conductive workpiece

Electrical discharge machining (EDM) removes material with repeated electrical discharges across a small gap. Local heating melts and vaporizes tiny amounts of material. The electrode does not cut by rubbing against the work.

Check conductivity before considering EDM. Hardened tool steel is a candidate; ordinary nonconductive glass or ceramic is not. Hardness is less restrictive than in cutting with a conventional tool, but composition and electrical and thermal properties still affect machining behavior.

Supporting detail: Addendum 87 — Why the fluid and the gap matter.

Use sinker EDM for cavities and wire EDM for through profiles

Use sinker EDM for cavities and wire EDM for through profiles

Sinker, ram or die-sinking EDM feeds a shaped electrode toward the work to make a cavity. The cavity is larger than the electrode because removal extends across the spark gap. Mold cavities and hardened dies are typical uses. Electrode wear must be allowed for.

Wire EDM feeds a thin wire through the cutting zone while controlled motion traces a profile. The wire is continuously renewed. An enclosed opening normally needs a start hole for threading; the wire must pass through the work. A blind pocket calls for another approach, such as sinker EDM.

Wire EDM is useful for intricate die openings and thin features with low cutting force. Internal corners still have a radius: the wire radius plus the working gap limits how tight a corner can be. Specify a small radius rather than a mathematically sharp corner.

Offset the wire center by its radius plus the spark gap; Practice

Offset the wire center by its radius plus the spark gap

Center-path offset = wire radius + spark gap. Measure this distance from the finished contour toward the material being removed. In a simple straight cut, the full cut width (kerf) is wire diameter plus twice the gap.

For an illustrative radius of 0.120 mm and a one-sided gap of 0.018 mm, the offset is 0.138 mm. These are teaching inputs, not machine settings. A control may apply compensation to a programmed part contour; do not also offset the geometry a second time.

Practice a wire offset

Supporting detail: Addendum 88 — Why one offset does not describe every pass.

Low cutting force does not mean no thermal change

Low cutting force does not mean no thermal change

EDM can hold fine features and produce a fine finish with suitable finishing passes, but its surface contains small discharge craters. Melted material can solidify again as a recast layer. Heat can alter nearby material, so surface integrity and any required finishing belong in process selection.

Supporting detail: Addendum 89 — Further reading on EDM surfaces and wire systems.

Compare Electrochemical Machining. Safety references: Electrical Safety, Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Electrochemical Machining

ECM dissolves conductive metal through an electrolyte rather than removing it with sparks or a cutting edge.

ECM removes metal by electrochemical dissolution

ECM removes metal by electrochemical dissolution

In electrochemical machining (ECM), the metal workpiece is the positive electrode (anode), and the tool is the negative electrode (cathode). Direct current passes through a flowing, electrically conductive liquid called an electrolyte. Metal dissolves from the work surface while the tool advances without cutting contact.

Consider ECM for conductive metals, including hard alloys and complex contours. The tool shape, gap and electrolyte flow govern the resulting feature. A suitable electrolyte must be matched to the metal; a generic salt solution is not a universal process recipe.

ECM uses a conducting liquid; EDM uses controlled breakdown

ECM uses a conducting liquid; EDM uses controlled breakdown

Two electrically powered processes with different removal mechanisms
QuestionECMEDM
What removes material?Electrochemical dissolutionHeat from discharges
What does the liquid do?Conducts current and carries reaction products awayInsulates between discharges; cools and flushes
Does the tool wear?No removal-related tool wear in principle; real tooling still needs maintenanceElectrode wear occurs; wire is renewed
What surface results?Can be smooth and burr-free, without a thermal recast layerDischarge craters and possible recast material

ECM is not a melting process and normally avoids a heat-affected zone. That does not mean the electrolyte stays cold: current flow heats it. Flow, temperature, chemistry and gap control all matter.

Supporting detail: Addendum 90 — Why hardness alone does not set ECM performance.

Compare Electrical Discharge Machining. Safety references: Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets and Electrical Safety.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Jigs, Fixtures and Repeatable Location

Locate a part repeatably, clamp it against supports, and distinguish tool-guiding jigs from workholding fixtures.

A jig guides the tool; a fixture locates and holds the work

A jig guides the tool; a fixture locates and holds the work

A drill jig locates and holds the part and guides the drill with a bushing. A fixture locates and holds the part while the machine controls the tool path. A plate with clamps is not automatically a jig: ask whether it guides the cutting tool.

Both reduce the need to recreate the part position for every cycle. Neither removes the need for trained setup, secure restraint and inspection. Follow the approved mounting method; do not infer that a jig may be held by hand.

For machine workholding and indicating procedures, use Milling Vises and Strap Clamps and Mill Indicators and Part Zero. For reading the part's views, see Orthographic Projection and the Glass Box. The drawing specifies the required relationships; the fixture must support making them.

Three, two and one contacts establish six independent constraints

Three, two and one contacts establish six independent constraints

A free rigid body can translate along X, Y and Z and rotate about X, Y and Z: six degrees of freedom. For an ideal rectangular block seated against perpendicular locating planes, the 3-2-1 arrangement establishes its position without redundant locating contacts.

ContactsPlane in this exampleAdditional motions constrained while seated
Three non-collinear supportsPrimary, XY undersideZ translation, rotation about X and Y: three
Two separated side locatorsSecondary, XZ sideY translation and rotation about Z: two
One end locatorTertiary, YZ endX translation: one

These contacts locate only while the work stays seated. Clamps maintain contact and resist forces that would lift or separate the part. Do not count positive and negative directions as twelve independent degrees of freedom.

Direct clamp force into supports and leave room for chips; Checklist

Direct clamp force into supports and leave room for chips

Place clamp forces toward locators and supported regions, not toward open space where the part can bend. Use enough restraint for the operation without distorting the part. Plan the load path from the cutting force through the work and supports into the machine.

A fourth fixed support under an imperfect surface may make the part rock instead of improving location. Extra supports can be useful for stiffness if they are adjusted to the already located part without shifting it. Avoid redundant locators that fight one another.

Foolproofing (poka-yoke) makes an incorrect loading orientation difficult or impossible—for example, a locating feature that accepts an asymmetric part in only one orientation. Keep chips away from locating contacts with accessible cleaning paths and relief spaces; a trapped chip can relocate every subsequent cut.

  • Identify the intended locating contacts and check that the part seats without rocking.
  • Check that clamps press into supports and that loading, cutting and unloading paths are clear.
  • Check that incorrect orientation is prevented or clearly detectable.
  • Verify the first part after setup before repeating the cycle.
Modular fixtures trade dedicated tooling for reusable components; Practice

Modular fixtures trade dedicated tooling for reusable components

A modular fixture combines a reusable base with locating pins, supports and clamps. It suits changing work when the arrangement can be documented and rebuilt repeatably. A dedicated fixture may reduce loading time for repeated production, but takes its own design and manufacturing effort.

A tombstone is an upright fixture carrier with mounting faces that can present several setups to a machining centre. It still needs suitable locating, clamping and tool clearance on each face.

Select fixture materials for stiffness, wear, temperature change and the required accuracy. Aluminium can be useful; thermal expansion is a design consideration rather than an automatic ban on close-tolerance work. Wear surfaces may need hardened inserts or replaceable components.

Count locating constraints Identify a jig or fixture

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Laser, Waterjet and Plasma Cutting

Compare focused light, moving water and a plasma arc by material, thickness, edge quality and thermal effects.

Distinguish a thermal cut from an erosive cut

Distinguish a thermal cut from an erosive cut

Laser and plasma use concentrated heat. Waterjet uses mechanical energy. A heat-affected zone (HAZ) is material beside a cut whose properties or structure have changed from heating without being melted away.

Laser cutting concentrates light into a small region

Laser cutting concentrates light into a small region

A focused laser beam supplies thermal energy; cutting gas commonly helps remove material. Laser cutting is a candidate for fine profiles in sheet material. Metals, wood and selected plastics require suitable laser systems; a machine that cuts acrylic is not automatically a metal cutter.

A narrow kerf and fine detail are possible, particularly in thinner material. Edge finish, taper and dimensional accuracy depend on material, thickness, focus, gas and cutting speed. Melting, discoloration or charring may affect the edge. Do not assume the HAZ is zero.

Supporting detail: Addendum 91 — Why the material and laser must be matched.

Waterjet cuts soft materials; added abrasive cuts hard materials

Waterjet cuts soft materials; added abrasive cuts hard materials

Pure waterjet uses a high-speed water stream for materials such as foam, rubber and other soft sheet. Abrasive waterjet adds hard particles to erode metals, stone, non-tempered glass and many ceramics. Electrical conductivity is not required.

Waterjet normally creates no thermal HAZ. It is a candidate for thick stock or a heat-sensitive edge, but thickness still affects speed and cut quality. Taper, where the cut width changes through the thickness, and striations, visible lines down the cut face, can limit accuracy and finish. Slower quality cuts may reduce these effects. Brittle edges may chip and need finishing.

Identify the glass type before choosing a process: tempered glass is not a candidate for ordinary waterjet cutting. A no-HAZ process is not a promise of no mechanical damage.

Supporting detail: Addendum 92 — Further reading on glass and waterjet limits.

Plasma is a thermal cutting candidate for conductive metal

Plasma is a thermal cutting candidate for conductive metal

A plasma cutter uses an electric arc through ionized gas to melt metal; the gas stream expels it. The work must conduct electricity. Steel, stainless steel and aluminum are candidates; ordinary glass and wood are not.

Plasma often suits productive plate cutting where its edge quality meets the drawing or later machining is planned. Compared with a fine laser cut in thin sheet, small details can be harder to hold. Edge bevel, attached solidified metal (dross) and a HAZ may need attention. Equipment and thickness determine actual capability; plasma is not automatically a rough-only process.

Supporting detail: Addendum 93 — Compare capability on the actual thickness.

Continue with Selecting a Material-Removal Process. Safety references: Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Electrical Safety, Fire Safety and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Material-Removal Process Families

Sort machine tools by how they remove material, then follow the process that fits the feature.

Start with what removes the material

Start with what removes the material

A machine tool controls motion between a tool and the workpiece, the part being made. In material removal, the final shape is what remains after unwanted material is taken away.

CNC is a control method, not a removal family. Computer numerical control can guide a mill, lathe, grinder, EDM machine or cutting jet. See G-code and Toolpaths. Forming moves material without removing it; see Manufacturing Process Categories for the wider manufacturing map.

Conventional cutting uses defined cutting edges

Conventional cutting uses defined cutting edges

  • Turning rotates the work past a cutting tool; milling rotates the cutter and feeds it relative to the work.
  • Drilling makes holes; sawing separates stock, the starting material, with successive teeth.
  • Broaching uses a sequence of teeth to progressively cut a profile, such as a keyway. Dedicated tooling often suits repeated production, but broaching is not limited to large runs.
  • Shaping and planing use a back-and-forth straight cutting stroke. A shaper normally moves the tool; a planer normally moves the work.

A process name describes the action, not every possible shape. Milling can make curved contours as well as flat faces.

Abrasive processes use many small cutting grains

Abrasive processes use many small cutting grains

Grinding wheels hold abrasive grains that remove material. Precision grinding controls size and surface texture, often on hardened parts. Grinding can also remove substantial stock; it is not restricted to light finishing.

Honing commonly uses abrasive stones with combined motions to refine a bore's size, form and surface. Lapping uses fine abrasive between a lap and the work to refine a surface. Neither is simply another name for grinding.

Nontraditional processes change the removal mechanism

Nontraditional processes change the removal mechanism

  • Thermal: EDM, laser and plasma remove material with concentrated heat. EDM's energy supply is electrical, but its removal mechanism is thermal.
  • Electrochemical: ECM uses electric current to dissolve metal.
  • Chemical: Chemical Milling and Etching uses an etchant to dissolve exposed material.
  • Mechanical energy: waterjets and Ultrasonic Machining erode material with moving water or abrasive particles.

Use Selecting a Material-Removal Process to narrow the candidates. Safety references: Machine Hazards and Housekeeping, Equipment Operating Procedure and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Process Capability and Variation

Compare the allowed tolerance band with the process's centre and spread, without mistaking five good parts for proof of capability.

The drawing sets the limits; the process produces the spread

The drawing sets the limits; the process produces the spread

A tolerance band is the permitted interval from the lower size limit to the upper size limit. Process spread describes how much the manufactured values vary. Changing a machine setting may shift the centre; it does not necessarily reduce the spread.

A capable process consistently fits its variation within the required limits with useful margin. A narrow spread near a limit can still produce rejects if the process drifts. A wide spread cannot be fixed simply by moving its average to the middle.

Read Tolerances and Fits for the size-limit method and Shop Inspection and Quality Control for how these observations guide checks.

Mean locates a sample; range describes its width

Mean locates a sample; range describes its width

Consider five invented readings: 24.98, 24.99, 25.00, 25.01 and 25.02 mm, with limits of 24.95 to 25.05 mm.

  • Mean: add all five readings and divide by five: 125.00 / 5 = 25.00 mm.
  • Range: subtract the smallest from the largest: 25.02 − 24.98 = 0.04 mm.
  • Midpoint of the limits: (24.95 + 25.05) / 2 = 25.00 mm. This sample mean is centred on that midpoint, and all five values are inside the limits.

Now add 0.04 mm to every reading. The mean becomes 25.04 mm and the range remains 0.04 mm, but the largest reading becomes 25.06 mm and fails. Centre and spread answer different questions.

Supporting detail: Addendum 94 — Why a small sample range is not the full process spread.

Passing parts are evidence, not proof of a capable process; Interactive; Practice

Passing parts are evidence, not proof of a capable process

Capability concerns a process over time, not a single successful part. First establish that the measurement method is suitable and the process is stable enough to describe meaningfully. Collect representative readings across the conditions the conclusion is meant to cover.

A stable process can still be too wide for the tolerance. An unstable process can happen to produce five passing parts. Neither case is resolved by averaging away the problem. Investigate a trend or sudden change using the inspection plan.

Supporting detail: Addendum 95 — Where capability indices fit.

Capability explorer: assume a stable process with roughly normal output. μ is the process mean; σ (standard deviation) measures spread. These are chosen teaching inputs, not estimates from the five readings above. The five-readings example above explains why passing parts are evidence, not proof of a capable process.

Cp = (USL − LSL) / (6σ) compares tolerance width with spread, ignoring centring. Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) / (3σ) uses the nearer limit. Cpk is negative when the mean lies outside the limits. LSL and USL are the lower and upper size limits.

Predict first: which case has the higher Cp? Does it also have fewer parts outside the limits?

Expected ppm means parts outside the limits per million under this normal model, not a measured reject count. Values are rounded; less than 1 ppm is not a guarantee of zero rejects. Requirements depend on the application; no universal pass threshold is used here.

Practice mean Practice range Check sample centring

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Selecting a Material-Removal Process

Screen candidates by material, feature access, thickness and surface requirements before comparing production cost.

Screen the material and feature before choosing a machine; Checklist

Screen the material and feature before choosing a machine

  • Identify the material, its condition and conductivity. Check Material Families and Material Properties.
  • Mark the feature: through profile, blind cavity, shallow recess or finished surface. Identify tool access and any start-hole requirement.
  • Record thickness, minimum internal radius and the thinnest remaining feature.
  • Read the drawing's dimensional and surface requirements. Decide whether a thermal HAZ or recast layer is acceptable.
  • Shortlist processes, then check actual equipment capability, finishing needs and production quantity.

Hardness alone does not select a process. A hard nonconductive ceramic rules out ordinary EDM even though EDM can cut hardened steel. See Tolerances and Fits and Surface Texture and Finish for what the finished part must meet.

Use the feature to narrow the candidates

Use the feature to narrow the candidates

Starting candidates, not guaranteed process approvals
Part requirementCandidate and reasonCheck next
Hardened steel die with a through opening and small inside radiiWire EDM: conductive work, low cutting force, fine profileWire radius plus gap, threading access and surface integrity
Blind cavity in hardened conductive metalSinker EDM: shaped electrode reaches a cavityElectrode manufacture, wear and flushing access
Thick non-tempered glass plate with a through profileAbrasive waterjet: no conductivity requirement or thermal HAZGlass type, thickness capability, piercing and edge quality
Shaped hole in a hard nonconductive ceramicUltrasonic Machining: abrasive impact removes brittle materialTool wear, depth, chipping and required finish
Fine profile in thin metal sheetLaser: concentrated beam and narrow kerfMaterial match, HAZ and edge quality
Conductive metal plate blank for later machiningPlasma: productive thermal cutting candidateThickness capability and machining allowance
Soft foam gasketPure waterjet: water alone can separate soft materialSupport, water compatibility and detail size
Repeated complex metal contours without an EDM recast layerECM: dissolution instead of meltingMaterial chemistry, electrolyte flow and tooling cost
Many shallow areas in metal sheetChemical milling: masked areas can be etched togetherUndercut, depth control and surface finish
Keep conventional machining on the candidate list; Practice

Keep conventional machining on the candidate list

For an accessible flat face, hole or round shaft in a machinable material, conventional cutting may be the simplest route. Use the family map to reach those methods. A part may combine sawing, milling and grinding, or use waterjet for a blank followed by machining of critical faces.

Increasing thickness can increase cutting time, taper or flushing difficulty. A thin remaining wall may deflect or be damaged even when cutting forces are small. Ask for evidence of capability on the actual material and geometry rather than relying on a universal tolerance ranking.

Practice selecting a process Practice HAZ reasoning

Safety references: Equipment Operating Procedure, Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Shop Inspection and Quality Control

Check the first part, watch the process during production, and use suitable measurements to decide whether parts meet requirements.

Inspect before a setup error becomes a batch of parts

Inspect before a setup error becomes a batch of parts

Quality control uses evidence to keep production meeting requirements. Inspection checks what was made; it does not repair a process or make a bad part good.

First-article inspection
Check the first part from a new or changed setup against the required features before releasing continued production. A good first part supports the setup decision; it does not prove that later parts will stay good.
In-process checks
Check selected features while production continues. Record results in production order so tool wear or a shifting setup is visible before many parts are affected.
Final inspection
Check the completed part or lot against the acceptance plan, including requirements that earlier operations could not verify. Keep its identity connected to its results.

If a check fails, identify and hold the affected material, report the result, and investigate before continuing under the applicable procedure. Consider parts made since the last known good check; checking only the next part leaves that interval unresolved.

A gauge gives a decision; a measurement gives a value

A gauge gives a decision; a measurement gives a value

Attribute gauging reports a category such as pass/fail. Variable measurement reports a number, such as 18.012 mm. A number can show how close the process is getting to a limit; a passing gauge alone cannot.

For a plain hole, the GO plug checks the small-hole limit and should enter over the specified inspection length. The NO-GO plug checks the large-hole limit and should not enter as defined by the gauging procedure. Do not force either end. For a plain shaft, a GO ring should pass over the specified length and a NO-GO ring should not pass: the GO ring checks the large-shaft limit.

A GO plug that will not enter is a failed check, not proof of one particular cause: an undersize hole, burr, dirt, poor alignment or form error can obstruct it. Clean and investigate using the approved method. A NO-GO plug that enters beyond the permitted engagement is also a failed check.

Use the correctly identified gauge with current calibration status. Do not derive gauge sizes directly from workpiece limits. This plain-gauge explanation does not supply the engagement rules for threaded gauges.

Supporting detail: Addendum 96 — Why the gauge itself needs limits and wear checks.

Build a clean, repeatable surface-plate setup; Checklist

Build a clean, repeatable surface-plate setup

A surface plate provides a reference plane. A height gauge measures from that plane; an indicator can compare the part with a reference or show variation as a surface is swept. Neither tool corrects a rocking part or dirt under a support.

  • Read the required feature and reference surfaces on the drawing; select a suitable instrument and range.
  • Clean the plate, supports and contact surfaces. Address burrs under the approved preparation method without altering the feature being inspected.
  • Support the part stably on the intended reference surfaces and allow temperature differences to settle as the measurement procedure requires.
  • Check the instrument against the appropriate reference, set zero or reference height, and use consistent contact force and alignment.
  • Repeat the reading, record the value and units, and investigate disagreement before accepting the result.

Instrument handling belongs in Choosing Shop Measuring Tools and Reading Measuring Scales. Machine alignment is covered in Mill Indicators and Part Zero. Size acceptance and surface finish are separate requirements: see Tolerances and Fits and Surface Texture and Finish.

A CMM relates measured points to the part's references

A CMM relates measured points to the part's references

A coordinate measuring machine (CMM) records positions in three dimensions using a probe or sensor. Software uses sampled points to evaluate features such as a plane, bore or hole location relative to the chosen part alignment.

The operator still needs a suitable setup, probe qualification, measurement strategy and drawing interpretation. A few points cannot reveal every possible surface defect. A CMM is a measurement system, not an automatic guarantee that every requirement has been checked.

Increase checks when the process is new or changing

Increase checks when the process is new or changing

Sampling means inspecting some parts to learn about a larger group or process. It reduces inspection effort but leaves a chance that unmeasured defects will escape. Select samples by a defined plan, not by choosing the nicest-looking parts.

A new setup, tool replacement, unexpected variation or a trend toward a limit calls for closer attention and potentially more frequent checks under the inspection plan. A demonstrated stable process may justify fewer checks; feature consequences and customer requirements still matter. Some features require every part to be inspected.

Keep the readings in order and compare their trend and spread, not just their pass/fail status. Process Capability and Variation explains that distinction. Do not repeatedly adjust a stable process just because its readings differ slightly.

Trust a result only as far as the measurement supports it; Practice

Trust a result only as far as the measurement supports it

Accuracy concerns agreement with a reference or true value; precision concerns agreement among repeated measurements under stated conditions. Readings can cluster tightly and still be consistently wrong.

Calibration compares instrument indications with reference values under specified conditions and establishes their relationship and uncertainty. It is not merely setting zero, and adjustment is a separate action. Traceability belongs to a measurement result supported by a documented chain of calibrations, each contributing uncertainty.

For classroom limit comparisons, treat the stated numbers as exact and include both endpoints. In real inspection, uncertainty matters near a limit: apply the specified acceptance decision rule rather than assuming the last displayed digit is exact.

Practice limit decisions Practice gauge interpretation

Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes

Ultrasonic Machining

A vibrating tool drives abrasive particles against hard, brittle work without requiring electrical conductivity.

Ultrasonic impact machining removes material with abrasive particles

Ultrasonic impact machining removes material with abrasive particles

A shaped tool vibrates rapidly with a small stroke, driving abrasive particles in a liquid slurry against the work. The removal energy at the work is mechanical, even though electricity powers the vibration system.

Consider this process for holes or shaped cavities in hard, brittle materials such as glass and ceramics. The work need not conduct electricity. It is generally less effective for soft, ductile materials that deform instead of breaking away under particle impacts.

No thermal HAZ does not mean a perfect surface

No thermal HAZ does not mean a perfect surface

Ultrasonic impact machining normally avoids a thermal heat-affected zone. Abrasive size, tool wear, slurry access and feature depth affect dimensional control and finish. Fine abrasive can improve the surface, but removal may be slow; edge chipping and subsurface damage remain possible in brittle work.

Distinguish this process from ultrasonic-assisted cutting, where vibration is added to another cutting or grinding process. The two names do not imply identical tooling or removal mechanisms.

Supporting detail: Addendum 97 — Why a shaped tool does not give an exact-size copy.

Compare Electrical Discharge Machining and Selecting a Material-Removal Process. Safety references: Machine Hazards and Housekeeping and Chemicals and Safety Data Sheets.
