Addendum

Additional evidence, standards context, and background referenced from the main text.

  1. Machining/Milling/Climb and Conventional Milling

    Addendum 1. Why some machines climb mill without trouble

    A feed drive can be designed to reduce backlash, for example with a preloaded ball nut. The important question is whether the machine controls that movement, not simply whether it is called CNC. The chip is the same shape either way; what changes is whether the machine can hold the table against the pull of the cut.

    Sources: Sandvik Coromant: down milling versus up milling explains chip formation, rubbing and the backlash condition. Harvey Performance: climb versus conventional milling describes the lifting and downward force tendencies in peripheral horizontal milling. The arrows illustrate directions; they do not calculate force magnitudes.

    Back to reference 1

  2. Machining/Milling/Diagnosing Milling Chatter

    Addendum 2. Several faults can look or sound like chatter

    • Runout or one damaged edge can make one flute carry more load and leave uneven tooth marks or non-uniform edge wear.
    • Rubbing or built-up edge can smear material, generate heat and produce a poor finish without a regenerative vibration.
    • Chip re-cutting can scratch the finish and damage edges when chips remain in the cutting zone.
    • A forced vibration follows a repeating input from the cutter, interrupted cut, drive or surrounding system. Chatter is the self-reinforcing case; both still require finding the flexible path and the excitation.

    After the approved safe stop, inspect the pattern, cutter and setup together. Sound is useful for noticing a change, not for identifying the failed component.

    Back to reference 2

  3. Machining/Milling/End Mill Anatomy and Cutter Selection

    Addendum 3. Public anatomy reference

    Harvey Performance: The Anatomy of an End Mill provides an illustrated reference for the dimensions found in a tool catalog.

    Back to reference 3

  4. Machining/Milling/End Mill Anatomy and Cutter Selection

    Addendum 4. Why the two-for-aluminum, four-for-steel rule is only a starting point

    Tool designers trade chip space against the core and cutting-edge arrangement. Purpose-built tools and controlled engagement can make other flute counts appropriate. See Harvey Performance: Why Flute Count Matters.

    Back to reference 4

  5. Machining/Milling/End Mill Anatomy and Cutter Selection

    Addendum 5. Check the coating's material recommendation

    Harvey Tool's coating guide distinguishes ferrous applications from aluminum applications. Its AlTiN and TiB2 entries illustrate why a coating name must be matched to the work material.

    Back to reference 5

  6. Machining/Milling/Feeds and Speeds

    Addendum 6. Feed per tooth is not always the thickness of the chip

    Feed per tooth is how far the work moves between teeth. The chip a tooth actually cuts is only that thick when the cutter is at least half buried across its diameter. In a narrower cut, each tooth meets the work at a slant and the chip comes out thinner. Climb and Conventional Milling shows this: at a width of cut of 10% of the diameter, the thickest part of the chip is 60% of the feed per tooth.

    Some cutting data raises the feed per tooth for narrow cuts to make up for this. Read what your data assumes before using its numbers, and ask if it does not say. Thinner chips also take more energy per cubic inch, which is one reason a power estimate is a band.

    The spindle-speed, table-feed and feed-per-tooth relations follow Sandvik Coromant’s milling formulas and definitions. The calculator’s cutting-speed and feed-per-tooth ranges are from GARR TOOL’s general purpose milling guide, and its cutting-energy bands are converted from Kennametal’s milling power factors.

    Sandvik’s specific cutting-force explanation shows why chip thickness and cutting-edge geometry affect the energy estimate. Haas’s spindle power curves illustrate why available power depends on RPM; read the machine’s own curve and duty rating rather than treating its headline horsepower as available everywhere.

    Back to reference 6

  7. Machining/Milling/G-code and Toolpaths

    Addendum 7. How the simulator reads and runs a program

    Each line is read in the order a control carries out the parts of a line: feed rate, spindle speed and tool first, then the tool change, the spindle, coolant, the modes, the move, and last the program end. So S2500 M3 G1 X20 F100 starts the spindle before it moves. Two codes from one group on a line, such as G0 G1, are an error.

    The interpreter first reads the whole program, and a second machine runs it at once to find its path, its time and the first place it would stop; that is the path drawn before you press Play. Pressing Play runs the program again on the block, move by move. The metal, the vise and the tools are those of the simulator in Milling Operations: every cut is kept as the space the tool swept, and a move that would break a tool rule or hit the vise stops where it would happen.

    An arc’s end point has to be on its circle to within 0.005 mm or 0.1 % of the radius, whichever is larger. A rapid, or a feed with the spindle stopped, stops a hair short of the first metal it would touch. The volume removed is an estimate from a 0.25 mm grid.

    Back to reference 7

  8. Machining/Milling/Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

    Addendum 8. Public reference for key forms

    Engineering Institute of Technology, Fundamentals of Mechanical Engineering introduces keys, keyways and the common key types in its keys section. No standard size table or shaft-to-key size rule is reproduced here.

    Back to reference 8

  9. Machining/Milling/Keys, Keyways and Shaft Keyseats

    Addendum 9. Why cutter selection includes more than width

    Reach, neck clearance and tooth arrangement affect access and cutting behavior. See Harvey Performance's keyseat cutter considerations. A nominal tool width does not certify the width of the finished slot.

    Back to reference 9

  10. Machining/Milling/Mill Indicators and Part Zero

    Addendum 10. Contact angle affects the reading

    Mitutoyo: Dial Test Indicators and the Cosine Effect shows the stylus geometry and correction. Do not apply a plunger-indicator correction rule to a lever indicator without checking its instructions.

    Back to reference 10

  11. Machining/Milling/Mill Indicators and Part Zero

    Addendum 11. Check both repeatability and the offset sign

    Repeat the touch from the same direction. On manual feed screws, account for backlash when reversing; a handwheel reading can change while the table has not yet moved. Do not use a rough saw edge as though it were a finished datum. The radius correction is geometry, independent of the control's button sequence.

    MIT's mill introduction covers mechanical edge finding and feed-screw backlash.

    Back to reference 11

  12. Machining/Milling/Mill Toolholders and Collets

    Addendum 12. Public toolholder references

    Haas: Tool Holder Essentials compares holder choices. Tormach's R8/TTS explanation is for the machine configuration named in that manual, not a statement of this shop's inventory.

    Back to reference 12

  13. Machining/Milling/Mill Toolholders and Collets

    Addendum 13. Manufacturer examples and the drill-chuck exception

    HAIMER's toolholder catalog (PDF) identifies Weldon-flat and shrink-fit products. SCHUNK explains hydraulic actuation and the expansion sleeve; hydraulic designs include milling-rated products, so a family-wide ban on milling would be wrong. BIG DAISHOWA describes its mechanical milling chucks.

    Albrecht's APC catalog (PDF) describes its geared special-collet mechanism. Its separate CNC Drill Chuck manual (PDF) explicitly includes finish milling among that named product's uses. Such a product rating does not qualify every chuck sold under the same brand. REGO-FIX explains the powRgrip collet, holder and press unit.

    Back to reference 13

  14. Machining/Milling/Mill Toolholders and Collets

    Addendum 14. A real trade-off within one product family

    BIG DAISHOWA's mechanical-chuck guidance describes two clamping configurations for its slim HMC(S): the roughing configuration increases clamping force at the expense of greater runout. That is a qualified product example, not permission to tighten another chuck farther or a ranking of all milling chucks.

    Back to reference 14

  15. Machining/Milling/Mill Toolholders and Collets

    Addendum 15. Why the snap matters

    The eccentric ring retains and extracts the collet as the nut is loosened. Missing that engagement can prevent correct seating. Use REGO-FIX's ER assembly instructions for the mechanism and Haas: ER Collet Essentials for a public demonstration.

    Back to reference 15

  16. Machining/Milling/Mill Toolholders and Collets

    Addendum 16. Why adding the tool can change the answer

    HAIMER's balancing guide (PDF) discusses assembly unbalance. Albrecht's APC catalog (PDF), Handling APC and Ultra, states that the marked balance condition excludes collet and tool and that shank slots affect the assembled result. A small runout reading is not a substitute for that separate balance and speed check.

    Back to reference 16

  17. Machining/Milling/Mill Toolholders and Collets

    Addendum 17. Check your selection reasoning without a video

    A defensible answer identifies the limiting feature or load, names a candidate mechanism, and states what its manufacturer must confirm. Different products can satisfy the same job. If the only justification is a brand name or a universal star rating, the selection is incomplete.

    Back to reference 17

  18. Machining/Milling/Milling Operations

    Addendum 18. How the inspection decides, and what its numbers are

    The part is kept as a list of every cut: the space each tool swept through. The top of the metal at any point is the raw top lowered by every cut that reaches that point. The inspection measures walls, floors, holes and chamfers at sampled locations on that surface, with numbers rounded to a hundredth of a millimetre. A display grid plus probes derived from each cut and drawing boundary look for excess metal and gouges. Passing means the modeled checks pass; it does not certify every point of a real surface. Removed volume is an estimate from the 0.25 mm grid; very small cuts can change the analytic surface without a resolved grid volume. Walls and holes pass within ±0.10 mm, the bore within ±0.05 mm, and floors and faces within ±0.05 mm.

    Tapped holes are accepted when their drilled diameter falls inside the minor-diameter limits for a 6H internal thread: 4.917 to 5.153 mm for M6×1, and 6.647 to 6.912 mm for M8×1.25. These are finished minor-diameter limits, used here as a teaching proxy for pilot quality; they are not universal tap-drill recommendations or a complete 6H inspection.

    Sources: Gühring’s metric table, page 46, distinguishes nominal tap-drill sizes from finished minor limits. Haas’s M6×1 example specifies a 5 mm tap drill and a 2P–3P chamfer, illustrating why the model’s 4P is not universal. Vermont Gage explains the separate thread and cylindrical gauge checks.

    Back to reference 18

  19. Machining/Milling/Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

    Addendum 19. Read the whole sweep, not just two endpoints

    A smooth change suggests angular misalignment. A sudden jump at one spot suggests a chip, burr, damaged jaw or unstable contact. Tightening can move the vise, which is why the final sweep matters. Equal endpoint readings alone cannot reveal a bowed or damaged face between them.

    Public demonstration: Haas: How to Square and Indicate a Vise. The alignment principle transfers; machine controls do not.

    Back to reference 19

  20. Machining/Milling/Milling Vises and Strap Clamps

    Addendum 20. Why the force divides this way—and what the model cannot tell you

    Take moments about the heel: Fpart(a + b) = Pb. Vertical balance gives Fpart + Fheel = P. These are upward reactions on the strap; the strap pushes downward on the part and heel with equal magnitudes.

    This neglects strap weight, friction, deformation and additional contacts. It does not calculate stud force from wrench torque, allowable loads, sliding resistance or the number of clamps needed. Those depend on the hardware, workpiece and cutting forces. See Carr Lane's strap-clamp guide for the underlying geometry and hardware guidance.

    Back to reference 20

  21. Machining/Milling/Tool Stickout and Deflection

    Addendum 21. The calculation and its units

    The solid round section has area moment of inertia I = πd⁴/64. With x measured from the clamp, displacement magnitude is y(x) = Fx²(3L − x)/(6EI). At the tip, x = L, so δ = FL³/(3EI). Both displacement and slope are zero at x = 0.

    Use N for force, mm for length and diameter, and N/mm² for E. The controls show E in GPa: multiply by 1,000 to get N/mm². The answer is in mm; multiply by 1,000 for µm.

    For F = 100 N, L = 40 mm, d = 10 mm and E = 600 GPa, I = 490.874 mm⁴ and δ = 0.007243 mm = 7.243 µm. Halfway along that tool, y(L/2) is 5/16 of the tip value, or 2.264 µm. These are calculated examples, not measured cutter data.

    Back to reference 21

  22. Machining/Milling/Tool Stickout and Deflection

    Addendum 22. Primary references

    • MIT OpenCourseWare: review of cantilever beam theory, lecture 2 appendix, equations 10–11 on PDF page 5. Derives the end-loaded shape and tip displacement with fixed-clamp boundary conditions.
    • Hyperion Materials & Technologies: Carbide vs. Steel. Its wear-grade comparison reports the modulus range; it does not specify the stiffness of a particular fluted cutter.

    Back to reference 22

  23. Machining/Milling/Vertical Mill Anatomy and Motion

    Addendum 23. Why facing can reveal a tram problem

    A tilted spindle puts opposite sides of a face cutter at different heights. Adjacent passes may leave steps even with the vise correctly aligned. Surface finish alone does not identify the cause: check the geometry before changing cutting data.

    MIT: Introduction to the Mill illustrates the distinction between head tramming and vise alignment on a knee mill.

    Back to reference 23

  24. Machining/Turning/Lathe Operations

    Addendum 24. Rake and chipbreakers depend on the whole cutting setup

    Rake describes the slope of the surface the chip flows over. Clearance keeps the tool below the edge from rubbing. Material matters, but hardness alone does not dictate positive, neutral or negative rake: tool material, edge strength, holder geometry and rigidity also matter. Use the tool maker's cutting geometry and range for the application.

    A chipbreaker guides a chip into a tighter curl so it can break. It may be molded into an insert or ground into a tool. It works within a range of feeds and depths; a very thin chip can curl without breaking. A chipbreaker is not a guarantee of short chips at every setting.

    Back to reference 24

  25. Machining/Turning/Lathe Operations

    Addendum 25. How a manual lathe keeps every pass on one helix

    The carriage is coupled to the leadscrew by closing the half-nut. On a lathe with an inch leadscrew cutting an inch thread, the thread dial shows when to close it so that each pass drops into the same groove. Many machinists also feed the tool in with the compound travel set near 30° from the radial cross-feed direction, so that most of the cut is taken by one flank of the tool.

    The simulator simplifies all of this. It keeps every pass on one helix for you, feeds the tool straight in, and checks a simplified 60° thread by its crest and root diameters. A real thread is checked against a thread table with thread gauges or measuring wires.

    Back to reference 25

  26. Machining/Turning/Single-Point Threading

    Addendum 26. Radial depth and compound travel are different quantities

    If compound travel is c at angle β from radial, its radial component is h = c cos(β); therefore c = h / cos(β). The corresponding diameter reduction is 2h. Check whether a dial reads actual slide travel or diameter change before using it.

    Back to reference 26

  27. Machining/Turning/Single-Point Threading

    Addendum 27. Why only certain threading-dial positions return to the groove

    The threading dial is geared to the leadscrew and carried with the carriage. Its rotation tracks their relative position. For a selected thread, certain dial positions repeat the relationship that lets the tool enter the same helical groove when the half-nuts close. Other positions can put the tool between previous passes, cutting a second groove.

    Back to reference 27

  28. Machining/Turning/Single-Point Threading

    Addendum 28. Verify the formula without a thread-depth table

    Split the symmetric 60° tooth down the middle. The right triangle has axial width P/2 and radial height H. Its 30° angle gives tan(30°) = (P/2)/H. Rearranging gives the formula above. If a defined profile removes radial heights a at the crest and b at the root from this triangle, its height is H − a − b. Neither a nor b can be guessed from pitch alone.

    For a hypothetical sharp-V, 20-per-inch thread, P = 0.050 in and H = 0.04330 in. At 29° from radial, ideal compound travel would be H/cos(29°) = 0.04951 in. These calculations isolate geometry; they are not settings for cutting a real 20-per-inch fastener.

    Back to reference 28

  29. Machining/Turning/Turning Tapers

    Addendum 29. Check the rate with a fresh example

    A taper goes from 1.100 to 0.950 in over 3.000 in. Its diameter changes 0.150 in, so the rate is 0.050 in/in, or 0.600 in/ft. At half the length, the diameter has changed half as much: 0.075 in. These are teaching dimensions, not a standard machine taper.

    Back to reference 29

  30. Machining/Turning/Turning Tapers

    Addendum 30. Why the factor of two belongs in the angle formula

    Cut the cone through its axis. One side forms a right triangle whose rise is (D − d)/2 and whose run is l. Tangent is rise divided by run. Using the whole diameter change as the rise gives the wrong tool path.

    Back to reference 30

  31. Machining/Turning/Turning Tapers

    Addendum 31. Why this is an estimate rather than an exact setting

    The taper gives tan(α) = TPI/2. If L is the actual distance along the tilted work between support points, the ideal geometric offset is L sin(α). At shallow angles sin(α) and tan(α) are nearly equal. The usual formula substitutes L tan(α); real center contact and setup error add further differences. It is not a method for steep cones.

    Back to reference 31

  32. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Drilling on a Drill Press or Mill

    Addendum 32. Why “always center drill first” is too broad

    The starting recess determines which part of the next drill touches first. An unsuitable angle or an oversized pilot can load the drill's outer corners before its center is supported. Accurate starting also depends on tool rigidity, alignment and the surface being entered. A center-drilling step alone does not guarantee location.

    Back to reference 32

  33. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Drilling on a Drill Press or Mill

    Addendum 33. Why changes in the cut matter

    Changes in chip shape, sound, thrust or finish can indicate rubbing, chip packing, a damaged point or unsuitable cutting data. Continuing to force the tool does not diagnose the cause.

    Back to reference 33

  34. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Reaming, Boring and Hole Seats

    Addendum 34. A nominal tool size is not a finished-hole guarantee

    Tool condition, alignment, runout, temperature and workholding affect the result. A reamer stamped with the desired diameter still needs an appropriate prepared hole and cutting conditions. Inspect the actual bore rather than accepting it from the tool marking.

    Back to reference 34

  35. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Tap Drills and Tapping

    Addendum 35. Chart basis and the approximation's limits

    The three comparisons were checked against page 1, cutting-tap column, of North American Tool's Tap Drill Sizes — Inch & Metric with Drill Size Formulas, using the supplied four-page copy. Only these selected rows are used here; the chart is not reproduced. The estimate and a selected stock drill need not be identical. The chart's metric percentage formula gives about 77% when the entire pitch is subtracted, which is why “about 75%” must remain approximate.

    Back to reference 35

  36. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Tap Drills and Tapping

    Addendum 36. Keep percentage and fraction separate

    For a metric cutting-tap estimate, the supplied chart gives hole diameter = major diameter − (percentage × pitch / 76.98), entering 75 for 75%. Equivalently, multiplying a reference thread depth by 75% requires the fraction 0.75. Mixing those conventions introduces a factor-of-100 error. This formula estimates geometry, not allowable joint load.

    Back to reference 36

  37. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Tap Drills and Tapping

    Addendum 37. Why the local setup decides what is permitted

    Recognizing a production process does not authorize it on a particular machine. Spindle speed, tapping attachment and power-tapping procedure depend on the particular machine and setup.

    Back to reference 37

  38. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Thread Callouts and Threaded Fasteners

    Addendum 38. Check the entire joint before substituting a fastener

    Diameter, pitch, length and head clearance are only part of the selection. The nut or tapped material, coating, bearing surfaces, installation conditions and intended load also matter. A bolt that can be screwed into the hole has passed an assembly check, not a strength calculation.

    Back to reference 38

  39. Machining/Drilling and Threading/Twist Drills and Drill Sizes

    Addendum 39. Why a damaged or uneven point makes a poor hole

    Unequal lip lengths or unequal angles make the two lips remove different amounts of material. The drill can cut oversize or wander. A rounded edge can rub instead of producing a chip. Inspect the point and replace or correctly sharpen a damaged drill before trying to compensate with more force.

    Back to reference 39

  40. Machining/CNC/Absolute and Incremental Positioning

    Addendum 40. Check the conversion in both directions

    Subtract endpoints: (26−6,4−4) = (20,0); (26−26,19−4) = (0,15); (11−26,19−19) = (−15,0). Add those changes to A: (6+20+0−15,4+0+15+0) = (11,19). The net move is (5,15), not the final absolute position.

    Back to reference 40

  41. Machining/CNC/CNC Axes and Offsets

    Addendum 41. Why positive compensation can use a negative offset

    Positive compensation describes addition, not the sign of the stored number: adding a negative value shifts the compensated Z position in the negative direction. The Haas mill programming workbook's tool-length compensation section explains G43's addition of the selected offset to commanded positions.

    Back to reference 41

  42. Machining/CNC/CNC Control Fundamentals

    Addendum 42. Where the sensor sits matters

    A motor encoder measures the motor, while a linear scale can measure the slide directly. Screw error, backlash and elastic deflection between the sensor and the cutting point may remain. Homing establishes a reference; repeating homing is not a general cure for lost motion. See Oriental Motor's closed-loop stepper overview for an example of feedback used with steppers.

    Back to reference 42

  43. Machining/CNC/CNC Programming and Prove-Out

    Addendum 43. Other ways to create a program

    A short program can be written directly in a text editor. Conversational programming asks for feature dimensions at the control. Manual data input (MDI) lets the operator enter commands at the control, often for immediate execution. These routes still require correct modes, geometry and setup data; they do not bypass prove-out. Tormach's post-processor guidelines identify control-specific requirements.

    Back to reference 43

  44. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Profiles and Cycles

    Addendum 44. Why a good diameter measurement does not prove a taper is correct

    The two axis touch-offs locate tangent lines, not every possible contact point on the nose. The normal to an angled surface points in another direction, so its tangency requires another offset. Haas's tool nose compensation discussion describes the resulting undercut or overcut on tapered and curved profiles.

    Back to reference 44

  45. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Profiles and Cycles

    Addendum 45. Where to check the control behavior

    The Haas G41/G42 entry connects the compensation side to the selected tool offsets. The Haas SL-10 Programming Workbook (hosted by the University of Florida), printed pages 59–61, explains the imaginary tool tip, tip direction and approach/depart moves. Use the current manual for the installed control when programming.

    Back to reference 45

  46. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Profiles and Cycles

    Addendum 46. Why no universal cycle template is shown

    The Haas G71 reference distinguishes path types and radial cut depth from diametral finish allowance. The Hurco ISNC G71 reference supplies its own two-block definition. A familiar cycle number does not establish compatible parameter meanings.

    Back to reference 46

  47. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Program Walkthrough

    Addendum 47. Check roughing depth and remaining material

    The first pass changes diameter from 24 to 22 mm, a 1 mm radial cut. The second changes 22 to 20.6 mm, a 0.7 mm radial cut. Finishing from 20.6 to 20 removes 0.3 mm radially. Extending the OD cuts beyond Z−25 leaves room for the cutoff blade and places the finishing departure on material that will not belong to the finished part.

    Back to reference 47

  48. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Setup and Offsets

    Addendum 48. Why an extra axis changes the work a turning center can do

    Ordinary turning produces surfaces around the spindle axis. A powered tool plus controlled work angle can reach features at selected angular positions. See the Haas options programming reference for one manufacturer's C-axis implementation.

    Back to reference 48

  49. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Setup and Offsets

    Addendum 49. Control example: separate geometry and wear fields

    The Haas lathe manual, Operation, describes separate X/Z geometry wear, radius and tip-direction fields. Its button sequences and offset conventions must not be assumed on another control.

    Back to reference 49

  50. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Spindle and Feed Modes

    Addendum 50. Calculate where a speed ceiling starts to matter

    With 90 m/min and a ceiling of 1800 RPM, the crossover diameter is 90 × 1000 / (π × 1800) = 15.92 mm. At 10 mm, unrestricted CSS would request 2865 RPM, so the simplified steady-state result is 1800 RPM. Acceleration and other machine limits can reduce actual speed further. See Haas's spindle-speed commands workbook for its G50/G96/G97 implementation.

    Back to reference 50

  51. Machining/CNC/CNC Turning Spindle and Feed Modes

    Addendum 51. Reference for the code convention used here

    The G96–G99 entries in the Haas lathe manual describe S in CSS versus RPM and F per minute versus per revolution. Consult the manual for your own control before transferring these meanings.

    Back to reference 51

  52. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Bench Work with Hand Tools

    Addendum 52. File selection and care resources

    The Crescent Nicholson file selection guide covers filing methods and selection. Its file card documentation describes cleaning the teeth.

    Back to reference 52

  53. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Cutoff Sawing

    Addendum 53. Why finer teeth do not fix every bad cut

    More teeth share the load, but smaller gullets have less room for chips. Too much feed can overload the teeth; too little can make them rub. A wandering cut also calls for checking the blade condition, tension, guides, and workholding against the manuals. Changing speed alone cannot correct loose work or a worn guide.

    Back to reference 53

  54. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Grinding Wheels and Abrasives

    Addendum 54. Manufacturer resources for abrasive selection

    Norton: choosing a grinding wheel discusses conventional abrasives. 3M: CBN and diamond superabrasives covers the superabrasive families. Use product-specific data for a real selection.

    Back to reference 54

  55. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Grinding Wheels and Abrasives

    Addendum 55. A manufacturer's explanation of the marking

    Norton: Grinding Wheel Basics explains the five fields and manufacturer-specific variations. A wheel specification and its separately marked maximum operating speed answer different questions.

    Back to reference 55

  56. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Offhand Grinding

    Addendum 56. Where to check the clearance requirements

    OSHA's abrasive-wheel machinery requirements address work rests and adjustable guards. Consult the applicable text and the machine manual for the dimensions and scope.

    Back to reference 56

  57. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Offhand Grinding

    Addendum 57. Why a wheel can glaze, and where ring testing applies

    Glazing depends on the wheel grade and operating conditions as well as the work material. Hard material alone does not diagnose it. Norton's ring-test guidance explains the method's application and limitations; follow the full manufacturer procedure before mounting.

    Back to reference 57

  58. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Offhand Grinding

    Addendum 58. Carbide needs consistent temperature control

    General Carbide: The Designer's Guide to Tungsten Carbide, page 50, explains thermal shock and the effects of interrupted coolant during grinding. Follow the tool manufacturer's cooling guidance for HSS as well; permission to cool a warm bit is not permission to quench an overheated one.

    Back to reference 58

  59. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Precision Grinding

    Addendum 59. Magnetic holding and release are equipment-specific

    Industrial Magnetics: grinding chucks shows different chuck arrangements. Industrial Magnetics: electromagnet chuck controllers describes an automatic release cycle that replaces manual demagnetizing. Use the manual for the installed chuck and control, not a generic switch sequence.

    Back to reference 59

  60. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Precision Grinding

    Addendum 60. Why a real grinding plan needs more than the quotient

    The calculation assumes a flat starting face and no wheel wear or elastic error. A real plan may reserve material for lighter finish cuts, include dressing and spark-out, and stop to measure. Stock removal from two faces must be assigned to each face; do not silently count it twice.

    Back to reference 60

  61. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Saw Blade Selection

    Addendum 61. Why the answer can be a fraction of a tooth

    The product counts tooth spacings across the contact length. Actual engaged tooth tips are discrete, and the number changes as the blade moves. Entry, exit, variable pitch, and curved sections also change contact. This estimate explains the selection principle; it does not guarantee a fixed count throughout a real cut.

    Back to reference 61

  62. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Saw Blade Selection

    Addendum 62. Manufacturer resources for the next selection step

    Consult the chart supplied with the blade. Public starting points include Starrett's carbon blade range and DoALL's blade FAQ. Product-specific recommendations govern; the estimates here are teaching calculations.

    Back to reference 62

  63. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Vertical Band Machining

    Addendum 63. Why relief cuts help with some outlines

    A relief cut runs in from a scrap edge toward the outline, allowing waste to separate in smaller pieces. Plan relief cuts on the waste side and preserve the finishing allowance. They can provide room to approach a contour from another direction; they do not make the blade itself capable of a smaller turning radius.

    Back to reference 63

  64. Machining/Sawing and Grinding/Vertical Band Machining

    Addendum 64. Why joining includes more than making a weld

    Alignment keeps the band running straight. The prescribed annealing or tempering cycle restores suitable flexibility at the joint, and finishing removes raised weld material. A sound-looking joint alone is not proof that the loop is ready to run. DoALL's blade welder range is a starting point for equipment-specific documentation.

    Back to reference 64

  65. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Coolant Concentration and Mixing

    Addendum 65. Measurement references

    Cimcool's refractometer FAQ covers zeroing, the boundary and factor conversion. Master Fluids' concentration guide discusses product factors and contamination. A refractometer is a concentration estimate, not a bacteria test or proof that the fluid is fit for reuse.

    Back to reference 65

  66. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Coolant Concentration and Mixing

    Addendum 66. Why mixing order matters

    The aim is small oil droplets dispersed throughout the water, rather than water trapped inside an oil-rich mixture. Cimcool's mixing explanation describes the emulsifier's role. Mixing order is separate from the arithmetic: the right measured amounts still need the right preparation method.

    Back to reference 66

  67. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Coolant Concentration and Mixing

    Addendum 67. Derive the balance, or solve for an unknown addition volume

    Concentrate already in the tank plus concentrate added equals concentrate in the final tank: VC/100 + AP/100 = FT/100. Multiply through by 100 and solve for P. This tracks concentrate, not the Brix number.

    If a premix concentration P is already chosen, solve for its addition volume: A = V(T − C) ÷ (P − T). Check that A is positive and that V + A fits within the allowed fill level. If P = T and C differs from T, no finite addition reaches T exactly. If C = T already, adding premix at T preserves it.

    Back to reference 67

  68. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance

    Addendum 68. Why inspection and measurement belong together

    Concentration alone does not describe contamination or biological condition. HSE's metalworking-fluid guidance calls for maintaining fluid quality and checking bacterial contamination. A supplier-directed fluid-management program may include pH and microbial checks as well as concentration; use its methods and action limits. Master Fluid Solutions' FAQ explains odor, residue and concentration-related skin irritation.

    Back to reference 68

  69. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance

    Addendum 69. Supplier instructions determine the cleaning treatment

    HSE's sump-cleaning guidance emphasizes supplier-selected cleaner and circulation times. An extensively contaminated system may need treatment before draining and additional cleaning cycles; the general checklist is not a microbial decontamination recipe.

    Back to reference 69

  70. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Coolant Condition and Tank Maintenance

    Addendum 70. Why the waste route depends on what is in the tank

    Washington State Department of Ecology's metalworking-fluid guide, pages 12–13, illustrates how formulation and contamination change waste management. Its state-specific rules are not a disposal authorization elsewhere. EPA's used-oil guidance also distinguishes qualifying used oil from other wastes and notes that state requirements can be stricter. The product SDS is a starting point; used coolant also contains material picked up during machining.

    Back to reference 70

  71. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Cutting Fluids and Application Methods

    Addendum 71. Why the family name does not settle performance

    Base fluid, additives, dilution and water quality all affect the result. A neat oil can use mineral, vegetable or other base oils; “straight” describes using it undiluted. A synthetic is not automatically harmless or maintenance-free. See the fluid-family comparison on page 7 of Washington State Department of Ecology's metalworking-fluid guide and HSE's exposure overview.

    Back to reference 71

  72. Machining/Cutting Fluids/Cutting Fluids and Application Methods

    Addendum 72. Why some milling runs dry while other milling needs fluid

    A milling tooth repeatedly enters and leaves the material. Coolant can increase its temperature swing and promote thermal cracking in susceptible edges. Other operations need lubrication to limit adhesion, cooling to control distortion, or flow to clear chips. Sandvik Coromant's dry and wet milling guidance explains these competing demands.

    Back to reference 72

  73. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Choosing Shop Measuring Tools

    Addendum 73. What a sweep can and cannot establish

    A sweep combines the part's shape with its orientation and support. Runout is not a direct measurement of formal concentricity. A height sweep relative to a plate can reveal variation, but calling it a flatness inspection requires the proper setup and evaluation. Follow the drawing's specified inspection method.

    Back to reference 73

  74. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Choosing Shop Measuring Tools

    Addendum 74. Instrument references

    Consult the actual tool's instructions and specifications. The Mitutoyo Quick Guide covers micrometers, calipers, height gages, gauge blocks, and indicators. The Starrett catalog separates graduations from accuracy and illustrates several instrument arrangements. The Mitutoyo ABSOLUTE caliper specifications provide examples of 0.0005 in / 0.01 mm display increments.

    Back to reference 74

  75. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Reading Measuring Scales

    Addendum 75. Other 0.001 in verniers can have different spacing

    A 50-division vernier can span 49 main-scale spaces of 0.050 in. Each vernier space is 0.049 in, again leaving a 0.001 in difference. Read the actual main scale; do not apply the trainer's 0.025 in spacing to that tool. The Starrett catalog, page 102, illustrates the 50-division arrangement.

    Back to reference 75

  76. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Reading Measuring Scales

    Addendum 76. Reading references

    The Starrett catalog, page 22, explains inch and vernier micrometer scales. The Mitutoyo Quick Guide, page 9, explains the metric micrometer. The examples and diagrams here are original teaching examples.

    Back to reference 76

  77. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Reliable Shop Measurement

    Addendum 77. The offset-and-angle relationship

    For a small angle, the error is approximately the offset multiplied by the tilt in radians. An offset of 2 in and a tilt of 0.0005 rad give about 0.001 in of error. This is distinct from simply looking at the scale from an angle. See the Abbe discussion in the Mitutoyo Quick Guide, page 11.

    Back to reference 77

  78. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Shop Layout and Angle Measurement

    Addendum 78. Finding the middle of two heights

    If the lower edge of a slot is 0.600 in above the reference and the upper edge is 0.900 in above it, the center is (0.600 + 0.900) / 2 = 0.750 in above that reference. Half the difference, 0.150 in, is half the slot height; it still must be added to the lower height.

    Back to reference 78

  79. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Shop Layout and Angle Measurement

    Addendum 79. Punch types and their uses

    Starrett's punch guide explains the sharper prick punch, the wider center punch, and why the locating mark is checked before it is enlarged.

    Back to reference 79

  80. Machining/Measurement and Fit/Shop Layout and Angle Measurement

    Addendum 80. Why the 5-minute vernier works

    On the arrangement described in the Starrett catalog, page 306, 12 vernier spaces span 23 main-scale degrees. Each vernier space is 23/12 degrees, or 1°55′: 5 minutes short of two degrees. The line alignment reveals that difference. Page 308 distinguishes a plain universal bevel from the graduated protractor used with it.

    Back to reference 80

  81. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Automated Manufacturing Cells

    Addendum 81. Cell, system and integration describe different scopes

    A flexible manufacturing system may coordinate multiple machines or cells with material handling and scheduling. Computer-integrated manufacturing is the broader idea of connecting manufacturing information and activities. These terms overlap in use, but are not interchangeable names for one machine configuration.

    Back to reference 81

  82. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Broaching

    Addendum 82. Why the finishing teeth need not keep getting taller

    Once the intended profile is reached, further rise would make the feature larger. Repeated finishing teeth can maintain the final size as earlier teeth wear. See Nidec's precision cutting tools reference for broach terminology.

    Back to reference 82

  83. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Broaching

    Addendum 83. Production advantages depend on the job

    Tool cost, material, cut length, machine capacity and required finish determine the economics. Broaching is not automatically the cheapest process. Pilot Precision's broach overview includes both short-run sets and one-pass production tools. Cutting Fluids and Application Methods explains lubrication choices.

    Back to reference 83

  84. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Broaching

    Addendum 84. Manufacturer reference for the pass sequence

    Pilot Precision, Engineering Section: How to Use Broaches, printed page 35 describes guided keyway broaching and the successive shim stack. The tool's own instructions govern the actual setup.

    Back to reference 84

  85. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Broaching

    Addendum 85. How the rotary holder produces the cutting motion

    Slater Tools' rotary broaching explanation describes the holder's angled spindle and the different tool/work motions on a lathe and mill. Its application guide covers preparation and operating requirements.

    Back to reference 85

  86. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Chemical Milling and Etching

    Addendum 86. Why thin-sheet patterns are a useful application

    A mask can define many features at once without a separate shaped cutting tool for each opening. Fotofab describes partial and through etching.

    Back to reference 86

  87. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Electrical Discharge Machining

    Addendum 87. Why the fluid and the gap matter

    The dielectric fluid normally insulates the gap. A voltage pulse breaks down that insulation locally and permits a discharge. Between pulses, the fluid helps cool the region and flush debris. Debris removal and gap control help keep discharges stable. Sinker EDM commonly uses dielectric oil; wire EDM commonly uses controlled deionized water, though oil-based wire machines also exist.

    Back to reference 87

  88. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Electrical Discharge Machining

    Addendum 88. Why one offset does not describe every pass

    Discharge energy, flushing and finishing passes change the working gap and surface. Actual compensation comes from the machine's process data and inspection. CHMER's EDM FAQ defines the offset as the wire radius plus the discharge gap, and notes that the gap changes with discharge energy.

    Back to reference 88

  89. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Electrical Discharge Machining

    Addendum 89. Further reading on EDM surfaces and wire systems

    Makino discusses thermal surface effects; Sodick explains wire EDM. Low mechanical force is not a guarantee of zero distortion or an unchanged surface.

    Back to reference 89

  90. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Electrochemical Machining

    Addendum 90. Why hardness alone does not set ECM performance

    The reaction removes metal without requiring a harder cutting edge. Metal chemistry and current conditions still affect dissolution, so “all metals machine at the same rate” is not a valid selection rule. Tooling and electrolyte control can make ECM attractive for repeated parts, while adding development effort for a one-off feature.

    Further reading: EMAG's ECM overview and the Electrochemical Society's machining explanation.

    Back to reference 90

  91. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Laser, Waterjet and Plasma Cutting

    Addendum 91. Why the material and laser must be matched

    Different materials absorb different wavelengths differently. Power and beam delivery also limit the usable thickness and quality. See TRUMPF's laser-cutting overview.

    Back to reference 91

  92. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Laser, Waterjet and Plasma Cutting

    Addendum 92. Further reading on glass and waterjet limits

    OMAX explains waterjet materials and cold cutting; its glass-cutting notes distinguish glass types and edge damage.

    Back to reference 92

  93. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Laser, Waterjet and Plasma Cutting

    Addendum 93. Compare capability on the actual thickness

    Hypertherm describes the energy sources and selection by material, thickness and cut quality. Qualitative comparisons narrow candidates; they do not replace a supplier's capability check.

    Back to reference 93

  94. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Process Capability and Variation

    Addendum 94. Why a small sample range is not the full process spread

    The range uses only the two extremes observed in this sample. More readings, different tools, temperature changes and later production may reveal variation not present in these five parts. Standard deviation is another measure of spread that uses every reading's distance from the mean; no standard-deviation calculation is needed for this example.

    Back to reference 94

  95. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Process Capability and Variation

    Addendum 95. Where capability indices fit

    Indices such as Cp and Cpk compare estimated process variation and its position with specification limits. Their interpretation depends on the data, stability, distribution and application requirements. A single threshold is not a universal acceptance rule, and a five-reading classroom example is not a capability study.

    Back to reference 95

  96. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Shop Inspection and Quality Control

    Addendum 96. Why the gauge itself needs limits and wear checks

    Gauges cannot be manufactured to an infinitely exact size. Their own tolerances and wear allowances are selected under the applicable gauging specification. Repeated use can shrink a plug or enlarge a ring and change its decision.

    Back to reference 96

  97. Machining/Production and Nontraditional Processes/Ultrasonic Machining

    Addendum 97. Why a shaped tool does not give an exact-size copy

    Abrasive particles occupy space around the tool and also wear it. The finished cavity therefore depends on the tool, abrasive action and process control, not simply on copying the tool's nominal dimensions. Bullen describes loose-abrasive ultrasonic machining.

    Back to reference 97
